docs.title: AI-Native Schools
docs.text:
Title: AI-Native Schools: Mornings with AI, Afternoons with Each Other

Target Audience: K-12 teachers, school principals and administrators, school board members, education policymakers, curriculum and instructional designers, education students, and parents who want to understand how AI will reshape the school day

Prerequisites: None. Readers should be comfortable using a web browser. Experience with an AI chat assistant is helpful but not required. No programming or statistics background is assumed; the few charts and growth curves in the book are explained from first principles.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
This book makes a prediction and then works out what follows from it. The prediction is that within three to four years almost every student will have access to a free, high-quality, interactive textbook that adapts to their needs. If that happens, schools will no longer need to spend most of the day on direct instruction, and they will have to decide what to do with the time that frees up. The book's answer is in its subtitle: mornings with AI, afternoons with each other.

The book is honest that this change can go well or badly. Real AI-first schools and products have produced both strong results and expensive failures. The book's goal is to strengthen the positives and reduce the negatives, and it uses stories to do this. Each part draws on real cases, collected in the AI-First Stories appendix, and on composite stories of students, teachers, and families. Every story about a risk is paired with what a school can do about it.

The book has five parts.

docs.title: Part 1: The Evidence for the Prediction
docs.text:
METR's task-horizon studies measure the length of task, in human working time, that an AI system can complete correctly. That horizon has been doubling about every five months. Readers learn how the measurement works, how to read a doubling curve on a logarithmic scale, and what steady exponential growth means over a three-to-four-year planning window. They also learn what could slow the trend, and why schools should plan for it anyway.

This growth is driving the intelligent textbook movement, which began in earnest in 2025. At the core of the book is the five-level model of intelligent textbooks, from McCreary's paper A Five-Level Classification Framework for Intelligent Textbooks: Lessons from Autonomous Vehicle Standards (EdArXiv preprint, December 2025). The model is based on the SAE J3016 levels for self-driving cars, which gave that industry a shared vocabulary, graduated regulation, and realistic expectations while the technology changed quickly. The five levels are:

  1. Static textbooks: fixed content with no interactivity, like traditional print and PDF textbooks
  2. Interactive textbooks: MicroSims, learning graphs, embedded simulations, and recommended learning paths
  3. Adaptive textbooks: content driven by each student's goals and progress, which requires storing student records
  4. Chatbot textbooks: conversational tutoring through chatbots and large language models
  5. Autonomous AI textbooks: real-time content generation and fully personalized instruction

Readers learn to place any textbook or AI product at its level and to use the levels as a shared vocabulary for buying decisions and policy. The levels also explain the economics. As AI improves, level 2 interactive content becomes cheap to produce, heading toward pennies per student per day, and is often free. Level 2 textbooks are being published in growing numbers, and level 3, 4, and 5 textbooks are on the horizon. Readers learn how the OpenBook QR Score measures the quality and reusability of open textbooks, and why those scores are rising quickly.

Level 3 marks a privacy inflection point. Below it, a textbook needs almost no student data. At level 3 and above, it needs detailed learning histories, which brings in FERPA, COPPA, and GDPR and calls for stronger governance and checks for algorithmic bias. The inBloom shutdown and the PowerSchool data breach show what happens when this is done badly. Readers learn how xAPI and Learning Record Stores (LRS) make personalization possible while students and families keep control of their own data.

docs.title: Part 2: The Shorter Academic Morning
docs.text:
If students can reach today's learning results in two to three hours a day with interactive intelligent textbooks, the traditional eight hours of sitting through direct instruction is no longer needed. In the morning, students follow their own curiosity through adaptive textbooks that pace the material, check mastery, and fill gaps.

The evidence for this is promising but mixed, and the book presents both sides. A carefully designed AI tutor helped Harvard physics students learn more in less time, and a low-cost AI tutoring pilot in Nigeria produced large gains. But a study in Turkish high schools found that students with open access to an AI chatbot did worse on later exams than students who never used it, while a version that gave hints instead of answers removed most of the harm. The lesson is that how the AI is designed matters more than how powerful it is.

Alpha School is the best-known working example of the morning-and-afternoon model. Its students spend about two hours a day on adaptive academic software and the rest of the day on life-skills workshops and projects led by adult guides. Tuition ranges from about $40,000 a year at the original Austin campus to about $65,000 a year at newer campuses in Boston, Miami, and New York, far beyond what public schools spend per student. Unbound Academy, a free online charter school in Arizona that uses the same software without in-person afternoons, reportedly scored below state averages in its early results. Together, the two stories show that the software alone is not the model.

The book's answer to the cost problem is a low-cost, energy-efficient, adaptive design built from:

  • Intelligent textbooks at level 2 and level 3, written once with AI and then served to every student as ordinary web pages at almost no cost
  • MicroSims, small interactive simulations that run in the browser with no server or AI model behind them
  • Learning graphs, which map each concept and its prerequisites so the textbook can choose a student's next step
  • xAPI and a Learning Record Store, which record what each student has done and mastered, so the textbook can adapt without a live AI model

AI does its expensive work once, when the content is written, instead of every time a student asks a question. Most students never send a request to a large language model, which keeps cost and energy use low and avoids the risk of students handing their thinking over to a chatbot. Chatbot tutoring (level 4) is used only where it adds real value, with guardrails that give hints instead of answers.

docs.title: Part 3: The Pro-Social Afternoon
docs.text:
The central question of the book is: what will fill the rest of the day? The answer is pro-social, hands-on activity: music, dance, theater, the visual arts, sports, coding and robotics clubs, maker spaces, and project-based learning. These activities draw on social constructionism, the idea that students learn the most when they build things and solve problems together. The afternoon focuses on creativity, collaboration, communication, and empathy.

AI can teach critical thinking and computational thinking well. Students still need to practice using those skills with other people, on teams, toward shared goals, and that is what the afternoon is for. The afternoon does not have to be invented from scratch. High Tech High's project-based learning, Finland's phenomenon-based learning, and El Sistema's youth orchestras already show it working. The book also warns about the opposite failure: afternoons that drift into unstructured free time.

docs.title: Part 4: Changing the Culture of a School
docs.text:
A new schedule on paper changes nothing if teachers, students, families, and school boards keep working the way they always have. Schools are known for absorbing reforms without changing much; Tyack and Cuban call the stable structure underneath this the "grammar of schooling." AltSchool, Summit Learning, and the Los Angeles iPad rollout all show technology-first reforms failing to change school culture. The book looks at change on two scales.

  • The whole organization. Readers learn technology adoption models: Rogers' diffusion of innovations and its adopter categories (innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, and laggards), Moore's chasm between early adopters and the early majority, and the hype cycle. They then study organizational change models: Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze, Kotter's eight steps for leading change, the ADKAR model, Bridges' transition model, Schein's levels of organizational culture, Senge's learning organization and systems thinking, and Fullan's research on educational change. The Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM) is covered in depth because it was built to track how teachers adopt new practices. Estonia's national AI Leap program shows a whole system adopting AI on purpose.
  • Microstrategies. These are small, concrete moves that leaders and teachers can make next week: recruiting teacher champions, running a single pilot classroom, getting visible early results, finding and copying "bright spots," shrinking the first step, peer observation, and professional learning communities. Readers also learn how to answer specific concerns, respond to resistance with empathy, and talk with families before rumors spread.

Readers learn to fit the strategy to where each group sits on the adoption curve and to each teacher's stage of concern, so that small moves add up to lasting change. The changing role of the teacher, from lecturer to coach and mentor, runs through this part. Tutor CoPilot, where AI coached human tutors instead of replacing them, shows how AI can make teachers better rather than make them unnecessary.

docs.title: Part 5: Putting the Model into Practice
docs.text: The final part is practical. Readers learn how to redesign a school schedule and staffing model, buy AI products safely, plan and run a pilot, protect student privacy, keep access equitable, assess learning, and measure whether the new model is working. The Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot, where a district spent millions on a startup that collapsed within months, shows why schools need procurement rules before they buy. AI cheating detectors, which wrongly flagged non-native English writers, show why assessment should be redesigned instead of policed.

  • The intelligent textbook movement since 2025
  • The five-level model of intelligent textbooks (the core framework of the book)
  • The SAE J3016 autonomous-vehicle levels as a model for classifying textbooks
  • Level 1, static textbooks: fixed content, no interactivity
  • Level 2, interactive textbooks: MicroSims, learning graphs, simulations, and path recommendations
  • Level 3, adaptive textbooks: goals, progress tracking, and student records
  • Level 4, chatbot textbooks: conversational tutoring with large language models
  • Level 5, autonomous AI textbooks: real-time content generation and full personalization
  • Precision in level terminology: avoiding vague "AI-powered" marketing claims
  • The economics of content creation: falling production costs and the penny-per-day vision
  • The commoditization of level 1 and level 2 content and what it means for publishers and schools

  • The level 3 privacy inflection point: why student records change everything
  • FERPA, COPPA, and GDPR obligations at level 3 and above
  • Algorithmic bias auditing and governance for adaptive systems
  • The trust paradox: personalization requires data, and data requires trust
  • xAPI and Learning Record Stores for student-controlled, portable learning data

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
These learning outcomes are organized using the 2001 revision of Bloom's Taxonomy: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create.

After this course, readers will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
• Define task horizon, doubling time, direct instruction, intelligent textbook, adaptive learning, cognitive offloading, and social constructionism
  • State the approximate doubling time reported by the METR task-horizon studies
  • List the five levels of intelligent textbooks and the defining feature of each
  • Recall the SAE J3016 standard that the five-level model is based on
  • Identify level 3 as the privacy inflection point
  • Recall the parts of the OpenBook QR Score and what Q and R stand for
  • Recall the Alpha School tuition range and how its school day is divided
  • Name the main categories of pro-social afternoon activities
  • Name the five adopter categories on the technology adoption curve
  • List the steps of Kotter's change model and the five elements of ADKAR
  • Recall the stages of concern in the Concerns-Based Adoption Model
  • Name the key case studies in the AI-First Stories appendix and the main lesson of each
  • List the main benefits and risks of moving to an AI-first school

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
• Explain how METR measures the length of task an AI system can complete
  • Explain why a five-month doubling time produces large changes over three to four years
  • Explain why the autonomous-vehicle levels are a useful model for classifying textbooks
  • Describe how a textbook adapts to a student's needs at each of the five levels
  • Explain why level 3 and higher textbooks need student records and stronger privacy protection
  • Explain how falling AI costs commoditize level 1 and level 2 content
  • Explain how intelligent textbooks, MicroSims, learning graphs, xAPI, and an LRS can adapt to students without live AI calls
  • Explain why writing content once costs far less, and uses far less energy, than calling a large language model for every student
  • Summarize the case that two to three hours of adaptive learning can match today's results, including the evidence against it
  • Explain why AI that gives hints helps learning while AI that gives answers can hurt it
  • Explain social constructionism and why students learn well when solving problems together
  • Describe how the teacher's role changes in an AI-native school
  • Explain why schools often absorb reforms without changing their underlying culture
  • Explain the chasm between early adopters and the early majority
  • Describe the difference between whole-organization change models and microstrategies, and why a school needs both

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
• Project an AI capability trend forward using a doubling time
  • Classify an existing textbook or AI learning product by its level in the five-level model
  • Use the OpenBook QR Score to compare two open textbooks
  • Write procurement criteria that state the required textbook level and its privacy requirements
  • Estimate the cost per student of an AI-first school built on open level 2 and level 3 textbooks
  • Draft a daily schedule that pairs a morning adaptive-learning block with afternoon pro-social activities
  • Match afternoon activities to the collaboration, creativity, and empathy skills they build
  • Place staff, student, and family groups on the technology adoption curve
  • Choose a microstrategy suited to a teacher's stage of concern
  • Apply Kotter's eight steps or ADKAR to a planned change at a specific school
  • Match each risk of the AI-first model to a specific way to reduce it
  • Use the lessons of a past failure, such as the Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot or Summit Learning, to write a risk checklist for a pilot

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
• Distinguish the skills AI can teach well (critical and computational thinking) from the skills that need practice with other people (teamwork, communication, empathy)
  • Compare the traditional school day with the AI-native school day in terms of time, cost, staffing, and outcomes
  • Compare Alpha School with Unbound Academy to separate the effect of the software from the effect of in-person guides and afternoons
  • Compare the cost structure of Alpha School with a low-cost model built on open textbooks
  • Identify the assumptions behind the book's prediction and what would happen if each one failed
  • Examine how the AI-native model could widen or narrow equity gaps
  • Analyze a school's culture using Schein's three levels
  • Diagnose why a past technology rollout stalled, using a case such as AltSchool or the Los Angeles iPad program
  • Separate legitimate concerns from general resistance to change
  • Analyze a story about AI in schools to find which benefits and which risks it shows

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
• Judge the strength of the evidence behind AI capability forecasts
  • Evaluate claims of results from AI-first schools, separating independent test results from self-reported growth
  • Critique an AI tutor or intelligent textbook for quality, guardrails, privacy, and fit with student needs
  • Evaluate a vendor's claimed textbook level against the five-level definitions
  • Assess whether a school's data governance is ready for level 3 and higher textbooks
  • Assess whether a school is ready to pilot a shorter academic morning
  • Evaluate afternoon programs on whether they build real collaboration and empathy skills
  • Judge which change model fits a given school's size, culture, and history
  • Evaluate whether a pilot has crossed the chasm and is ready to scale
  • Judge whether a proposed AI-first program builds on its strengths and deals with its risks
  • Justify a recommendation to a school board for or against adopting the model

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
• Design an AI-native school day for a specific grade level and community
  • Design a low-cost technology plan that uses learning graphs, MicroSims, and an LRS instead of live AI for most students
  • Create an afternoon program built around team projects that apply critical and computational thinking
  • Develop a pilot plan with goals, a timeline, staffing, family communication, and success measures
  • Construct an assessment plan that combines morning mastery data with afternoon portfolios and performances
  • Construct a culture-change plan that combines a whole-organization change model with specific microstrategies
  • Write a story about a student, teacher, or family in an AI-native school that shows a benefit, a risk, and how the school responds

docs.title: Sample Capstone Projects
docs.text:
1. AI-Native School Day Design

    • Description: Design a full weekly schedule for a real or imagined school that uses a morning adaptive-learning block and afternoon pro-social activities
    • Skills Demonstrated: Scheduling, staffing, matching activities to skills
    • Deliverables: A weekly schedule, a staffing plan, and a one-page rationale

  2. Pilot Program Proposal

    • Description: Write a proposal to a school board for a one-semester pilot of the AI-native model
    • Skills Demonstrated: Using evidence, assessing risk, planning for privacy and equity
    • Deliverables: A written proposal with goals, timeline, budget impact, success measures, and a risk checklist drawn from the AI-First Stories

  3. Forecast Briefing

    • Description: Prepare a short briefing that explains the METR task-horizon trend and what it means for schools over the next four years
    • Skills Demonstrated: Reading exponential trends, communicating uncertainty
    • Deliverables: A slide deck or one-page briefing with a projection chart

  4. Afternoon Club Design

    • Description: Design a club or team project that requires students to apply critical and computational thinking together
    • Skills Demonstrated: Project-based learning design, collaboration, empathy goals
    • Deliverables: A club charter, a sample project, and a rubric for teamwork

  5. Five-Level Product Audit

    • Description: Audit three AI learning products or textbooks a school is considering, assign each a level in the five-level model, and check their privacy practices and guardrails against that level
    • Skills Demonstrated: Classification, vendor evaluation, privacy governance
    • Deliverables: A comparison table and a recommendation memo

  6. School Culture Change Plan

    • Description: Write a two-year plan for moving a real or imagined school to the AI-native model
    • Skills Demonstrated: Assessing culture, mapping the adoption curve, combining a change model with microstrategies, engaging stakeholders
    • Deliverables: A culture assessment, an adoption-curve map of stakeholders, a staged change plan, and a family communication plan

  7. Affordable Alpha

    • Description: Redesign the Alpha School model so a public school could afford it, using open intelligent textbooks, MicroSims, learning graphs, xAPI, and an LRS, while keeping the in-person afternoon that Unbound Academy lacked
    • Skills Demonstrated: Cost modeling, technology design, comparing energy use
    • Deliverables: A cost-per-student comparison, a technology diagram, and a list of trade-offs

  8. Two-Sided Story

    • Description: Write a short story about one day in an AI-native school that shows one benefit growing stronger and one risk being reduced
    • Skills Demonstrated: Storytelling, risk analysis, empathy
    • Deliverables: A 1,500-word story with a one-page commentary linking it to the book's risk-and-response framework

docs.title: Interactive Elements
docs.text:
• Estimated Number of MicroSims: 15-25
  • Types of Simulations: Exponential-growth projection charts, log-scale explorers, intelligent textbook level classifiers, school-day schedule builders, cost-per-student calculators, technology adoption curve explorers, change-model step-throughs, stakeholder adoption maps, timelines of the intelligent textbook movement, causal-loop diagrams, benefit-and-risk balance charts, and comparison infographics
  • Primary Libraries: p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network.js, vis-timeline
  • Stories: Illustrated stories and short graphic-novel scenes in most chapters, each showing a benefit, a risk, and how the school responds

docs.title: AI-First Stories
docs.text:
This book uses stories to show that moving to an AI-first school has real benefits and real risks. Our goal is to strengthen the positives and reduce the negatives. This appendix collects the real cases the chapters draw on. Each story is labeled as positive, cautionary, or both-sided, and each ends with the lesson it teaches.

Check the facts before citing

Many of these stories are still unfolding, and the figures come from news coverage, preprints, and the schools' own claims. Before a chapter quotes a number, check it against the original source and note the date.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Story Type Year Main lesson Alpha School Both-sided 2014– The morning-and-afternoon model can work, but it is expensive Nigeria AI tutoring pilot Positive 2024 Low-cost AI tutoring can help where resources are scarce Harvard physics AI tutor Positive 2024 A well-designed AI tutor can teach more in less time Tutor CoPilot Positive 2024 AI that coaches people works better than AI that replaces them David Game College Both-sided 2024 An AI-taught class still needs human learning coaches Estonia's AI Leap Positive 2025 A whole country can adopt AI on purpose Unbound Academy Cautionary 2025– The model does not carry over automatically when it goes online The LA Unified chatbot "Ed" Cautionary 2024 Rushed purchasing and reliance on one vendor put students at risk AltSchool Cautionary 2013–2019 Technology without a lasting school culture does not last Summit Learning Cautionary 2018–2019 Too much screen time drives students and families away inBloom Cautionary 2014 Student data projects fail without the trust of families PowerSchool data breach Cautionary 2024 Centralized student records are a large target LA Unified iPad rollout Cautionary 2013 Buying devices before planning the teaching wastes money The Turkish high-school study Both-sided 2024 Open AI access can hurt learning; guardrails fix most of the harm "Your Brain on ChatGPT" Both-sided 2025 Writing with AI can lower engagement and memory Khanmigo Both-sided 2023– Careful design still meets the reality of classroom use AI cheating detectors Cautionary 2023 Fighting AI can create its own equity problems The non-AI afternoon Positive ongoing Project-based and arts-based afternoons are already proven

docs.title: Nigeria AI Tutoring Pilot
docs.text:
Positive · 2024 · World Bank

In a six-week after-school program in Edo State, Nigeria, students used a GPT-4-based tutor to practice English while teachers were in the room. The World Bank team reported large learning gains for a very small cost per student.

Lesson: Low-cost AI tutoring, with a teacher present, can help students in places with few resources. This supports the book's claim that AI-first learning does not have to be a luxury.

docs.title: Harvard Physics AI Tutor
docs.text:
Positive · 2024–2025 · Kestin et al.

In a randomized study in an introductory Harvard physics course, students who used a carefully designed AI tutor learned more, in less time, than students in an active-learning class led by an instructor. The tutor was built on proven teaching practices instead of being an open chatbot.

Lesson: A well-designed AI tutor can make the shorter academic morning work. Design matters more than raw AI power.

docs.title: Tutor CoPilot
docs.text:
Positive · 2024 · Stanford University

Tutor CoPilot gave human tutors live AI suggestions during their sessions instead of replacing them. Students' mastery improved, the weakest tutors improved the most, and the cost per tutor for a year was small.

Lesson: AI works well when it makes people better at helping students. This supports the book's picture of the teacher as a coach.

docs.title: Estonia's AI Leap
docs.text:
Positive · 2025 · Estonia (TI-Hüpe)

Estonia launched a national program giving secondary students and teachers access to AI learning tools, along with teacher training. It builds on the country's earlier success bringing computers into schools.

Lesson: A school system can adopt AI on purpose, with a plan, training, and public support. This is a useful example for the change-management chapters.

docs.title: Unbound Academy
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2025– · Arizona

Unbound Academy is a free, online charter school for grades 4–8 that uses Alpha School's 2 Hour Learning software. The Arizona State Board for Charter Schools approved it by a 4–3 vote. A board slideshow reportedly showed 10% proficiency in math and 28% in English Language Arts, below state averages. The school had projected 90%+ within two to three years, and separately claims students learn 2.8 times faster on its own growth tests. The reports do not say where students started, so it is unclear how much they grew.

Lesson: This is the key story to pair with Alpha. The morning software alone is not the whole model. When the program moves online and opens to everyone without in-person afternoons and adult guides, the results do not carry over automatically.

docs.title: The LA Unified Chatbot "Ed"
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2024 · Los Angeles Unified School District

LA Unified committed about $6 million to the startup AllHere for an AI chatbot called "Ed" and spent about $3 million of it. The company collapsed within months of launch. In November 2024 its founder was charged with defrauding investors of nearly $10 million. In 2026 the FBI searched the superintendent's home and office in an investigation reported to be connected to AllHere; he has not been charged with a crime.

Lesson: Rushed purchasing, depending on one vendor, and sending student data to an unproven company all put students at risk. Schools need procurement rules, such as those based on the five-level model, before they buy AI products.

docs.title: AltSchool
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2013–2019 · Silicon Valley

AltSchool raised more than $170 million to build a network of "personalized learning" microschools run on its own software. It closed its schools within a few years and shifted to selling software.

Lesson: Personalization led by technology, without a lasting school culture and community, does not last.

docs.title: Summit Learning
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2018–2019 · Brooklyn and Kansas

Summit Learning, a personalized-learning platform backed by Facebook engineers, was rolled out to many schools. Students walked out in Brooklyn and families protested in Kansas, complaining about long hours on screens and too little contact with teachers.

Lesson: This is the clearest real example of the screen-time risk. An AI morning must stay short, and the afternoon must be truly with other people.

docs.title: inBloom
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2014

inBloom was a $100 million, Gates Foundation-funded project to store and share student data across states. It closed after parents pushed back over privacy.

Lesson: Any xAPI and Learning Record Store system needs the trust of families from the start, with clear rules about who owns and controls student data.

docs.title: PowerSchool Data Breach
docs.text:
Cautionary · December 2024

A breach at PowerSchool, one of the largest student information system vendors, exposed records for tens of millions of students and teachers.

Lesson: Level 3 textbooks and higher need student records. The more centralized those records are, the bigger the target. This makes the level 3 privacy threshold concrete.

docs.title: LA Unified iPad Rollout
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2013 · Los Angeles Unified School District

LA Unified began a $1.3 billion plan to give every student an iPad loaded with Pearson curriculum. The plan was cancelled amid technical problems, weak curriculum, and a scandal over how the contract was awarded.

Lesson: Buying devices before having a plan for teaching wastes money and public trust.

docs.title: Alpha School
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2014– · Austin and other cities

Alpha School students spend about two hours a day on adaptive academic software and the rest of the day on life-skills workshops and projects led by adult guides. Tuition ranges from about $40,000 a year at the original Austin campus to about $65,000 a year at newer campuses in Boston, Miami, and New York.

Lesson: The morning-and-afternoon structure can work, but at private-school prices. The book asks how to offer the same structure to every student using open intelligent textbooks, MicroSims, learning graphs, xAPI, and a Learning Record Store instead of costly live AI.

docs.title: David Game College
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2024 · London

David Game College opened what was described as the UK's first GCSE class taught mainly by AI. Students work with AI learning platforms and are supported by learning coaches instead of traditional teachers.

Lesson: It shows the AI-first idea spreading beyond the United States. It also shows the same open question as Alpha: how much of the result comes from the software and how much from the adults around it.

docs.title: The Turkish High-School Study
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2024 · Bastani et al., Wharton

In a study at a high school in Turkey, students given open GPT-4 access did much better on practice problems. On later exams taken without AI, however, they did about 17% worse than students who never had access. A second version with guardrails, which gave hints instead of answers, removed most of the harm.

Lesson: This is the book's thesis in one experiment. The same AI can help or hurt depending on how it is designed. It also supports the book's low-cost design: guided, structured adaptation is safer than an open chatbot.

docs.title: "Your Brain on ChatGPT"
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2025 · MIT Media Lab

In this study, students who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed lower brain engagement in EEG readings and remembered less of what they had written than students who wrote on their own. The study was small and is still a preprint.

Lesson: It supports the risk of students handing their thinking over to AI, and shows why the book puts writing, debate, and making things into the afternoon.

docs.title: Khanmigo
docs.text:
Both-sided · 2023– · Khan Academy

Khanmigo is an AI tutor built specifically for learning. It guides students with questions instead of giving answers, and it has been rolled out in many school districts. Early versions made math mistakes, and students in some districts used it less than expected.

Lesson: Even careful design meets the reality of how classrooms actually use a tool. A level 4 chatbot is not automatically better than a well-built level 2 or level 3 textbook.

docs.title: AI Cheating Detectors
docs.text:
Cautionary · 2023 · Liang et al., Stanford

A Stanford study found that popular AI-writing detectors often wrongly flagged essays by non-native English writers as written by AI.

Lesson: Fighting AI can create its own equity problems. Schools should redesign assignments instead of relying on detection.

docs.title: The Non-AI Afternoon
docs.text:
Positive · ongoing

The pro-social afternoon does not need to be invented from scratch. These programs already show it working:

  • High Tech High (San Diego): project-based learning, where students work in teams on real projects and present them in public exhibitions
  • Finland's phenomenon-based learning: students study real-world topics across subjects, often in groups
  • El Sistema (Venezuela and worldwide): youth orchestras that use group music-making to build discipline, belonging, and community

Lesson: The afternoon half of the AI-native school day is already proven. AI frees the time; these models show how to use it.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 23 chapters covering 532 concepts from the learning graph.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning - This chapter introduces the core vocabulary of schools, students, teachers, and learning theory — education, curriculum, learning outcomes, the school day, direct instruction, spaced and retrieval practice, Bloom's Taxonomy, and formative assessment.
  2. Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling - This chapter covers how educators judge what works — evidence-based practice, randomized controlled trials, effect size, and case study methods — alongside the motivational side of learning: curiosity, boredom, engagement, and productive struggle.
  3. School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy - This chapter examines the structural and historical scaffolding of the school system: the bell schedule, the Carnegie unit, seat time, age-based grade levels, and the industrial-era school model, alongside achievement and equity gaps and alternatives like charter, virtual, and microschools.
  4. Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies - This chapter introduces artificial intelligence, machine learning, and large language models, then explains how METR measures AI capability through the task-horizon studies — benchmark task suites, the 50% time horizon, and human working time as the unit of measurement.
  5. Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty - This chapter teaches readers to project the METR task-horizon trend forward: reading a logarithmic scale, the five-month doubling time, and the difference between linear and exponential growth.
  6. The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks - This chapter presents the book's central organizing idea: the five-level model of intelligent textbooks, adapted from the SAE J3016 levels for self-driving cars.
  7. Content Economics and Open Educational Resources - This chapter covers the economics behind falling content-creation costs: open educational resources, open licenses, the OpenBook QR Score, content commoditization, and how publisher business models are changing as AI makes level 1 and level 2 content cheap to produce.
  8. Tracking Mastery: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, and MicroSims - This chapter introduces the technical building blocks that let a textbook adapt to a student without a live AI model: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, mastery data, learning analytics, and MicroSims, together with student-controlled, portable learning data.
  9. Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale - This chapter covers learning graphs as directed acyclic graphs of concept nodes, the interoperability standards (IMS Global, IEEE) that let these pieces work across products, and the practical requirements of delivering content at scale: device access, connectivity, offline access, and a "generate once, serve many" delivery model.
  10. Student Privacy and Data Governance - This chapter covers the level-3 privacy inflection point: why adaptive and higher-level textbooks need detailed student data, and what that triggers — FERPA, COPPA, GDPR, data governance, and algorithmic bias auditing — illustrated by the inBloom shutdown and the PowerSchool data breach.
  11. Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning - This chapter makes the case for a shorter academic morning: adaptive and mastery learning, personalized pacing, Bloom's two-sigma problem, one-on-one tutoring, and what AI tutors do well, alongside the critical- and computational-thinking skills a compressed morning is meant to protect time for.
  12. AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance - This chapter covers how an AI tutor should be designed rather than just how powerful it is: guardrails, hints instead of answers, Socratic questioning, and the risk of cognitive offloading and over-reliance, alongside the specific thinking skills (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithmic thinking) AI can teach well.
  13. Social Learning and Human Skills - This chapter introduces social constructionism and constructivism as the theoretical basis for the pro-social afternoon, along with the specific human skills it targets: collaboration, teamwork, communication, empathy, creativity, and social-emotional learning.
  14. The Pro-Social Afternoon - This chapter covers what fills the pro-social afternoon in practice: the arts, sports, clubs, maker spaces, service learning, and project-based learning, with proven models such as High Tech High, phenomenon-based learning, and El Sistema, plus the risk of an unstructured afternoon.
  15. Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation - This chapter introduces the technology adoption curve: Rogers' diffusion of innovations, the five innovation attributes, adopter categories from innovators to laggards, the chasm between early adopters and the early majority, and the hype cycle.
  16. Organizational Change Models - This chapter names the major organizational change models used later in the book — Kotter's eight steps, Lewin's unfreeze-change-refreeze, ADKAR, Bridges' transition model, Schein's culture model, Senge's learning organization, Fullan's educational change, and the Concerns-Based Adoption Model — along with organizational and school culture.
  17. Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns - This chapter goes deeper into the early stages of leading change: Lewin's unfreezing, Kotter's guiding coalition and shared vision, Bridges' endings and losses, Schein's levels of culture, and the first stages of ADKAR and the Concerns-Based Adoption Model.
  18. Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption - This chapter completes the change models with their later, sustaining stages: Senge's systems thinking and mental models, the later stages of ADKAR and CBAM, Bridges' new beginnings, the "grammar of schooling," and Estonia's national AI Leap as a whole-system example.
  19. Microstrategies for Leading Change - This chapter covers the concrete, next-week moves that make change stick: teacher champions, pilot classrooms, bright spots, shrinking the first step, professional learning communities, and engaging stakeholders — including resistance, family communication, and the changing role of the teacher from lecturer to coach and mentor.
  20. Designing the AI-Native School Day - This chapter covers redesigning the school day itself: the morning-afternoon model, scheduling and staffing, the changing teacher role, and grade-level design choices for a real AI-native school.
  21. Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly - This chapter covers putting the model into practice responsibly: safe procurement, avoiding vendor lock-in, equity and access, redesigning assessment instead of policing it, and measuring whether a pilot is actually working.
  22. AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril - This chapter presents a first set of real cases that show both the promise and the peril of AI-first schools: Alpha School, the Turkish high school chatbot study, the Harvard physics AI tutor, and the risk-and-response framework used to weigh them.
  23. AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice - This chapter presents a second set of cases focused on lessons for practice: AltSchool, Summit Learning, the Los Angeles iPad rollout and "Ed" chatbot, and other cautionary and positive examples, closing with how to evaluate result claims and make a recommendation to a school board.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Work through the chapters in order. Each chapter's concepts depend only on concepts introduced in earlier chapters, so completing chapters sequentially ensures every prerequisite has already been covered. The Part structure of the course description groups these 23 chapters into five broader parts plus a closing set of case studies.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the core vocabulary of schools, students, teachers, and learning theory — education, curriculum, learning outcomes, the school day, direct instruction, spaced and retrieval practice, Bloom's Taxonomy, and formative assessment. It gives readers the shared terms the rest of the book builds on, with no AI yet in the picture. After completing it, readers can describe how a traditional classroom and school day work today.

docs.title: Before We Change Anything, Let's Name It
docs.text:
This book argues that the school day is about to change more in the next few years than it has in the last hundred. Before we can talk sensibly about that change, we need a shared vocabulary for the thing being changed. Teachers, principals, board members, and parents all use words like curriculum, learning, and assessment, but they often mean slightly different things by them. Those small differences turn into large arguments once money, schedules, and children's futures are on the table.

So this chapter does something deliberately modest. It describes how schools work today, using terms that education researchers and practitioners would recognize, and it does so without any artificial intelligence in the picture. Every later chapter leans on these words. When Chapter 11 argues that adaptive textbooks can compress academic work into a shorter morning, it depends on what you learn here about direct instruction, the learning gap, and self-paced learning. When Chapter 20 redesigns the school day, it starts from the school day described here.

Hello — I'm Indigo

I'm Indigo, a barn owl, and like most owls I prefer to look carefully before I swoop. I'll pop up in these chapters to do six jobs:

  1. Welcome you at the start of each chapter and tell you why it matters.
  2. Think with you when an idea asks you to rebuild a mental model.
  3. Tip you off to a shortcut or a useful test you can use right away.
  4. Warn you about a common trap, and show you how to step around it.
  5. Encourage you when a passage is genuinely hard.
  6. Celebrate with you when you finish something worth naming.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Let's find the balance.

We will move from the broadest ideas to the most specific ones. First come education and learning, then the institutions and people involved, then what schools try to teach and how they describe it, and finally the daily mechanics of teaching, practice, and checking for understanding. Along the way we follow one composite student, Maya, a seventh grader at a public middle school, and her math teacher, Ms. Rivera. Neither is a real person. They are composites built to make the ideas concrete.

docs.title: Education and Learning: Two Words That Are Not Synonyms
docs.text:
The broadest concept in this book is education: the organized, intentional effort by a society, community, or family to help people acquire knowledge, skills, values, and ways of thinking. The key words are organized and intentional. A grandmother deliberately teaching a grandchild to bake bread is education. So is a university lecture, an apprenticeship, a driver's education course, and a public school. Education is something people do for or with a learner, and it always has a purpose behind it.

Learning is different. Learning is a relatively lasting change in a person's knowledge, skills, or understanding that results from experience. Learning happens inside the learner. It can happen with no education involved at all: a child who touches a hot stove learns something durable without anyone intending to teach. And education can happen with little learning: a lecture delivered to a room of students who forget it by Friday was education in intent and not much learning in result.

The phrase "relatively lasting" matters more than it first appears. Researchers distinguish performance, what a learner can do right now, from learning, what the learner can still do days or weeks later. A student who crams the night before a test may perform well in the morning and retain little by the next month. That student showed strong performance and weak learning. This gap between how learning feels in the moment and what actually lasts will come back later in this chapter, when we reach spaced and retrieval practice, and it shapes nearly every argument in the book about what an AI tutor should and should not do.

Learning happens in the learner

Notice where each word lives. Education lives in the plans, people, and places a society builds; learning lives only inside the student's head. Every reform in this book is a bet that changing the first will change the second — so always ask what evidence shows the second actually moved.

A third word, schooling, is often blurred with both. Schooling is education delivered through the specific institution of a school. Most of this book is about schooling, because that is the institution AI is about to reshape. The table below summarizes the three terms you have just met; it adds no new ideas, but it is a useful reference when later chapters use the words carefully.

Term What it is Where it lives Can it happen without the others? Education Organized, intentional effort to help people learn Families, communities, institutions Yes — a lecture no one remembers is education with little learning Learning A relatively lasting change in knowledge or skill from experience Inside the learner Yes — a child learns from touching a hot stove with no teacher present Schooling Education delivered through the institution of a school Schools No — schooling is one form of education

docs.title: Worked Example: Is This Education, Learning, or Both?
docs.text:
Consider four short scenes from Maya's week and decide which concept each one illustrates.

  1. Monday, 9:10 a.m. Ms. Rivera explains how to add fractions with unlike denominators. Maya is texting under her desk and absorbs none of it. This is education (intentional, organized teaching) with almost no learning.
  2. Monday, 6:00 p.m. Maya watches an older cousin fix a bicycle chain, and the next weekend fixes her own. This is learning with no formal education; the cousin was not trying to teach.
  3. Wednesday. Maya's grandfather spends an evening deliberately teaching her to read a bus map, and she navigates to the library alone the following Saturday. This is both: intentional education outside school, and lasting learning.
  4. Friday. Maya scores 95 percent on a vocabulary quiz she crammed for that morning; three weeks later she recalls four of the twenty words. This is strong performance with weak learning, which is exactly the distinction researchers warn about.

The fourth scene is the one that matters most for the rest of this book. A school that measures only Friday's quiz will believe it is succeeding even when little lasting learning occurred.

docs.title: Schools, Students, Teachers, and Classrooms
docs.text: With education and learning defined, we can name the institution and the people where most formal education for children happens.

docs.title: School
docs.text:
A school is an institution, usually with dedicated buildings and staff, that a society sets up to provide education to a defined group of learners on a regular schedule. In the United States, public schools serve roughly 49 million students in about 99,000 schools, according to the National Center for Education Statistics, with private schools and homeschooling serving millions more. A school is more than a building. It is a bundle of decisions about who attends, what they study, who teaches them, when they show up, how they are grouped, and how their progress is judged.

That bundle has been remarkably stable. Historians David Tyack and Larry Cuban called the durable structure underneath it the "grammar of schooling": age-graded classes, one teacher per room, subjects divided into periods, and a bell schedule. Chapter 3 traces where that grammar came from. For now, notice that most of the features we think of as "what a school is" were design choices made more than a century ago, and design choices can be revisited.

A school also performs several jobs at once, and confusing them causes trouble in any reform conversation. Schools teach academic content. They also provide safe supervision for children while parents work, meals for students who need them, a place to make friends, access to counseling and special-education services, sports, the arts, and a sense of community. A reform that improves academic learning but breaks the supervision or community job will meet fierce resistance, and it should.

docs.title: Worked Example: Listing a School's Jobs
docs.text:
Suppose a parent asks the principal of Maya's school, "What is this school actually for?" A complete answer lists at least six distinct jobs:

  1. Academic instruction in reading, writing, mathematics, science, history, and other subjects.
  2. Supervision: a safe, adult-supervised place for children roughly from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.
  3. Nutrition: breakfast and lunch, often free or reduced-price for students from low-income families.
  4. Support services: special education, counseling, health screening, English-language support.
  5. Social development: friendships, teamwork, conflict resolution, belonging.
  6. Enrichment: music, art, athletics, clubs.

When a later chapter proposes moving academic instruction into a shorter morning, this list is a checklist. Every job still has to be done by someone, somewhere, during the day.

docs.title: Student
docs.text:
A student is a person enrolled in a course of study at an educational institution. That definition is administrative; the more useful view for this book is that each student arrives as a different learner. Students differ in prior knowledge, reading level, interests, motivation, language background, disabilities, home circumstances, sleep, and confidence. A seventh grader like Maya might read at a ninth-grade level, do math at a fifth-grade level, love drawing, and be quietly anxious about speaking in front of the class.

Traditional schools group students mainly by age, not by readiness. Two students born a week apart sit in the same grade regardless of what each already knows. This is efficient for scheduling and fair in a rough sense, but it means every classroom contains students at very different starting points. That fact drives the concept of the learning gap later in this chapter.

docs.title: Worked Example: One Student, Several Starting Points
docs.text:
Here is a profile of Maya, drawn as a composite, to make "each student is different" concrete:

  • Reading: finishes young-adult novels quickly; reads about two grade levels above her grade.
  • Mathematics: never fully mastered fractions in fifth grade, so ratio problems in seventh grade stall her.
  • Interests: drawing, graphic novels, animals.
  • Constraints: cares for a younger brother after school, so homework time is short.
  • Confidence: high in English class, low in math class, and she hides confusion rather than ask.

Notice that "seventh grader" describes almost nothing useful about what Maya needs next. Her next step in reading and her next step in math are years apart.

docs.title: Teacher
docs.text:
A teacher is a professional whose job is to help students learn: planning instruction, explaining ideas, designing practice, assessing progress, giving feedback, managing a group of young people, and building relationships with them and their families. In most countries, public school teachers hold a license that requires a degree, supervised practice, and examinations.

The job is far larger than the time spent talking at the front of a room. Teachers make hundreds of small decisions every hour: who to call on, when to slow down, whether a student's silence means confusion or boredom, how to calm a conflict. Researchers who study classroom teaching consistently find that the teacher is the most important school-based factor in how much students learn. That is why this book will argue that AI should change what teachers spend their time on, not whether schools need them.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Arithmetic of a Teacher's Week
docs.text:
Ms. Rivera teaches five sections of seventh-grade math, each with 28 students. That is \( 5 \times 28 = 140 \) students. Suppose she wants to give each student five minutes of written feedback on one homework assignment per week:

\[ 140 \text{ students} \times 5 \text{ minutes} = 700 \text{ minutes} \approx 11.7 \text{ hours} \]

That is nearly twelve hours a week for one round of feedback on one assignment, on top of roughly 25 hours of teaching and the time needed to plan lessons. The arithmetic explains why so much student work gets a checkmark rather than a comment. It also explains why any tool that takes routine feedback off a teacher's desk is attractive, and why a tool that gives bad feedback is dangerous: it scales errors across 140 students at once.

docs.title: Classroom
docs.text:
A classroom is the room, and the group of students and teacher within it, where scheduled instruction happens. It is both a physical space and a social one. The physical classroom has seats, a board or screen, and supplies. The social classroom has norms (raise your hand, do your own work), routines (warm-up, lesson, practice, exit ticket), and a culture that can make students feel safe to try or afraid to be wrong.

The classroom's central constraint is simple: one adult, many students, fixed time. That constraint shapes almost every teaching method.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Much One-on-One Time Is There?
docs.text:
Maya's math period lasts 50 minutes and has 28 students. If Ms. Rivera spent the entire period moving from student to student, with no whole-class teaching, no transitions, and no interruptions, each student would get:

\[ \frac{50 \text{ minutes}}{28 \text{ students}} \approx 1.8 \text{ minutes per student} \]

In practice, after taking attendance, opening the lesson, and managing transitions, a student might get less than a minute of individual attention per period. This single number is a large part of why one-to-one tutoring is so effective and so expensive, a theme Chapter 11 explores through Bloom's two-sigma problem.

docs.title: Curriculum and Learning Outcomes: What Schools Intend to Teach
docs.text: Schools do not leave the content of education to chance. They describe it.

docs.title: Curriculum
docs.text:
A curriculum is the planned body of knowledge, skills, and experiences that a school or system intends students to learn, along with the sequence in which they will learn it. In the United States, states usually set standards (broad statements of what students should know at each grade), districts adopt or write a curriculum aligned to those standards, and teachers turn the curriculum into daily lessons. Textbooks, unit plans, pacing guides, and assessments are all parts of a curriculum's machinery.

Researchers often distinguish three versions of any curriculum. This distinction, used in international studies such as TIMSS, is one of the most useful ideas a school leader can carry:

  • The intended curriculum is what the documents say students should learn.
  • The enacted curriculum is what teachers actually teach in their classrooms.
  • The attained curriculum is what students actually learn and can show.

Every gap between the three is a place where learning leaks out. A standard can be in the documents and never taught because the class ran out of time. A topic can be taught and never learned because it moved too fast.

docs.title: Worked Example: One Standard, Three Curricula
docs.text:
Take a seventh-grade math standard: students compute unit rates involving ratios of fractions. Trace it through Maya's school year:

Curriculum layer What happened Evidence Intended The state standard and district pacing guide schedule three weeks of unit rates in October Pacing guide Enacted A fire drill, a school assembly, and a review day cut instruction to eight class periods Ms. Rivera's lesson plans Attained Students fluent with fractions mastered unit rates; Maya and several others did not, because the lessons assumed fraction skills they lacked Unit test results

The table shows the same standard looking fully covered on paper and only partly learned in practice. Most of this book's proposals are about narrowing the distance between the intended and attained curriculum for each individual student.

docs.title: Learning Outcome
docs.text:
A learning outcome is a specific, observable statement of what a learner will be able to do after instruction. Where a curriculum describes a whole course, a learning outcome describes one target. Good outcomes have three properties: they name an observable action, they name specific content, and they make it possible to tell whether the learner succeeded.

Compare two statements:

  • Weak: "Students will understand fractions."
  • Strong: "Students will add two fractions with unlike denominators and simplify the result, correctly solving at least four of five problems."

The weak version uses understand, which cannot be observed directly. You cannot watch someone understand. The strong version names an action (add and simplify), specific content (unlike denominators), and a criterion (four of five). A teacher, a parent, or a piece of software could check it.

The watch-them-do-it test

Here's a shortcut for checking any learning outcome: ask, "Could I watch a student do this and agree with a colleague on whether they succeeded?" If the verb is understand, know, appreciate, or learn about, the answer is no — swap in a verb you can see, like explain, calculate, compare, or design.

docs.title: Worked Example: Rewriting Outcomes
docs.text:
Here are three outcomes taken from a typical unit plan, rewritten to pass the test above.

Original outcome Problem Rewritten outcome Students will know the causes of the Civil War Know is not observable Students will explain three causes of the Civil War, citing one primary source for each Students will appreciate poetry Appreciate is not observable and not assessable Students will identify two uses of figurative language in an unfamiliar poem and describe the effect of each Students will learn about ecosystems Learn about names a topic, not an action Students will predict how removing one species changes a given food web and justify the prediction

Outcomes matter to this book for a practical reason. An adaptive textbook can only decide what a student should do next if it knows what the student is trying to be able to do. Precise learning outcomes are the raw material for the learning graphs and mastery tracking introduced in Chapters 8 and 9.

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy and Higher-Order Thinking
docs.text:
Learning outcomes differ not only in content but in the kind of thinking they demand. Reciting a definition and designing an experiment are both outcomes, but they ask for very different mental work.

Bloom's Taxonomy is a framework for classifying learning outcomes by the kind of cognitive work they require. Benjamin Bloom and colleagues published the original version in 1956. In 2001, Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl published a revision that renamed the levels as verbs and moved Create to the top. The revised taxonomy has six levels, listed here from least to most complex:

  1. Remember — retrieve facts and terms from memory (list, define, recall).
  2. Understand — explain ideas in one's own words (summarize, explain, classify, compare).
  3. Apply — use a procedure or idea in a given situation (calculate, solve, use).
  4. Analyze — break material into parts and see how they relate (compare, organize, differentiate).
  5. Evaluate — make judgments against criteria (judge, critique, justify).
  6. Create — put elements together into something new (design, compose, construct).

The levels are cumulative in a loose sense. You cannot evaluate an argument about ecosystems without remembering what a food web is, understanding how energy moves through it, and analyzing which species depend on which. This book uses the 2001 revision throughout, including in its own learning outcomes in the course description.

The MicroSim below, reused from the companion book Automating Instructional Design, lets you hover over each level to see its meaning, typical verbs, and examples.

docs.title: Diagram: Bloom's Taxonomy
docs.text:
Run the Bloom's Taxonomy MicroSim fullscreen

Bloom's Taxonomy (reused MicroSim)

Type: infographic sim-id: bloom-taxonomy Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/automating-instructional-design/sims/bloom-taxonomy/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/bloom-taxonomy Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: recall Learning Objective: The learner will recall the six levels of the 2001 revised Bloom's Taxonomy in order, with one typical verb for each.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.7534).

docs.title: Higher-Order Thinking
docs.text:
Higher-order thinking refers to the cognitive work in the top three levels of Bloom's Taxonomy: analyzing, evaluating, and creating. The lower three levels (remember, understand, apply) are sometimes called lower-order thinking. The labels are not a ranking of importance. Higher-order thinking depends on a large store of remembered and understood knowledge; a student cannot critique a historical argument without knowing the history.

Higher-order thinking matters to this book for two reasons. First, it is the kind of thinking employers, universities, and citizens most need, and the kind that traditional lecture-and-test schooling exercises least. Studies of classroom tasks repeatedly find that most assignments sit at the Remember and Apply levels. Second, it is exactly the kind of thinking a student can skip by asking a chatbot for the answer. Chapter 12 returns to this risk under the name cognitive offloading.

The pyramid is not a ladder you climb once

A common trap is reading Bloom's Taxonomy as "teach facts first, then never return to them," or as "lower levels are for weak students." Both are wrong: experts move up and down the levels constantly, and a hard Remember task (recall 50 capitals) can be harder than an easy Analyze task. Classify an outcome by the kind of thinking it asks for, not by how difficult or impressive it sounds.

docs.title: Worked Example: One Topic at Six Levels
docs.text:
The water cycle can be taught at every level of the taxonomy. Here is a set of tasks on the same topic, one per level:

Level Task Remember List the four main stages of the water cycle Understand Explain in your own words why puddles disappear on a sunny day Apply Use the water cycle to predict where dew will form on a cool morning Analyze Compare rainfall data from two cities and identify which stage of the cycle explains the difference Evaluate Judge which of two proposed school rain-garden designs will capture more runoff, and defend your judgment Create Design an experiment to measure evaporation rates in different locations around the school

A unit that contained only the first two rows would be easy to teach and test. It would also leave students unable to use what they know. In the sim specified below, you practice classifying tasks from many subjects.

docs.title: Diagram: Bloom Level Task Sorter
docs.text:
Bloom Level Task Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: bloom-level-task-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify twelve classroom tasks into the six levels of the 2001 revised Bloom's Taxonomy, correctly placing at least ten of twelve on the first attempt.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/bloom-taxonomy

Prerequisites: Bloom's Taxonomy, the six levels (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create), learning outcome, higher-order thinking (all defined in the section "Bloom's Taxonomy and Higher-Order Thinking" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of the 12 tasks to one of six level bins and submits it. An assignment is correct when it matches the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt. Reading level descriptions and hovering over bins is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The verb alone decides the level (for example, any task containing "explain" must be Understand). (2) Harder or longer tasks are always at higher levels. (3) Writing anything is automatically Create.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying is an Understand-level skill: the learner must recognize which level definition fits an unfamiliar task and commit to an answer before seeing feedback. Mixing subjects prevents the learner from sorting by topic instead of by kind of thinking.

Content:

Six bins, in this order, each with its one-line definition shown on request:

Bin Definition shown Remember Retrieve facts and terms from memory Understand Explain ideas in your own words Apply Use a procedure or idea in a given situation Analyze Break material into parts and see how they relate Evaluate Make judgments against criteria Create Put elements together into something new

Twelve tasks:

# Task shown to the learner Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 List the planets in order from the Sun. Remember The learner only retrieves a memorized sequence. 2 State the year the U.S. Constitution was signed. Remember Recalling a single fact is retrieval, even though it is a history task. 3 Explain in your own words why ice floats on water. Understand Restating an idea in one's own words shows comprehension, not a new use of it. 4 Summarize the main argument of a newspaper editorial in three sentences. Understand Summarizing condenses meaning without judging or restructuring it. 5 Use the area formula to find how much paint is needed to cover a 3 m by 4 m wall. Apply A known procedure is carried out in a given situation. 6 Conjugate five new regular -ar verbs in the Spanish preterite tense. Apply A learned rule is applied to new cases; nothing is analyzed or invented. 7 Compare two accounts of the same battle and identify where they disagree. Analyze The learner breaks two sources into parts and examines how they relate. 8 Break a persuasive speech into its claims, its evidence, and its emotional appeals. Analyze Separating a whole into its structural parts is analysis. 9 Judge which of two experiment designs better tests whether fertilizer increases plant growth, and defend your choice. Evaluate The learner makes and justifies a judgment against a criterion (a fair test). 10 Score a classmate's essay with the class rubric and justify each score. Evaluate Applying criteria to reach a defended judgment is evaluation. 11 Design an experiment to test whether background music affects reaction time. Create The learner produces an original plan that did not exist before. 12 Write an original short story that uses foreshadowing. Create The learner composes a new work, not a summary or analysis of an existing one.

Provenance: Bin definitions are from the chapter section "Bloom's Taxonomy and Higher-Order Thinking," which follows Anderson and Krathwohl (2001). Tasks are illustrative, written for this sim.

Rules: Each task has exactly one correct level, given in Content. A task is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 12. Mastery is a score >= 10.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one task at a time and the six bins.
  2. The learner places the task in a bin and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. The next task appears. After all 12, the learner sees the score and a list of any misplaced tasks with their correct levels.
  5. The learner should notice that tasks 3 and 7 both involve explaining or comparing, yet sit at different levels, and that task 2 is short but still Remember while task 12 is a writing task at Create.

Feedback: 12 tasks, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct — [level]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the task counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 12" is shown. Final message for a score >= 10: "You can classify tasks by the kind of thinking they ask for." For a score < 10: "Review the level definitions and try again; the tasks will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Task 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the six empty bins and the score "First-try correct: 0 of 12." The prompt reads "What kind of thinking does this task ask for?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names six levels in the order Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create. The chapter states that higher-order thinking means the top three levels. The objective's mastery bar is 10 of 12.

docs.title: The School Day and Direct Instruction
docs.text: We now know what schools intend to teach. The next question is how they spend their time teaching it.

docs.title: School Day
docs.text:
The school day is the daily schedule during which students attend school: start and end times, the division of time into periods or blocks, and the transitions, meals, and breaks between them. A typical U.S. public school day runs about six and a half to seven hours, for about 180 days a year, according to NCES surveys. Middle and high schools usually divide the day into six to eight subject periods of 45 to 55 minutes each, separated by passing time. Elementary schools more often keep one class with one teacher for most of the day, with blocks for reading, math, and specials such as art and physical education.

The school day is one of the most stubborn parts of the grammar of schooling. Bus routes, teacher contracts, parents' work hours, athletics, and state instructional-time requirements are all built around it. That is why proposals to change what happens during the day, as this book makes, are far more realistic than proposals to change its total length.

Before you look at how the minutes are actually spent, one more term is needed.

docs.title: Direct Instruction
docs.text:
Direct instruction is a teacher-led method in which the teacher explicitly explains and models new content, guides students through practice, checks understanding, and then has students practice independently. The pattern is often summarized as I do, we do, you do. In lowercase, "direct instruction" names this general approach. In capitals, "Direct Instruction" refers to a specific, tightly scripted program developed by Siegfried Engelmann and colleagues in the 1960s, which performed strongly in the large federal Project Follow Through evaluation.

Direct instruction has a good research record for teaching well-defined skills to novices, especially when lessons are broken into small steps, students practice frequently, and the teacher checks understanding before moving on. Barak Rosenshine's widely used Principles of Instruction summarize this evidence. The method's weakness is not that explanation is bad. It is that a single explanation, at a single pace, is delivered to a whole classroom of students who are ready for different things.

docs.title: Worked Example: An I-Do, We-Do, You-Do Lesson
docs.text:
Here is how Ms. Rivera's 50-minute lesson on unit rates might run:

  1. Warm-up (5 minutes). Students solve two review problems on fractions while she takes attendance.
  2. I do (10 minutes). She models, aloud, how to find the price per ounce for a 12-ounce bottle costing $3.00: \( \$3.00 \div 12 = \$0.25 \) per ounce, explaining each step.
  3. We do (10 minutes). The class solves three problems together; she cold-calls students for each step and watches for errors.
  4. You do (20 minutes). Students practice ten problems independently while she circulates.
  5. Exit ticket (5 minutes). Each student solves one problem on a slip of paper she collects at the door.

This is a well-designed lesson. Yet for Maya, step 2 already assumes fraction division skills she lacks, while for two classmates who mastered unit rates last year, steps 2 and 3 are fifteen minutes of waiting. Both problems come from pacing the whole room together, not from the quality of the teaching.

The sim below asks you to estimate how a full day of minutes like these adds up.

docs.title: Diagram: Where the Minutes Go in a Traditional School Day
docs.text:
Where the Minutes Go in a Traditional School Day

Type: chart sim-id: school-day-minute-map Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate the minutes of an illustrative middle-school day into whole-class direct instruction, practice, and non-instructional time, estimating the direct-instruction total to within 10 minutes.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-strategy-for-education/tree/main/docs/sims/school-day-comparison-timeline

Prerequisites: school day, direct instruction, the I-do/we-do/you-do pattern, classroom (all defined in the section "The School Day and Direct Instruction" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the chart is revealed, the learner enters two estimates: (a) total minutes of whole-class direct instruction in the day, and (b) which category is the largest single use of time. Estimate (a) is correct when it is within ±10 minutes of 100. Estimate (b) is correct when it is "Whole-class direct instruction" or "Practice" (they tie at 100 minutes each). Viewing the chart after reveal is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Most of the school day is spent with a teacher explaining new material. (2) Almost all of a seven-hour day is academic time. (3) Non-instructional time (passing, lunch, settling in) is negligible.

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level differentiation requires the learner to separate a familiar whole (a school day) into categories and see their proportions. Committing to an estimate before the reveal exposes the learner's mental model so the chart can correct it.

Content:

The illustrative schedule, shown as a list before the reveal:

Time Block Minutes 8:00–8:10 Homeroom 10 8:10–8:15 Passing 5 8:15–9:05 Period 1: English 50 9:05–9:10 Passing 5 9:10–10:00 Period 2: Mathematics 50 10:00–10:05 Passing 5 10:05–10:55 Period 3: Science 50 10:55–11:00 Passing 5 11:00–11:50 Period 4: Social Studies 50 11:50–12:20 Lunch 30 12:20–12:25 Passing 5 12:25–1:15 Period 5: World Language 50 1:15–1:20 Passing 5 1:20–2:10 Period 6: Art 50 2:10–2:15 Passing 5 2:15–3:05 Period 7: Physical Education 50

Each of the five academic periods (Periods 1–5) is divided as: 5 minutes settling and attendance, 20 minutes whole-class direct instruction, 20 minutes guided and independent practice, 5 minutes wrap-up.

Category totals revealed in the chart:

Category Minutes Share of 425 minutes Whole-class direct instruction 100 23.5% Guided and independent practice 100 23.5% Arts and physical education 100 23.5% Settling, attendance, and wrap-up 50 11.8% Passing time 35 8.2% Lunch 30 7.1% Homeroom 10 2.4% Total 425 100%

Provenance: Illustrative composite schedule written for this chapter; the sim must label it "Illustrative schedule." Period lengths follow the chapter's statement that middle-school periods run 45 to 55 minutes.

Rules: Shares are minutes ÷ 425, shown to one decimal place. Estimate (a) is correct when |estimate − 100| <= 10. Estimate (a) accepts whole numbers from 0 to 425. Estimate (b) is chosen from the seven category names; either of the two tied categories named in Evidence of Mastery is correct.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the schedule and enters estimate (a) and selects estimate (b).
  2. The learner reveals the chart. The day appears as categories with minutes and shares, and the learner's estimates appear beside the true values.
  3. The learner selects any category to see which blocks of the schedule contribute to it.
  4. The learner should notice that whole-class direct instruction is less than a quarter of the day, and that non-instructional categories (settling, passing, lunch, homeroom) add up to 125 minutes, more than direct instruction.

Feedback: One attempt per estimate before reveal. Estimate (a) correct: "Within 10 minutes — 100 minutes of the 425-minute day is whole-class direct instruction." Incorrect, too high: "Higher than the schedule shows. Teachers explain new material for about 20 minutes of each 50-minute academic period, and only five of the seven periods are academic." Incorrect, too low: "Lower than the schedule shows — five academic periods with about 20 minutes of explanation each make 100 minutes." Estimate (b) correct: "Right — direct instruction and practice tie at 100 minutes, and arts and PE also take 100." Incorrect: "That category is smaller. Three categories tie at 100 minutes each." After reveal, the estimates cannot be changed; a "Try again" action clears them and hides the chart.

Starting State: The schedule list is visible, the chart is hidden, and the prompt reads "In this seven-hour day, how many minutes does a student spend listening to a teacher explain new material to the whole class?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a typical U.S. school day runs about six and a half to seven hours and that middle-school periods run 45 to 55 minutes.
