The worked example lesson uses a 50-minute period. The illustrative day totals 425 minutes, with 100 minutes of whole-class direct instruction.

docs.title: The Learning Gap
docs.text:
Direct instruction to a whole class works best when students arrive at roughly the same starting point. They rarely do.

A learning gap is the difference between what a student is expected to know or be able to do at a given point, as defined by learning outcomes, and what the student actually knows or can do. The term is used at two scales. For an individual, it names specific missing pieces: Maya's gap is fraction operations from fifth grade. For a group, it describes average differences between groups of students, such as the gaps that widened during pandemic school closures.

Learning gaps compound. Mathematics is the clearest case, because so much of it is built on earlier skills. A student who misses fractions struggles with ratios, then with proportional reasoning, then with algebra. Each year's lessons assume last year's outcomes were attained. When they were not, the student falls further behind even while sitting through every lesson. Chapter 9 will show how a learning graph makes these prerequisite chains explicit, which is the first step toward closing gaps one concept at a time.

A gap is a missing prerequisite, not a missing effort

Think of a learning gap like a missing stair in the middle of a staircase. Running harder up the stairs doesn't help; someone has to go back and build the stair. Many students who look unmotivated are standing at a missing stair, and the lesson in front of them assumes it is there.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Wide Is One Classroom?
docs.text:
It is common for a single classroom to span several grade levels of readiness. Here is an illustrative seventh-grade math class of 28 students, with each student's readiness expressed as a grade level:

Readiness (grade level) 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10 Number of students 1 2 4 6 7 5 2 1

Suppose a lesson is "in reach" for a student if it sits at their readiness level or one level above it. Ms. Rivera pitches her lesson at grade 7. Then:

  • Students at grades 6 and 7 find it in reach: \( 6 + 7 = 13 \) students.
  • Students at grades 3–5 find it too hard: \( 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 \) students.
  • Students at grades 8–10 already know it: \( 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 \) students.

Fewer than half of the class, 13 of 28, is in the zone where this lesson can produce learning. Moving the pitch does not fix it, as the next sim lets you confirm: no single pitch reaches more than 13 of these 28 students.

docs.title: Diagram: One Lesson, Many Readiness Levels
docs.text:
One Lesson, Many Readiness Levels

Type: microsim sim-id: one-lesson-many-readiness-levels Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine how the pitch of a single whole-class lesson determines how many students in a mixed-readiness class are in reach, too far behind, or already ahead, and identify the pitch that reaches the most students.

Prerequisites: learning gap, direct instruction, classroom, readiness expressed as a grade level, the "in reach" rule (all defined in the section "The Learning Gap" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers three questions with committed answers: (Q1) the pitch that puts the most students in reach — correct answer 7; (Q2) the number of students in reach at that best pitch — correct answer 13; (Q3) the number of students at pitch 7 for whom the lesson is too hard — correct answer 7. Mastery is 3 of 3. Moving the pitch freely is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Teaching "to the middle" reaches most of the class. (2) A skilled enough teacher can find one pitch that works for everyone. (3) Students ahead of the lesson are learning something; in this model they are waiting.

Instructional Rationale: Analyzing requires the learner to see how one variable (pitch) splits a fixed group into parts. Predicting before exploring, then testing every pitch, lets the learner discover for themselves that the best single pitch still misses more than half the class.

Content:

Class of 28 students, each shown as an individual marker grouped by readiness:

Readiness (grade level) 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10 Students 1 2 4 6 7 5 2 1

Three student states, with the label shown in the legend:

  • In reach: the lesson is at the student's readiness level or one level above.
  • Too hard: the lesson is more than one level above the student's readiness.
  • Already known: the lesson is below the student's readiness.

In-reach counts for every pitch, used to check the sim:

Pitch 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10 In reach 1 3 6 10 13 12 7 3

Provenance: The class distribution is illustrative, written for this chapter; the sim must label it "Illustrative class." The in-reach rule is defined in the chapter section "The Learning Gap."

Rules: Lesson pitch p: min 3, max 10, step 1, default 7, unit grade level. For a student with readiness r: in reach when 0 <= p − r <= 1; too hard when p − r > 1; already known when p − r < 0. Counts are recomputed whenever p changes. The best pitch is the one with the highest in-reach count; in this class it is unique (p = 7).

Learner Activity:

  1. Before the pitch can be changed, the learner answers Q1 and Q2 as predictions.
  2. The learner moves the pitch from 3 to 10. Each student marker changes state and the three counts update at once.
  3. The learner should notice that the in-reach count rises to 13 at pitch 7 and falls on either side, and that at every pitch at least 15 students are too hard or already known.
  4. The learner sets the pitch to 7 and answers Q3.
  5. The learner submits all three answers for checking.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Q1 correct: "Yes — pitch 7 puts 13 students in reach, the most of any pitch." Q1 incorrect: "Try each pitch and watch the in-reach count; it peaks at one value." Q2 correct: "Right — 13 of 28, fewer than half the class." Q2 incorrect: "Count the students at readiness 6 and 7 when the pitch is 7." Q3 correct: "Correct — the 7 students at readiness 3, 4 and 5 are more than one level behind." Q3 incorrect: "Count students whose readiness is more than one level below the pitch." After the second wrong attempt, the answer and its explanation are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown after submission.

Starting State: The pitch is at 7 but locked, all 28 markers are shown by readiness without state colors, and the prompt reads "Where should one lesson be pitched to reach the most students — and how many will it reach?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter uses a class of 28 with the distribution above, pitches the lesson at grade 7, and states that 13 students are in reach, 7 find it too hard, and 8 already know it. The chapter states that no single pitch reaches more than 13 of the 28 students.

docs.title: Self-Paced Learning and Student Agency
docs.text: If one pace cannot fit a whole class, an obvious alternative is to let each student move at their own pace. That idea is old, and it comes with an important companion idea about who makes decisions.

docs.title: Self-Paced Learning
docs.text:
Self-paced learning is an arrangement in which each student moves through learning material at their own speed, advancing when ready rather than when the class calendar says to. The material is usually broken into small units, each with a check, so a student who needs more time on fractions takes it, and a student who already knows unit rates moves on.

Self-pacing has a long history. In 1968 the psychologist Fred Keller described the Personalized System of Instruction, in which college students worked through written units at their own pace and took short unit tests, advancing only after passing. Studies of the system found good results, but it spread slowly. Before cheap computers, self-pacing required a teacher to manage dozens of students on dozens of different pages, with a separate test ready for each. That logistical burden, not a lack of evidence, kept it on the margins. Much of this book's argument is that interactive textbooks remove that burden.

Self-pacing also has real risks. Without structure, some students drift, procrastinate, or move quickly through material without learning it. Students who most need support are often the least able to regulate their own pace. A self-paced system needs frequent checks, visible progress, deadlines that still exist, and adults who notice when a student stalls.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Students, One Unit
docs.text:
Imagine Ms. Rivera reorganizes her ratios unit into eight short lessons, each ending in a five-question check that a student must pass at four of five to advance.

Student Starting point Path through the unit Days to finish Maya Missing fraction skills Two review lessons on fractions first, then all eight lessons, retaking the check for lesson 3 once 14 Jordan Mastered ratios last year Passes the checks for lessons 1–5 on the first day, completes lessons 6–8 4

Under whole-class pacing both students would spend the same ten days on the unit: Maya would leave without the foundation, and Jordan would spend six days waiting. Under self-pacing, Maya takes longer and actually learns it; Jordan finishes early and has ten days for something else. Notice the new problem this creates: what does Jordan do with those ten days? That question, scaled up to a whole school, is the central question of this book.

docs.title: Student Agency
docs.text:
Student agency is the capacity and opportunity for students to make meaningful choices about their own learning: what to study, how to study it, how to show what they learned, and when to move on. The OECD's Learning Compass 2030 describes agency as a student's ability to set goals, reflect, and act responsibly to bring about change. Agency has two parts that are easy to blur. Capacity is the student's skill and confidence in making decisions. Opportunity is whether the school actually gives them decisions to make.

Agency is a matter of degree. A student who chooses which of two essay prompts to answer has a little agency. A student who chooses a semester-long research question, plans the steps, and decides how to present the result has a great deal. Most traditional schools give students little agency over academic work, because a whole-class schedule leaves little room for choice.

Self-paced learning and student agency are related but distinct. Self-pacing is about speed: a student controls how fast they move through a fixed sequence. Agency is about choice: a student controls what and how. A self-paced program can offer almost no agency (every student does the same lessons in the same order, only at different speeds), and a project can offer great agency with a fixed deadline.

docs.title: Worked Example: Four Degrees of Agency
docs.text:
The same assignment, a report on a local ecosystem, can be offered at different degrees of agency:

Degree What the student decides Example None Nothing Everyone writes a five-paragraph report on the pond behind the school, due Friday Low One choice within a set Choose the pond, the creek, or the park woodland Moderate Topic and format Choose any local ecosystem and present it as a report, a video, or a field guide High Question, method, and product Pose your own question about a local ecosystem, plan how to investigate it, and decide how to share what you found

Higher agency is not automatically better. A student new to research may flounder at the "High" row without support, while a confident student may be bored at "None." Good teaching gradually hands over more decisions as students build the capacity to make them well.

docs.title: Formative Assessment: Checking Learning While It Happens
docs.text:
Self-paced learning depends on knowing when a student is ready to move on. Whole-class teaching depends on knowing whether to slow down. Both depend on assessment.

Formative assessment is the process of gathering evidence of student learning during instruction and using it to adjust teaching and learning while there is still time to act. It is contrasted with summative assessment, which measures learning at the end of a unit or course to assign a grade or report results. The terms come from Michael Scriven's 1967 work on evaluation, and Benjamin Bloom applied them to classroom learning shortly after. A useful shorthand: formative assessment is a check-up, summative assessment is an autopsy.

The definition's key phrase is uses it to adjust. A quiz is not formative because of its format. It is formative only if the results change what happens next: the teacher reteaches, the student practices a specific skill, or the class moves on with evidence that it is ready. In their influential 1998 review Inside the Black Box, Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam concluded that strengthening formative assessment produced some of the largest learning gains of any classroom intervention they reviewed.

Common formative techniques include exit tickets (one or two questions at the end of a lesson), hinge questions (a single multiple-choice question mid-lesson whose wrong answers each reveal a specific misconception), mini whiteboards that every student holds up at once, and short low-stakes quizzes.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Hinge Question in Action
docs.text:
Midway through her unit-rate lesson, Ms. Rivera asks one question and has every student hold up the letter of their answer:

A 6-pack of juice costs $4.50. What is the price per bottle?

  • A. $0.75 (correct: \( 4.50 \div 6 = 0.75 \))
  • B. $1.33 (divided 6 by 4.50 — reversed the division)
  • C. $27.00 (multiplied instead of divided)
  • D. $1.50 (guessed from rounding)

She sees 17 A's, 8 B's, and 3 C's. Instead of moving on, she pulls the 11 students with B or C to the side board for five minutes on which quantity goes on top, while the other 17 begin practice. That is formative assessment: the evidence changed what happened next for 11 students, in the same period, before the misconception was practiced ten more times.

The following table contrasts the two kinds of assessment you have now seen.

Formative assessment Summative assessment When During learning At the end of a unit or course Purpose Adjust teaching and learning Judge and report what was learned Typical stakes Low or none Often high (grades, promotion, accountability) Example Hinge question, exit ticket Unit exam, state test, final project Who acts on the result Teacher and student, right away Teachers, families, administrators, later

The constraint, again, is the classroom. A teacher can run one hinge question per lesson for 28 students and act on the result. Running a different check for each student after every small step, and responding to each, is beyond what one adult can do. That is exactly the work an interactive textbook can take on, as Chapter 8 shows.

docs.title: Spaced Practice and Retrieval Practice: How Learning Lasts
docs.text: Earlier we separated performance from learning. Two of the most reliable findings in all of learning science explain how to turn short-term performance into lasting learning, and both are underused in most schools.

docs.title: Spaced Practice
docs.text:
Spaced practice (also called distributed practice) is the strategy of spreading study or practice sessions over time, with gaps between them, instead of concentrating them in one long session. The opposite, massed practice, is cramming: doing all the practice at once.

The finding goes back to Hermann Ebbinghaus, who in 1885 measured his own forgetting of nonsense syllables and charted what is now called the forgetting curve: memory fades quickly at first, then more slowly. He also found that reviews spread over days held up far better than the same number of reviews done in one sitting. More than a century of later research, summarized in a large 2006 meta-analysis by Nicholas Cepeda and colleagues, confirms that spacing improves long-term retention across ages, subjects, and kinds of material.

Why does spacing work? A useful explanation is that a review is most valuable when the memory has started to fade. Pulling back a half-forgotten idea takes effort, and that effort strengthens the memory more than reviewing something you already have in mind. Psychologist Robert Bjork calls this a desirable difficulty: a condition that makes practice feel harder and slower but improves long-term learning.

docs.title: Retrieval Practice
docs.text:
Retrieval practice is the strategy of learning by actively recalling information from memory, through practice questions, flashcards, or trying to write down what you remember, rather than by rereading or reviewing the material. It is sometimes called the testing effect, because low-stakes testing turns out to be one of the most powerful ways to learn, not just a way to measure learning.

In a well-known 2006 study, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students read a short passage and then either reread it or take a recall test on it. Five minutes later, the rereading group remembered slightly more. One week later, the retrieval group remembered substantially more. Rereading produced better short-term performance; retrieval produced better learning. A 2013 review by John Dunlosky and colleagues rated retrieval practice and spaced practice the two highest-utility study strategies of the ten they examined, while rereading and highlighting, the strategies students use most, rated low.

This one fights your instincts

If spacing and retrieval feel wrong to you, that's normal — they feel less productive than rereading, which is exactly why students and teachers avoid them. You already made sense of the performance-versus-learning distinction earlier in this chapter; this is that same idea in action. Try the sim below and predict before you look, so your own guess becomes the evidence.

docs.title: Worked Example: Planning Three Reviews
docs.text:
Maya has a science test on cell structure on day 30. She has time for three short review sessions after the first lesson on day 0. Compare three plans:

Plan When she reviews How she reviews What the research predicts Cram Three sessions back-to-back on day 0 Rereads her notes Feels confident on day 0; most is forgotten by day 30 Spaced reread Days 1, 3, and 7 Rereads her notes Much better retention on day 30 than cramming Spaced retrieval Days 1, 4, and 12 Closes her notes and writes down everything she remembers, then checks The strongest retention of the three on day 30

The total study time is the same in all three plans. Only the timing and the method change. This is why spacing and retrieval matter so much for the AI-native model: an adaptive textbook can schedule reviews for each student at the right moment, something no teacher with 140 students can do by hand.

docs.title: Diagram: Spacing and Retrieval Retention Explorer
docs.text:
Spacing and Retrieval Retention Explorer

Type: chart sim-id: spacing-retrieval-retention-explorer Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare predicted retention under massed, evenly spaced, and expanding review schedules, each done by rereading or by retrieval, and correctly predict which schedule and method retain the most on a day-30 exam.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-sciences/tree/main/docs/sims/spaced-retrieval-timeline

Prerequisites: learning versus performance, forgetting curve, spaced practice, massed practice, retrieval practice, desirable difficulty (all defined in the sections "Education and Learning" and "Spaced Practice and Retrieval Practice" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before any curve is shown, the learner makes two committed predictions: (P1) which of the four schedules gives the highest day-30 retention — correct answer "Expanding"; (P2) which method, reread or retrieval, gives higher day-30 retention for the same schedule — correct answer "Retrieval." A third check (P3) asks, after the learner has viewed the exam-day options, which schedule gives the highest retention on a day-1 exam — correct answer "Massed." Mastery is 3 of 3. Switching schedules and exam days after the predictions is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Cramming is efficient because it gives the best score on tomorrow's test, so it must be the best way to learn. (2) Rereading is as good as testing yourself. (3) The total time spent studying is what matters, not when it happens.

Instructional Rationale: Understanding a comparison is strongest when the learner first commits to a prediction that may be wrong and then sees the curves. Including a day-1 exam option lets the learner discover why cramming feels effective while still failing at day 30.

Content:

Four schedules (review times in days after the first lesson at day 0):

Schedule Review times (days) No review none Massed 0.042, 0.083, 0.125 (1, 2 and 3 hours after the lesson) Evenly spaced 1, 3, 7 Expanding 1, 4, 12

Two methods: Reread, Retrieval.

Three exam days: 1, 7, 30.

Predicted retention at the exam (model values, rounded to whole percents), used to check the sim:

Schedule Exam day 1, Reread Exam day 1, Retrieval Exam day 7, Reread Exam day 7, Retrieval Exam day 30, Reread Exam day 30, Retrieval No review 72% 72% 10% 10% 0% 0% Massed 76% 78% 12% 14% 0% 0% Evenly spaced 72% 72% 60% 74% 20% 43% Expanding 72% 72% 72% 83% 40% 65%

Provenance: The model is illustrative, written for this chapter to show the direction of effects reported by Ebbinghaus (1885), Cepeda et al. (2006), and Roediger and Karpicke (2006). Its numbers are not measured data, and the sim must label every curve "Illustrative model, not experimental data."

Rules: Retention R(t) = exp(−(t − t_last) / S), where t is days since the first lesson, t_last is the time of the most recent review (0 at the start), and S is memory stability in days. Initial S = 3 days. At each review at time t, compute R at that moment, then update S_new = S × (1 + k × (1 − R)), with k = 2 for Reread and k = 4 for Retrieval, and set t_last = t. A review whose time is greater than or equal to the exam day is skipped. Retention is shown as a percent rounded to the nearest whole number. The curve is plotted from day 0 to the selected exam day.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner makes predictions P1 and P2 and submits them. Nothing is plotted before submission.
  2. The sim plots the four schedules for the Reread method, exam day 30, and marks the day-30 retention of each.
  3. The learner switches the method to Retrieval. The four curves update; the Reread curves remain visible as faint references for comparison.
  4. The learner switches the exam day to 1, then 7. The learner should notice that Massed is highest on day 1, but falls to 0% by day 30, while Expanding with Retrieval holds 65%.
  5. The learner answers P3 and submits it.

Feedback: P1 and P2 have one attempt each and are scored before the curves appear. P1 correct: "Yes — expanding gaps let each review come when the memory has faded a little, which strengthens it most." P1 incorrect, chose Massed: "Massed reviews come before any forgetting happens, so they add little lasting strength." P1 incorrect, chose Evenly spaced: "Close — spacing helps, but longer later gaps help more in this model." P1 incorrect, chose No review: "Without review, retention falls close to zero within a month." P2 correct: "Right — retrieval strengthens memory more than rereading." P2 incorrect: "Rereading feels effective, but recalling from memory builds more lasting strength." P3 has two attempts. P3 correct: "Yes — cramming wins tomorrow's test, which is why it feels like it works." P3 incorrect: "Look at the day-1 exam: the spaced reviews have not happened yet." After the second wrong attempt, the answer is shown. Score "n of 3" is shown at the end.

Starting State: No curves are drawn. The four schedules are listed with their review days, and the prompt reads "Maya has three short reviews before a test on day 30. Which schedule, and which way of reviewing, will help her remember the most?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses a test on day 30, three reviews, a cram plan on day 0, an evenly spaced plan on days 1, 3 and 7, and an expanding retrieval plan on days 1, 4 and 12. The chapter states that rereading gave better recall after five minutes and retrieval gave better recall after one week in Roediger and Karpicke (2006).

The two-question study habit

Want to put this to work tomorrow? Open each class with two quick questions on material from last week and last month — not yesterday. That single habit adds both spacing and retrieval to a lesson in under five minutes, without changing the rest of your plan.

docs.title: Educational Technology
docs.text:
Everything in this chapter so far could happen with paper, chalk, and a teacher. The last group of concepts concerns the tools schools add to that picture and the money that pays for all of it.

Educational technology, often shortened to edtech, is the use of tools, devices, software, and media to support teaching and learning, together with the practices for using them well. The definition includes the practice, not just the device: a projector is hardware, but how a teacher uses it to show student work for discussion is educational technology.

Edtech has a long and humbling history. In the 1920s the psychologist Sidney Pressey built a machine that gave students multiple-choice questions and advanced only when they answered correctly. In the 1950s B. F. Skinner promoted "teaching machines" that broke material into small steps with immediate feedback. In 1960 the University of Illinois launched PLATO, a computer-based instruction system that pioneered features later familiar online. Each wave came with predictions that it would transform schools. The historian Larry Cuban documented a recurring pattern across decades: new technology is purchased with great enthusiasm, then used far less, and in more traditional ways, than its promoters expected. His 2001 book on school computers was titled Oversold and Underused.

The following table gathers the edtech waves just described, along with later ones, so you can see the pattern at a glance.

Era Technology Promise What mostly happened 1920s Pressey's testing machine Automate drill and free teachers Little adoption; seen as a curiosity 1950s–1960s Skinner's teaching machines, programmed instruction Each student learns at their own pace with instant feedback Brief enthusiasm, then decline 1960s–1970s PLATO and mainframe instruction Computer-based lessons at scale Influential, but costly and limited to a few institutions 1980s Classroom microcomputers Computers in every school Machines often sat in labs, used for typing and games 1990s–2000s Internet, interactive whiteboards Access to the world's information; engaging lessons Whiteboards often used as expensive projector screens 2000s–2010s One-to-one laptops and tablets, learning management systems, online video lessons Personalized learning for every student Mixed results; strongest where teaching practice changed too

The lesson of this history is not that technology fails. It is that technology alone rarely changes the grammar of schooling: the age-graded classroom, the bell schedule, the single pace. When the tool is bolted onto an unchanged school day, it tends to be absorbed into old habits.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Uses of the Same Tool
docs.text:
A district buys a tablet for every seventh grader. Consider how two classrooms use them for the same unit:

Classroom A Classroom B How tablets are used Students read the textbook as a PDF and type answers to the same worksheet Students work through self-paced lessons with immediate checks; the teacher's dashboard shows who is stuck Learning job the tool does None that paper didn't already do Practice with feedback, and formative assessment data for the teacher What the teacher does Lectures, then grades typed worksheets Pulls small groups based on the dashboard Change to the grammar of schooling None Pace becomes individual; teacher time shifts from lecturing to targeted help

Both classrooms "use technology." Only one used it to change how learning works. This distinction, between digitizing the old model and changing the model, is the thread that connects this chapter to the five-level model of intelligent textbooks in Chapter 6.

docs.title: Paying for It: Public School Funding and Per-Pupil Spending
docs.text: Every design choice in a school, from class size to the tablet cart, is constrained by money. Two terms describe where it comes from and how it is usually measured.

docs.title: Public School Funding
docs.text:
Public school funding is the system of revenues, mainly taxes, that pays for public schools. In the United States, funding comes from three levels of government. Local revenue comes mostly from property taxes. State revenue comes from income and sales taxes and is often distributed through formulas meant to help districts with less local wealth. Federal revenue, historically under 10 percent of the total, is targeted at specific purposes such as supporting students from low-income families (Title I) and students with disabilities (IDEA). The federal share rose temporarily during the pandemic-relief years. State and local sources have each historically provided a little under half of the total.

Because local revenue depends on property values, districts in wealthier areas can raise more money with the same tax rate than districts in poorer areas. State formulas reduce this gap but rarely close it. School funding lawsuits in many states have turned on exactly this question. Equity in funding comes back in Chapter 3 and again in Chapter 21, where the book asks whether an AI-native school would narrow or widen such gaps.

docs.title: Per-Pupil Spending
docs.text:
Per-pupil spending is the total amount spent on a group of public schools in a year divided by the number of students enrolled, giving the average cost to educate one student for one year. It is the standard unit for comparing school costs across districts, states, and countries. Most published figures use current spending, which covers day-to-day operations such as salaries, benefits, supplies, and transportation, and excludes construction and debt payments.

According to the U.S. Census Bureau's annual survey of school finances, U.S. public schools spent about $15,600 per pupil in current spending in fiscal year 2022, with wide variation between states. Roughly 60 percent of current spending goes to instruction, mostly teacher salaries and benefits. Check the latest Census release before citing these figures, since they rise most years.

docs.title: Worked Example: Computing Per-Pupil Spending
docs.text:
An illustrative district reports the following for one year:

Item Amount Current spending (salaries, benefits, supplies, transportation, services) $180,000,000 Construction of a new middle school (capital outlay) $40,000,000 Enrollment 12,000 students

Per-pupil current spending excludes the construction cost:

\[ \text{per-pupil spending} = \frac{\$180{,}000{,}000}{12{,}000 \text{ students}} = \$15{,}000 \text{ per student} \]

Including the construction would give \( \$220{,}000{,}000 \div 12{,}000 \approx \$18{,}333 \), a misleading figure for comparing everyday costs, because a new building is a once-in-decades expense.

Now divide by the school year to get a daily figure. With 180 school days:

\[ \frac{\$15{,}000}{180 \text{ days}} \approx \$83 \text{ per student per day} \]

Keep that daily figure in mind. Later chapters compare it with the cost of interactive textbooks, which the course description describes as heading toward pennies per student per day, and with the tuition of private AI-first schools.

An average hides the spread

A common trap is treating one per-pupil number as "what a student costs." Averages blend students who need far more (special education, English learners) with students who need less, and they mix current spending with capital spending. When comparing two figures, first check that both use current spending and the same year.

docs.title: Putting the Building Blocks Together
docs.text:
You have now met 21 concepts, and they are not a list of unrelated vocabulary words. They depend on one another in a structure. Learning outcome depends on learning. Bloom's Taxonomy classifies learning outcomes, and higher-order thinking is defined by the taxonomy's top levels. Direct instruction requires a teacher, a classroom, and an idea of learning. Per-pupil spending only makes sense once you know what public school funding is.

This structure has a name in this book: a learning graph, a map of concepts in which each arrow points from a concept to a prerequisite it depends on. Chapter 9 explains learning graphs in detail. The map below shows the dependencies among this chapter's 21 concepts, taken directly from the book's own learning graph, and asks you to read it.

docs.title: Diagram: Building Blocks Concept Map
docs.text:
Building Blocks Concept Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: building-blocks-concept-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain which earlier concepts each Chapter 1 concept depends on by identifying its direct prerequisites in the chapter's concept map, correctly answering at least five of six prerequisite questions.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/chapter1-concept-map

Prerequisites: all 21 concepts defined in this chapter, and the meaning of a dependency arrow (an arrow points from a concept to a prerequisite it depends on), defined in the section "Putting the Building Blocks Together" above.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner answers six prerequisite questions by selecting nodes in the map. An answer is correct when the selected set exactly equals the direct-prerequisite set given in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Clicking nodes to read definitions is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) The concepts are independent vocabulary words. (2) Advanced-sounding concepts (Higher-Order Thinking) must have many prerequisites. (3) Arrows point from a prerequisite to what it enables; in this book they point from a concept to what it depends on.

Instructional Rationale: Explaining relationships is an Understand-level skill, shown here by locating each concept's prerequisites. Answering by selecting nodes in the actual graph forces the learner to read arrow direction correctly, which later chapters on learning graphs depend on.

Content:

Nodes (21), each with the one-sentence definition shown when the node is selected:

Node Definition shown Education The organized, intentional effort to help people acquire knowledge, skills, values, and ways of thinking. Learning A relatively lasting change in knowledge, skills, or understanding that results from experience. Student A person enrolled in a course of study at an educational institution. Teacher A professional whose job is to help students learn through planning, explaining, assessing, and feedback. School An institution a society sets up to provide education to a defined group of learners on a regular schedule. Curriculum The planned body of knowledge, skills, and experiences a school intends students to learn, and its sequence. Educational Technology Tools, devices, software, and media used to support teaching and learning, with the practices for using them well. Classroom The room, and the group of students and teacher within it, where scheduled instruction happens. School Day The daily schedule of periods, transitions, meals, and breaks during which students attend school. Public School Funding The system of revenues, mainly local, state, and federal taxes, that pays for public schools. Per-Pupil Spending Total annual spending on public schools divided by the number of students enrolled. Learning Outcome A specific, observable statement of what a learner will be able to do after instruction. Learning Gap The difference between what a student is expected to know and what the student actually knows. Bloom's Taxonomy A framework that classifies learning outcomes into six levels of cognitive work. Higher-Order Thinking The cognitive work of the top three Bloom levels: analyzing, evaluating, and creating. Formative Assessment Gathering evidence of learning during instruction and using it to adjust teaching and learning. Direct Instruction A teacher-led method of explaining, modeling, guided practice, and independent practice. Spaced Practice Spreading practice sessions over time instead of concentrating them in one session. Retrieval Practice Learning by actively recalling information from memory rather than rereading it. Student Agency The capacity and opportunity for students to make meaningful choices about their own learning. Self-Paced Learning An arrangement in which each student advances through material at their own speed.

Edges (20), each pointing from a concept to a prerequisite it depends on:

From (depends) To (prerequisite) Curriculum Education School Education Educational Technology Education Student Agency Student Student Agency Learning Self-Paced Learning Student Agency Learning Outcome Learning School Day School Public School Funding School Per-Pupil Spending Public School Funding Learning Gap Learning Outcome Classroom School Direct Instruction Teacher Direct Instruction Learning Direct Instruction Classroom Spaced Practice Learning Retrieval Practice Learning Bloom's Taxonomy Learning Outcome Higher-Order Thinking Bloom's Taxonomy Formative Assessment Learning Outcome

Six questions, in this order:

# Question Correct selection Why (shown as feedback) 1 Select every direct prerequisite of Per-Pupil Spending. Public School Funding You need to know where school money comes from before you can divide it per student. 2 Select every direct prerequisite of Higher-Order Thinking. Bloom's Taxonomy Higher-order thinking is defined as the top three levels of the taxonomy. 3 Select every direct prerequisite of Self-Paced Learning. Student Agency Letting a student control their pace is one form of giving them agency. 4 Select every direct prerequisite of Learning Gap. Learning Outcome A gap is measured against an expected outcome. 5 Select every direct prerequisite of Direct Instruction. Teacher, Learning, Classroom Direct instruction is a teacher leading a classroom toward learning; it needs all three. 6 Select every direct prerequisite of Formative Assessment. Learning Outcome Formative assessment checks progress toward a specific outcome.

Provenance: Nodes and edges are taken from docs/learning-graph/learning-graph.json in this repository, restricted to the 21 Chapter 1 concepts; copy the values listed here into the sim rather than reading the file at run time. Definitions come from the chapter prose.

Rules: Foundational nodes (Education, Learning, Student, Teacher) have no outgoing edges and must be visually distinguished as having no prerequisites. A question's answer is correct only when the selected set equals the correct set exactly (no missing and no extra nodes). The learner can zoom and reset the view with buttons; mouse-wheel zoom is disabled.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner explores the map, selecting nodes to read their definitions.
  2. The learner starts the quiz. Question 1 appears; the learner selects one or more nodes and submits.
  3. The sim marks the answer and highlights the correct prerequisite nodes and their edges.
  4. The learner continues through question 6, then sees the score.
  5. The learner should notice that Higher-Order Thinking has only one direct prerequisite even though it sounds advanced, and that four concepts have no prerequisites at all.

Feedback: Six questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct. [Why text]." Incorrect with missing nodes: "You're missing at least one prerequisite. Follow every arrow leaving [concept]." Incorrect with extra nodes: "At least one selected concept is not a direct prerequisite. Only count arrows that leave [concept] directly." After the second wrong attempt, the correct nodes are highlighted with the Why text. Score "n of 6" is shown at the end.

Starting State: The full map of 21 nodes and 20 edges is shown, with no node selected, and the prompt reads "Every concept in this chapter rests on others. Which ones?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that it covers 21 concepts, that arrows point from a concept to a prerequisite it depends on, that Learning Outcome depends on Learning, that Higher-Order Thinking is defined by Bloom's Taxonomy, that Direct Instruction requires a Teacher, a Classroom, and Learning, and that Per-Pupil Spending depends on Public School Funding.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
The vocabulary in this chapter describes a school system that works, often well, within a hard constraint: one teacher, one pace, many students, fixed time.

  • Education is the organized effort; learning is the lasting change inside the learner. Strong performance on today's test is not the same as learning.
  • A school does many jobs besides academic instruction, and any redesign of the school day must still do all of them.
  • Every student arrives at a different starting point, while a classroom gives one teacher less than two minutes per student per period for individual attention.
  • A curriculum exists in three versions (intended, enacted, attained), and precise learning outcomes with observable verbs are how you tell the three apart.
  • Bloom's Taxonomy classifies outcomes by the kind of thinking they ask for, and higher-order thinking (analyze, evaluate, create) depends on a strong base of the lower levels.
  • Direct instruction is effective for novices but paces the whole room together, which turns ordinary differences in readiness into learning gaps.
  • Self-paced learning and student agency answer the one-pace problem in different ways (speed versus choice) and both need structure to work.
  • Formative assessment uses evidence during learning to change what happens next; spaced practice and retrieval practice turn performance into lasting learning.
  • Educational technology has repeatedly been oversold when bolted onto an unchanged school day; it matters when it changes which learning job is done and by whom.
  • Public school funding comes from local, state, and federal sources, and per-pupil spending of roughly $15,000 a year, about $83 a school day in our example, is the baseline any new model will be compared against.

You can now describe how a school works

You just built the vocabulary to describe a traditional school day from the per-pupil budget down to a single hinge question — and to spot exactly where one pace for 28 students leaves learning on the table. Chapter 2 asks who has a stake in changing that, and why. One step at a time, together.

docs.title: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers how educators judge what works — evidence-based practice, randomized controlled trials, effect size, and case study methods — alongside the motivational side of learning: curiosity, boredom, engagement, and productive struggle. It also introduces the people involved in a school decision: parents, principals, administrators, and school boards. Readers finish able to weigh a claim about an educational intervention and name the stakeholders it affects.

docs.text:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning

docs.title: A Vendor, a Principal, and a Number
docs.text:
On a Tuesday in October, a sales representative visits Lincoln Middle School, the composite school where Maya from Chapter 1 is a seventh grader. The representative hands the principal, Ms. Okafor, a glossy brochure for an AI-assisted math program called MathPath. It says three things: "Effect size of 0.8," "94% of teachers love it," and "Evidence-based." The district is about to decide whether to buy it for every middle school.

Ms. Okafor has three problems at once. She needs to know whether those three claims mean anything. She needs to know whether a program that helps some students will actually engage Maya, who hides her confusion, and Jordan, who is bored. And she needs to know who has to be consulted before anything is bought: the teachers, the families, the district office, the school board.

This chapter gives you the vocabulary to follow her through all three problems. It has three parts: how to judge evidence, how motivation and engagement work, and who the stakeholders of a school decision are. It matters now because AI products will arrive in schools far faster than the research that evaluates them, and the people making the decisions will mostly be educators and board members, not statisticians.

Before you sign anything

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to read a vendor brochure the way a careful principal does, and say which of its claims you'd trust and which you'd test. You'll also know exactly who needs a seat at the table before a school adopts anything new. Let's find the balance between healthy skepticism and open-minded curiosity.

We start with the setting every example in this chapter lives inside.

docs.title: K-12 Education: The Setting
docs.text:
K-12 education is the span of publicly and privately provided schooling from kindergarten (usually age five) through twelfth grade (usually age seventeen or eighteen), roughly thirteen years of schooling. The "K" stands for kindergarten and the "12" for the final high school grade. In the United States it is commonly divided into three bands, though the boundaries differ by district.

Band Typical grades Typical ages Typical structure Elementary K–5 5–11 One teacher for most subjects; one classroom Middle 6–8 11–14 Subject teachers; periods; a bell schedule High 9–12 14–18 Subject teachers; credits toward graduation; electives

Almost every state requires children to attend school for part of this span, though the starting and ending ages vary. K-12 is also the scope of this book. We do not cover preschool, higher education, or corporate training. The reason to keep the scope narrow is that the decision-makers, the money, and the rules that govern K-12 schools differ sharply from those that govern a university.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Thirteen Years Add Up To
docs.text:
A student who attends school from kindergarten through twelfth grade spends, using the Chapter 1 figures of about 180 days a year and about 6.5 hours a day:

\[ 13 \text{ years} \times 180 \text{ days} = 2{,}340 \text{ days} \qquad 2{,}340 \times 6.5 \text{ hours} \approx 15{,}200 \text{ hours} \]

At the Chapter 1 per-pupil figure of about $15,600 a year, the public cost of those thirteen years is about \( 13 \times \$15{,}600 = \$202{,}800 \), or roughly $200,000 per student. Those two numbers, 15,200 hours and $200,000, frame every decision in this book. An idea that saves even ten percent of the hours or improves the use of the money is worth a serious look. An idea that costs more than it returns is not.

docs.title: Evidence-Based Practice: Judging What Works
docs.text:
When a salesperson says a program is "research-based" or "proven," what are they claiming? Often very little. This section defines the terms researchers and policymakers use to separate strong claims from weak ones.

Evidence-based practice is the use of the best available research evidence, combined with professional judgment and knowledge of the local students and setting, to decide what to do. Three parts matter: research evidence about what has worked elsewhere, professional judgment from teachers who know their students, and context such as the students' ages, languages, and prior knowledge. Drop any one of them and the approach fails. Research alone ignores the classroom in front of you. Judgment alone is a collection of habits that may never have been tested.

The phrase gained legal force in the United States through the Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) of 2015, which ties some federal school funds to the use of interventions backed by evidence. ESSA defines four levels of evidence, and the What Works Clearinghouse, run by the U.S. Department of Education's Institute of Education Sciences, reviews studies against standards of this kind. This book adds a fifth bin for claims that are not evidence of effect at all.

Level What the evidence looks like Plain-language meaning Strong At least one well-designed, well-implemented experimental study (random assignment) Students were randomly placed in groups, and the program group did better Moderate At least one well-designed quasi-experimental study (a comparison group, but no random assignment) A comparison group existed, but it was chosen, not drawn by lot Promising At least one well-designed correlational study with statistical controls for who chose the program Users did better after adjusting for obvious differences Demonstrates a rationale A logical explanation based on research, with an evaluation planned or under way A good reason to expect it to work, but no results yet No evidence of effect Testimonials, satisfaction surveys, usage counts, uncontrolled before-and-after gains Doesn't show that the program caused learning

A few things stand out. First, the ladder is about the design of the study, not the size of the claim. A modest effect found by random assignment is stronger evidence than a huge effect from a satisfaction survey. Second, the lowest bin is not a criticism of teachers' opinions, which matter for other reasons. It simply says an opinion is not a measurement of learning.

docs.title: Worked Example: Reading the MathPath Brochure
docs.text:
Return to the three claims in Ms. Okafor's brochure and assign each to a level.

Claim Level Why "94% of teachers love it" No evidence of effect A satisfaction survey says teachers like the program, not that students learned more "Evidence-based" Unknown until asked The label alone is not a study; the question is which study, of what design "Effect size of 0.8" Unknown until asked A size means nothing until you know how it was measured and compared

The right next step is not to reject MathPath but to ask three questions of any vendor: Who was compared with whom? How were they chosen? What was measured, and by whom? The next two sections explain why those questions matter.

Three questions for any vendor

Keep these on an index card: "Compared with whom? Chosen how? Measured by whom?" If the answer to the last one is "the vendor," ask for an independent study as well.

docs.title: Randomized Controlled Trials
docs.text:
A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is a study design in which participants are assigned by chance, like a coin flip, to either a treatment group that receives the intervention or a control group that does not, and the two groups are then compared on the same measure. The randomness is the whole point. If assignment is truly by chance, then on average the two groups start out alike in prior knowledge, motivation, family support, and every other factor, including factors nobody thought to measure. Any later difference is then much more likely to be caused by the intervention.

Compare this with letting students choose. In a school that offers an optional AI tutor, the students who sign up are likely to be more motivated, better organized, or have more supportive homes. If those students score higher, you cannot tell whether the tutor helped or whether motivated students would have done well anyway. This problem is called selection bias, and randomization is the main cure for it.

The most famous education RCT in the United States is Project STAR, run in Tennessee from 1985 to 1989. About 11,600 students in kindergarten through third grade were randomly assigned to small classes of 13 to 17 students or regular classes of 22 to 25, and the small classes produced modest but lasting benefits. RCTs are also now appearing in the AI-tutoring literature the course description mentions: the Turkish high school study that found open chatbot access harmed later exam scores, and a Nigerian after-school tutoring pilot with large gains, were both designed as randomized comparisons.

RCTs have limits. They are expensive, slow, and sometimes impossible: you cannot randomly assign children to different school funding levels. They tell you what happened on average in the studied setting, which may not match your school. And a poorly run RCT, with many students dropping out or the control group getting the treatment anyway, can be less trustworthy than its label suggests.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Pilot That Randomizes
docs.text:
Lincoln Middle has 280 seventh graders. Instead of buying MathPath for everyone, Ms. Okafor runs a six-week pilot. A coin flip, done by a computer, assigns 140 students to use MathPath for 30 minutes a day in addition to regular class, and 140 to continue as normal. All 280 take the same 50-point test at the start and again after six weeks. Suppose the results are:

Group Students Mean score at six weeks Standard deviation MathPath (treatment) 140 34 10 Regular class (control) 140 30 10

The treatment group scored four points higher. Is that a real effect or chance? If the groups were drawn by lot, the random wobble in the difference of two group averages is about

\[ 10 \times \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{140} + \tfrac{1}{140}} \approx 1.2 \text{ points}, \]

so a four-point gap is about three times larger than chance alone would usually produce. That makes a real effect likely. But how big is the effect, and is four points a lot? Answering that question is the job of effect size.

docs.title: Effect Size
docs.text:
Effect size is a standardized measure of how large the difference between two groups is, expressed in units of the spread of scores rather than in raw points. The most common form is Cohen's d: the difference between the two group averages divided by the pooled standard deviation. The standard deviation measures how widely students' scores vary around the average, so d tells you how many "typical spreads" the groups differ by.

\[ d = \frac{\bar{x}_{\text{treatment}} - \bar{x}_{\text{control}}}{s_{\text{pooled}}} \]

Standardizing is what lets you compare a 4-point gain on a 50-point test with a 40-point gain on a 500-point test. In the MathPath pilot, \( d = (34 - 30)/10 = 0.4 \).

To make d intuitive, translate it into a percentile. If scores are roughly bell-shaped, then at \( d = 0.4 \) the average treated student scores above about 66 percent of the control group. The table below summarizes a few reference points; each follows from the same bell-curve arithmetic.

Effect size d The average treated student scores higher than this share of the control group 0.0 50% 0.1 54% 0.2 58% 0.4 66% 0.5 69% 0.8 79%

Now the claim "effect size of 0.8" has a meaning: the average student on the program would outscore about four in five students who were not on it. That would be spectacular, and that is exactly why a skeptic should ask whether it is believable.

How big is "big"? Jacob Cohen suggested in 1988 that 0.2 is small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large, but he meant these as rough guides for lab psychology. In education, researchers have learned that real interventions, tested on standardized tests in real schools, rarely produce effects that large. Matthew Kraft's 2020 review of education studies suggests that for well-designed studies of standardized achievement, an effect below 0.05 is small, 0.05 to 0.20 is medium, and above 0.20 is large. By that standard, even an effect of 0.2 is a major result, and a claim of 0.8 should prompt questions about the study's design before celebration. John Hattie's widely cited syntheses use 0.40 as a "hinge point" for a worthwhile effect, but that number has drawn criticism because it mixes studies of very different designs and quality.

The sim below lets you see how much the two groups overlap at different effect sizes.

docs.title: Diagram: Effect Size Visualization
docs.text:
Run the Effect Size Visualization MicroSim fullscreen

Effect Size Visualization (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: effect-size-visualizer Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/statistics-course/sims/effect-size-visualizer/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/statistics-course/tree/main/docs/sims/effect-size-visualizer Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: interpret Learning Objective: The learner will interpret Cohen's d values from 0 to 2.0 by describing how much two score distributions overlap at each value.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.7557).

Significant is not the same as big

Notice that "is the effect real?" and "is the effect large?" are different questions. A huge study can find a real but tiny effect; a tiny study can find a large one by luck. Always ask for both the size and how the groups were formed.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is 0.8 Believable?
docs.text:
Suppose the MathPath brochure's 0.8 comes from a study. Walk through what you would ask:

  1. Design. Was assignment random? If students chose MathPath, selection bias could create a large "effect" with no learning gain at all.
  2. Outcome measure. Was the test the standard state test, or a test the vendor wrote about exactly the skills MathPath practices? A test written to match the program inflates effects.
  3. Time and size. A two-week pilot with 30 students may give a big number that does not hold up in 3,000 students over a year.
  4. Who ran it. An independent evaluator is more credible than the company's own team, which has a stake in the result.

The pilot at Lincoln Middle, with its random assignment, school-wide test, and independent scoring, would produce a number you can trust. That number, 0.4, is lower than 0.8, and it is still a strong result by Kraft's benchmarks.

docs.title: Case Study Method
docs.text:
An RCT answers "did it work, on average?" The case study method answers a different question: how and why did it work, or not work, in a particular place? A case study is an in-depth examination of one or a few real situations, such as a school, a classroom, or a district, using interviews, observation, documents, and data, with attention to the context that numbers leave out. The term also names a teaching method, used in business and law schools, in which students analyze a real case and argue about what to do. This book uses both senses: it studies cases, and it asks you to reason about them.

Cases are strong where RCTs are weak. A case can show that a program worked beautifully in one school because the principal protected teachers' time, and failed in another because the tablets arrived in January. It can surface problems nobody thought to measure. Its weakness is that one story does not prove a general rule: a vivid success may be an exception. The sound approach is to use both. The course description's stories of Alpha School, Unbound Academy, and the Los Angeles "Ed" chatbot are cases; the effect sizes in the research are the statistics; and a careful reader looks for where the two agree.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Case Study of the Pilot
docs.text:
After the MathPath pilot, Ms. Okafor asks a district researcher to do a short case study. The researcher interviews six teachers, observes four classes, and reads the usage logs. The findings:

  • What worked: Students who got stuck received a hint within seconds, and teachers could see on a dashboard who needed help.
  • What did not: In two classrooms the tablets were used only on Fridays, because teachers lacked planning time to use the dashboard.
  • Context: The classrooms with the largest gains had a teacher who stopped the lesson each day to address the most common error the dashboard showed.

The RCT said the program helped on average. The case study says the average hides a difference in how teachers used it. Both are needed to decide what to do next.

The tool below practices the central evaluation skill of this section: matching a claim to the level of evidence behind it.

docs.title: Diagram: Evidence Tier Claim Checker
docs.text:
Evidence Tier Claim Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: evidence-tier-claim-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge the strength of the evidence behind ten vendor claims by assigning each to one of five evidence levels, correctly placing at least eight of ten on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: evidence-based practice, randomized controlled trial, selection bias, the five evidence levels (Strong, Moderate, Promising, Demonstrates a rationale, No evidence of effect), all defined in the section "Evidence-Based Practice: Judging What Works" above.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 10 claims in one of five level bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A large sample makes a claim strong whatever the study design. (2) Teacher satisfaction is evidence of learning. (3) Any before-and-after gain shows the program worked.

Instructional Rationale: Judging is an Evaluate-level act: the learner must apply criteria (how groups were formed) to unfamiliar claims and commit to a verdict. Including a very large self-selected sample and a before-and-after gain forces the learner to rely on design, not on impressive-sounding numbers.

Content:

Five bins, each with its one-line definition shown on request:

Bin Definition shown Strong Random assignment, well designed and well carried out Moderate A comparison group, but no random assignment Promising A correlational study that adjusts for who chose the program Demonstrates a rationale A research-based reason to expect it to work; results not yet in No evidence of effect Testimonials, surveys, usage counts, uncontrolled before-and-after or self-selected comparisons

Ten claims about the fictional program "MathPath":

# Claim shown to the learner Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 "In a study where 1,200 students were randomly assigned to MathPath or a control group, the MathPath group gained 0.15 standard deviations more on the state test." Strong Random assignment and a standardized outcome measure. 2 "A district compared 800 MathPath students with 800 matched students who did not use it, matched on prior scores and demographics; MathPath students gained more." Moderate There is a comparison group, but it was chosen, not drawn by lot. 3 "Across 40 schools, students who used MathPath more hours scored higher, after statistical adjustment for prior scores and family income." Promising A correlational study with controls; it still cannot rule out unmeasured differences. 4 "MathPath's design is based on research about spaced and retrieval practice, and an independent evaluation is under way." Demonstrates a rationale A research-based reason to expect it to work, with results still to come. 5 "94% of teachers surveyed said they love MathPath." No evidence of effect A satisfaction survey does not measure learning. 6 "Students in one pilot classroom raised their average score by 12 points from fall to spring." No evidence of effect Students usually gain over a school year; with no comparison group the gain cannot be credited to the program. 7 "Among 12,000 students, those who chose to use the optional MathPath program scored higher than those who did not." No evidence of effect Students who choose a program differ from those who do not, and a large sample does not fix that. 8 "Two separate randomized trials in different states, with 2,000 students in total, found gains of 0.10 and 0.18 standard deviations." Strong Repeated random-assignment results strengthen the case. 9 "A state analysis compared the 30 schools that adopted MathPath with 30 similar schools that did not, using the same tests." Moderate A comparison group of similar schools, but not randomly formed. 10 "MathPath uses mastery learning, which has strong research support in general; no study of MathPath itself has been done." Demonstrates a rationale A sound reason to expect results, but no evidence yet about this product.

Provenance: The five levels follow the chapter section "Evidence-Based Practice: Judging What Works," which summarizes the Every Student Succeeds Act evidence tiers and adds one bin for non-evidence. The claims are illustrative, written for this chapter; the sim must label them "Fictional claims about a fictional program."

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct level, given in Content. A claim is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 10. Mastery is a score >= 8.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one claim at a time and sees the five bins.
  2. The learner places the claim in a bin and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place the claim again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 10 claims, the sim shows the score and lists any misplaced claims with their correct levels.
  5. The learner should notice that claim 7, with 12,000 students, sits in the lowest bin while claim 1, with 1,200, sits in the highest.

Feedback: 10 claims, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [level]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the claim counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 10" is shown. Final message for a score >= 8: "You can judge a claim by how its comparison was built." For a score < 8: "Review the level definitions and try again; the claims will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Claim 1 of the shuffled order is shown with five empty bins and the score "First-try correct: 0 of 10." The prompt reads "How strong is the evidence behind this claim?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names five evidence levels in the order Strong, Moderate, Promising, Demonstrates a rationale, No evidence of effect. The chapter states that a large sample does not fix self-selection and that satisfaction surveys do not measure learning. The mastery bar is 8 of 10.

docs.title: Prior Knowledge and Prerequisite Concepts
docs.text:
Evidence tells you whether something works on average. Learning, as Chapter 1 stressed, happens inside one learner at a time, and what that learner already knows shapes everything.

Prior knowledge is the set of facts, skills, concepts, and beliefs a learner already holds when they begin a new lesson. The educational psychologist David Ausubel wrote in 1968 that the single most important factor influencing learning is what the learner already knows, and that teachers should find this out and teach accordingly. That remains one of the best-supported ideas in the field, and it explains much of the learning gap you met in Chapter 1.

Prior knowledge has three effects. It enables new learning: a student who knows what a fraction is can learn to add fractions. It organizes memory: new facts attach to existing ones, which is why experts remember more of a new fact in their field than novices do. And it can mislead: prior knowledge sometimes includes wrong ideas. In a well-known 1987 documentary, A Private Universe, graduates and faculty at Harvard were asked why it is hot in summer and cold in winter, and many confidently explained that the Earth is closer to the Sun in summer, which is wrong. A teacher who does not find out about such beliefs may teach on top of them without correcting them.

A prerequisite concept is a concept that must be understood before another concept can be learned. Prior knowledge is what the student has; a prerequisite is what a given idea requires. A teacher's work is to compare the two. Prerequisites form chains, and the learning graph introduced in Chapter 1 and covered in depth in Chapter 9 is a map of those chains, with every arrow pointing from a concept to what it depends on.

docs.title: Worked Example: Maya's Missing Stair
docs.text:
Maya's difficulty with ratios in seventh grade traces back to a chain of prerequisites in mathematics. The table lists a simplified chain of eight concepts and what each depends on.

# Concept Depends directly on 1 Whole-number multiplication and division none 2 Fractions as parts of a whole none 3 Equivalent fractions 1, 2 4 Adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators 3 5 Multiplying and dividing fractions 1, 2 6 Ratios 3 7 Unit rates 5, 6 8 Proportional equations 7

Ms. Rivera sees that Maya fails unit-rate problems (concept 7). Reteaching unit rates again will not help if the gap lies earlier. A short diagnostic gives Maya a few problems on each concept. She passes concepts 1, 2, and 5 but fails concepts 3, 4, and 6. Failing 3 explains the other two: concepts 4 and 6 both depend on equivalent fractions. The problem is not in unit rates, or even ratios; it is two steps down, at equivalent fractions. This is why a diagnosis needs a map and not just a score.

The practical rule is this: the root gap is a failed concept all of whose own prerequisites passed. A failed concept whose prerequisites also failed is a symptom, not the cause. Fix the root gap and the dependent failures often resolve; reteach a symptom and nothing changes. The sim below lets you practice that diagnosis.

docs.title: Diagram: Prerequisite Chain Diagnosis
docs.text:
Prerequisite Chain Diagnosis

Type: graph-model sim-id: prerequisite-chain-diagnosis Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: attribute Learning Objective: The learner will attribute a student's failure on a target concept to its root gap by examining a prerequisite map and a set of pass/fail results, correctly identifying the root gap in at least four of five cases.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/learning-dependency-network

Prerequisites: prior knowledge, prerequisite concept, root gap, the meaning of a dependency arrow (all defined in the section "Prior Knowledge and Prerequisite Concepts" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 5 cases, the learner selects exactly one node as the root gap and submits it. A selection is correct when it matches the "Root gap" column in Content. Mastery is 4 of 5 correct. Selecting nodes to read their descriptions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The target concept the student failed is always the place to reteach. (2) Every failed concept needs reteaching. (3) A concept that failed must have a failed prerequisite.

Instructional Rationale: Attributing a failure to a cause requires reading structure, which here is the prerequisite map. Cases include a root gap at the target itself and cases with several dependent failures, so the learner cannot use a single shortcut.

Content:

Eight nodes, each with its name shown on the node and a one-sentence description shown when it is selected:

# Node Description shown 1 Whole-number multiplication and division Multiplying and dividing whole numbers fluently. 2 Fractions as parts of a whole Understanding a fraction as equal parts of one whole. 3 Equivalent fractions Recognizing that different fractions can name the same amount, such as 1/2 and 2/4. 4 Adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators Combining fractions after rewriting them with a common denominator. 5 Multiplying and dividing fractions Multiplying and dividing fractions, including by whole numbers. 6 Ratios Comparing two quantities, such as 3 apples for every 2 oranges. 7 Unit rates Finding the amount per one unit, such as price per ounce. 8 Proportional equations Writing and solving equations that relate two proportional quantities.

Nine arrows, each pointing from a concept to a prerequisite it depends on:

From (depends) To (prerequisite) 3 1 3 2 4 3 5 1 5 2 6 3 7 5 7 6 8 7

Five cases. Each shows a student's pass (P) or fail (F) result on every node, and the target concept the student failed in class:

Case Target N1 N2 N3 N4 N5 N6 N7 N8 Root gap Why (shown as feedback) 1 7 P P P P F P F F 5 Node 5 failed while both its prerequisites (1 and 2) passed; nodes 7 and 8 fail because they sit above node 5. 2 8 P P F F P F F F 3 Node 3 failed while its prerequisites (1 and 2) passed; nodes 4, 6, 7 and 8 fail because they depend on 3, directly or through 6. 3 4 P P P F P P P P 4 Node 4 failed while its only prerequisite (3) passed, so the gap is at the target itself. 4 8 P P P P P P F F 7 Node 7 failed while both its prerequisites (5 and 6) passed; node 8 fails because it depends on 7. 5 6 P F F F F F F F 2 Node 2 has no prerequisites and failed; every other failure lies above it.

Provenance: The map is the simplified fractions-to-proportions chain written for this chapter. The pass and fail results are illustrative, and the sim must label them "Illustrative student results."

Rules: The root gap in a case is the failed node whose direct prerequisites all passed (or that has none). Each case has exactly one root gap. The learner selects one node per case. Nodes with no prerequisites (1 and 2) are visually marked as having none. Zoom and reset are available by buttons; mouse-wheel zoom is disabled.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner explores the map, selecting nodes to read their descriptions.
  2. The learner starts the cases. For case 1, the map shows pass/fail marks on every node and highlights the target.
  3. The learner selects the node they judge to be the root gap and submits.

  5. The learner continues through case 5, then sees the score.

Feedback: 5 cases, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct. [Why text]." Incorrect, selected a failed node whose prerequisite also failed: "That node failed because something below it failed. Look for a failed node whose prerequisites all passed." Incorrect, selected a passed node: "That node passed, so it is not a gap." After the second wrong attempt, the root gap is highlighted with the Why text. Score "n of 5" is shown at the end.

Starting State: The full map of 8 nodes and 9 arrows is shown with no node selected, and the prompt reads "A student failed one concept. Where should we reteach?"
