Logs trip up almost everyone

If a log scale feels backwards at first, that's normal; most of us learned charts where equal steps mean equal amounts. You already read two kinds of scale in Chapter 1 when you compared minutes and dollars. Try the sim above with the slider on one value and watch which axis the line straightens on.

docs.title: Projecting the Trend
docs.text:
Now we can state the forecast and its logic.

Trend extrapolation is the practice of extending a pattern observed in past data into the future, on the assumption that the forces that produced the pattern will continue. It is the most common forecasting method, since it needs no theory, only a line. Its strength is that, over short spans, the future often resembles the recent past. Its weakness is that it fails exactly when the forces behind the pattern change, which is when the forecast matters most.

History offers both successes and failures. Moore's law, Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that the number of transistors on a chip doubles at a steady interval, which he revised in 1975 to about every two years, held for decades and shaped an entire industry. It also slowed as chips approached physical limits. Many other exponential-looking trends turned out to be the early part of an S-curve: growth that accelerates, then levels off as it runs into a ceiling. The adoption of any new technology follows an S-curve, with the exponential phase lasting until the market is saturated.

A planning window is the span of time over which a decision has to hold up: the years a purchase, schedule, or training commitment will be in use. Schools plan in windows of about three to five years. Device fleets are replaced every three to five years, textbook adoptions last five to seven, and a kindergartner who starts in 2026 graduates in 2039. A forecast is useful only to the extent it covers the planning window of the decision it informs.

The book's central projection is the three-to-four-year forecast: applying five-month doubling to the task horizon over the next three to four years. From a start of about 50 minutes in early 2025, the Chapter 4 arithmetic gives a horizon of roughly 122 hours after three years and 647 hours after four. These figures are central estimates, not promises; the next section shows how wide the honest range around them is.

docs.title: Worked Example: When Could AI Build a Textbook Chapter?
docs.text:
Suppose a skilled team needs about 40 hours of human working time to write one chapter of an interactive textbook with its simulations. When does the 50 percent horizon cross 40 hours, which is 2,400 minutes? Solve \( 50 \times 2^{t/5} = 2{,}400 \):

\[ 2^{t/5} = 48 \qquad \frac{t}{5} = \log_2 48 \approx 5.6 \qquad t \approx 28 \text{ months} \]

So on the central trend the horizon passes 40 hours about 28 months after early 2025, around mid-2027. But a 50 percent horizon means the system finishes such a chapter correctly only half the time. If reliable output requires the 80 percent horizon, which in Chapter 4's simple model is a quarter of the 50 percent horizon, the 50 percent horizon must reach 160 hours, or 9,600 minutes:

\[ 2^{t/5} = 192 \qquad \frac{t}{5} = \log_2 192 \approx 7.6 \qquad t \approx 38 \text{ months} \]

That is about three years, mid-2028. This is the reasoning behind the book's prediction that interactive textbooks will become cheap and widely available within three to four years: not a guess about "intelligence," but arithmetic on a measured trend with a stated reliability bar.

docs.title: Forecast Uncertainty
docs.text:
Forecast uncertainty is the range of outcomes a forecast could reasonably turn out to have, which grows the further into the future the forecast looks. A single number, such as "122 hours," conceals that range. An honest forecast gives a range and says what it depends on.

The main source of uncertainty in an exponential forecast is the doubling time, because it sits in the exponent. Using an illustrative range of four to six months around the five-month planning figure:

Doubling time Horizon after 36 months Horizon after 48 months 4 months about 427 hours about 3,413 hours 5 months about 122 hours about 647 hours 6 months about 53 hours about 213 hours 10 months (trend halves in speed) about 10 hours about 23 hours

A shift of one month either way moves the three-year answer by a factor of about two or three, and the two ends of the range, four and six months, differ by a factor of eight. A trend that slows to half speed produces a three-year horizon about twelve times smaller than the central one. These are the same arithmetic as the Chapter 4 formula, applied to different inputs, and they show why precision about the doubling time matters more than precision about the starting value.

Uncertainty has other sources too: the measurement itself (a preprint on one set of tasks), whether horizons on benchmark tasks match horizons on messy real-world work, and whether progress on the 50 percent horizon carries over to the reliability that matters.

Don't mistake a line for a law

A common trap is reading a trend line as a guarantee, in either direction: "it will certainly happen" or "it's obviously hype." Instead, ask what the line assumes, how far it extends past the data, and how much the answer changes if the doubling time shifts by a month. If the answer swings by a factor of eight, say so in the plan.

The sim below lets you try these sensitivities yourself.

docs.title: Diagram: Doubling Time Projection Calculator
docs.text:
Doubling Time Projection Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: doubling-time-projection-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate how many months a 50-minute task horizon takes to reach 40 hours for doubling times of 4, 5, and 6 months, to within one month, and describe how the answer changes with the doubling time.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/microsims/tree/main/docs/sims/projecting-ai

Prerequisites: exponential growth, doubling time, number of doublings, trend extrapolation, forecast uncertainty (all defined in the sections "Linear Versus Exponential Growth," "Projecting the Trend," and "Forecast Uncertainty" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the doubling time can be changed, the learner commits three answers using the stated number of doublings: the months to reach 40 hours for doubling times of 5, 4, and 6 months. An answer is correct when it is within ±1 month of the value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Moving the slider afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) A small change in doubling time makes only a small change in the date. (2) The time to reach a target is proportional to the target. (3) A forecast has one answer.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating time to a target from the number of doublings makes the multiplication of doubling time by doublings explicit. Committing to three calculations first, then exploring, shows the learner that a one-month change in doubling time moves the date by about five or six months.

Content:

Rule shown: the time to reach a target = (number of doublings needed) × (doubling time). The number of doublings needed is log base 2 of (target ÷ starting value). For a start of 50 minutes and a target of 40 hours (2,400 minutes), the target is 48 times the start, which needs about 5.6 doublings.

Inputs:

Input Min Max Step Default Unit Doubling time 3 12 1 5 months Target horizon 3 choices 40 hours

The three targets: 5 hours (6 times the start, about 2.6 doublings), 40 hours (48 times the start, about 5.6 doublings), and 160 hours (192 times the start, about 7.6 doublings).

Check values at the 40-hour target:

Doubling time (months) Months to reach 40 hours 4 22 5 28 6 34 10 56

Check values for other targets at a 5-month doubling time: 5 hours takes 13 months and 160 hours takes 38 months.

Provenance: The start value of 50 minutes and the formula come from the chapter and Chapter 4. The targets are illustrative. The sim must label its output "Illustrative projection, not a forecast."

Rules: Start value = 50 minutes. Number of doublings n = log2(target in minutes ÷ 50). Months to target = n × doubling time, rounded to the nearest whole month. Targets in minutes are 300, 2,400, and 9,600.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner is shown the number of doublings for the 40-hour target and answers the three questions (doubling times of 5, 4, and 6 months).
  2. The learner submits. The sim checks the answers and shows the 28, 22, and 34 months on a timeline.
  3. The learner moves the doubling time from 3 to 12 months and switches targets. The months to target update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that a one-month change in doubling time moves the date for the 40-hour target by about five or six months.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: about [value] months." Incorrect: "Multiply the number of doublings, 5.6, by the doubling time in months." After the second wrong attempt, the value and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The doubling time is locked at 5 months, the 40-hour target is selected, and the prompt reads "How many months until the horizon reaches 40 hours?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states a 50-minute start, targets of 40 hours (28 months at a 5-month doubling) and 160 hours (about 38 months), and sensitivities of 22 and 34 months for doubling times of 4 and 6 months.

docs.title: Limits to AI Growth
docs.text:
A trend is a statement about the past. What keeps it going, and what could stop it? This section defines the main factors.

Compute scaling is the practice of improving AI capability by using more computing power to train and run models. Epoch AI, a research group that tracks AI trends, has estimated that the computing power used to train the largest AI models has grown by roughly four to five times per year since around 2010. A large share of recent capability gains has come from this scaling, in combination with better algorithms and more data.

The limits to AI growth are the constraints that could slow the trend. Researchers point to several:

  • Money. Training the largest models now costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and each step costs more than the last.
  • Chips and power. Advanced chips are made by a small number of factories, and data centers need large amounts of electricity and grid connections.
  • Data. The supply of high-quality human-written text is finite, and some analyses suggest the best of it could be used up within years.
  • The gap between benchmarks and the world. Gains on tasks with clear right answers may not carry over to messy, open-ended work.
  • Reliability. Progress at the 50 percent horizon may not translate into the reliability needed to trust a system with a long task.
  • Regulation and trust. Laws, safety concerns, and public opinion can slow deployment even when the technology is ready.

None of these is certain to bind. Each is a reason the trend might bend, and each has an offsetting argument: algorithmic efficiency improves, synthetic data can supplement human text, and chips keep getting more efficient.

docs.title: AI Energy Use and Data Center Energy
docs.text:
AI energy use is the electricity consumed by training and running AI models, and data center energy is the electricity consumed by the large facilities that house the computers doing the work. Both matter because energy is one of the limits above and because a school's choice of AI tool has an environmental footprint.

The International Energy Agency estimated that data centers used roughly 1.5 percent of the world's electricity in 2024, and projected that their consumption could roughly double by 2030, with AI a main driver. A typical text exchange with a chatbot is estimated at a few tenths of a watt-hour, about the energy of a web search; generating images, video, and long agentic tasks use much more.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Energy of a Tutoring Year
docs.text:
Take the Chapter 4 tutoring session, about 40 exchanges, and assume 0.3 watt-hours per exchange, an illustrative figure.

\[ 40 \times 0.3 \text{ Wh} = 12 \text{ Wh per session} \]

For a class of 28 students, one session each per day for 180 days, the total is \( 28 \times 12 \times 180 = 60{,}480 \) watt-hours, or about 60 kilowatt-hours, less than one percent of what a typical U.S. household uses in a year (about 10,000 kilowatt-hours). Scaled to 50 million students it is about 108 gigawatt-hours, or about 0.1 terawatt-hours, about three hundredths of one percent of the data centers' 2024 total of about 415 terawatt-hours. Chatbot tutoring is therefore not an energy problem on its own. The picture changes if every student runs long agent tasks, generates video, or uses the largest models all day, which is one reason the course description's design uses AI mainly to write content once and serve it as ordinary web pages. Writing a chapter once and serving it to a million students costs about the same energy as one run, not a million.

docs.title: Falling AI Costs and Chatbots
docs.text:
Chapter 4 defined AI inference cost. Falling AI costs names the trend that the price of a given level of AI capability keeps dropping. The Stanford AI Index 2025 reported a more than 280-fold drop in the price of GPT-3.5-level performance in under two years, and analyses by Epoch AI found large but uneven declines across capability levels, from roughly tenfold to hundreds-fold per year. As with the horizon, two forces combine: the capability available at a fixed price rises, and the price of fixed capability falls.

A decline of ten times per year compounds. A yearly tutoring cost of $72, the Chapter 4 figure at the 2022 price, would become $7.20 after one year, $0.72 after two, and $0.07 after three, about a thousandfold in all. The same caveat holds: the fall applies to a fixed capability level, and the newest systems cost more.

A chatbot is a conversational interface to an AI system, usually an LLM, through which a person exchanges messages with it in natural language. A chatbot is a way of using a model, and it is the form in which most students and teachers first meet AI. It is also the basis of level 4 in the book's five-level model of intelligent textbooks (Chapter 6). Because a chatbot can answer almost anything, it is flexible, and because it answers fluently whether or not it is right, it is also risky.

docs.title: AI Hallucination and AI Literacy
docs.text:
AI hallucination is the generation by an AI system of content that is fluent and confident but false or unsupported, such as an invented fact, a fabricated quotation, or a citation to a paper that does not exist. It happens because an LLM generates likely-sounding text, and it has no built-in check on whether the statement is true. Rates vary widely by model and task, and independent leaderboards that test summarization have found rates from about one percent to over ten percent depending on the model, with higher rates on harder questions.

The consequences are not hypothetical. In 2023 a New York lawyer submitted a legal brief containing court cases that a chatbot had invented, and a federal judge sanctioned the lawyers involved. For students, a hallucinated quotation in an essay or a wrong step in a math explanation can be learned as fact.

There are partial remedies. A model can be grounded in a vetted source, so that it answers from a given document rather than from memory; it can be asked to cite its sources, which can then be checked; and a human can verify anything that matters. None eliminates the problem, so people need the skills to catch it.

AI literacy is the set of knowledge and skills that lets a person understand what AI systems are, use them effectively, evaluate their outputs critically, and recognize their risks and ethical implications. It is to AI what reading comprehension is to text: a skill that everyone needs, not only specialists. The European Union's AI Act, which began requiring organizations to ensure AI literacy among their staff in February 2025, and curriculum frameworks developed by the OECD and the European Commission for primary and secondary schools, treat it as a basic competence.

docs.title: Worked Example: A One-Hour "Verify It" Lesson
docs.text: A teacher gives students a short passage and an AI-written summary of it that contains six statements, two of which are wrong. Students mark each statement as supported by the passage or not supported, and find the sentence in the passage that proves each answer. After the activity students know three things from direct experience: the AI summary was mostly right, it was wrong in a confident tone, and the only way to tell was to check against the source. The sim below practices the same skill.

docs.title: Diagram: Verify the AI Summary
docs.text:
Verify the AI Summary

Type: microsim sim-id: verify-the-ai-summary Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of six statements in an AI-written summary is supported by a source passage, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: AI hallucination, grounding in a source, AI literacy (all defined in the section "AI Hallucination and AI Literacy" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner marks each of 6 statements as Supported or Not supported and submits it. A mark is correct when it matches the "Correct mark" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the passage is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A confident, fluent statement is probably correct. (2) A statement that sounds plausible is supported. (3) A summary that is mostly right can be trusted whole.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a statement requires the learner to compare it with a source, which is the central habit of AI literacy. Mixing statements that are correct, subtly changed, and invented shows that fluency gives no clue to accuracy.

Content:

Source passage shown in full (fictional, written for this chapter):

"Lincoln Middle School ran a six-week pilot of a math program with 280 seventh graders. A computer randomly assigned 140 students to use the program for 30 minutes a day and 140 to continue as normal. At the end of the pilot, the program group scored an average of 34 points on a 50-point test and the comparison group scored an average of 30. The standard deviation of scores was 10 points. Six teachers were interviewed. They said the dashboard was useful, but two teachers used the tablets only on Fridays."

Six statements in an AI-written summary:

# Statement Correct mark Why (shown as feedback) 1 The pilot involved 280 seventh graders. Supported The passage states 280 seventh graders. 2 Students were assigned to groups at random. Supported The passage says a computer randomly assigned them. 3 The program group scored 34 on average, four points above the comparison group. Supported The passage gives 34 and 30. 4 The pilot lasted a full semester. Not supported The passage says six weeks, not a semester. 5 All six teachers used the tablets every day. Not supported Two teachers used the tablets only on Fridays. 6 An independent university team ran the evaluation. Not supported The passage does not say who ran the evaluation.

Provenance: The passage is the Chapter 2 pilot rewritten as a short text. The statements are illustrative. The sim must label the passage and summary "Fictional, for practice."

Rules: Each statement has exactly one correct mark. A statement is scored on its first submitted mark only. The score counts first-attempt correct marks out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5. Missing information counts as Not supported.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the passage and the six statements.
  2. For each statement, the learner marks Supported or Not supported and submits. The sim marks it and shows the feedback and the matching sentence of the passage, if any.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may re-mark; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct mark and reason are shown.
  4. After all 6, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that statement 6 sounds reasonable but has no support in the passage.

Feedback: 6 statements, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [mark]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Look for a sentence in the passage that says this. [Why text]." After the second attempt the correct mark is revealed and the statement counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You checked the summary against its source." For a score < 5: "Reread the passage and try again."

Starting State: The passage and the first statement are shown, with the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the prompt "Does the passage support this statement?"

Chapter Anchors: The passage uses the Chapter 2 pilot figures: 280 students, 140 per group, 30 minutes a day, six weeks, averages of 34 and 30, standard deviation 10, and six teachers. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

docs.title: Planning Under Uncertainty
docs.text:
A forecast with a wide range still has to be turned into a decision. Planning under uncertainty is the practice of making decisions that remain sensible across a range of possible futures instead of betting on one. Several techniques are standard.

  • Scenarios. Describe two or three distinct futures, such as "trend continues," "trend halves," and "trend stalls," and test each decision against all of them.
  • No-regret moves. Prefer actions that pay off in every scenario, such as training teachers in AI literacy, tightening student data governance, and piloting mastery-based pacing.
  • Reversible decisions. Choose short contracts, pilots, and options that can be undone, and avoid long lock-in until the picture clears.
  • Trip-wires. Decide in advance which observations, such as a vendor's independent evaluation or a stalled horizon measurement, would change the plan.

Prediction assumptions are the conditions that must hold for a forecast to be right. Stating them is a discipline: it turns "AI will do X" into "AI will do X if these things stay true." For the book's three-to-four-year forecast the main assumptions are:

  1. The doubling trend of the task horizon continues at about five months.
  2. Gains on benchmark tasks carry over to real work.
  3. Reliability, not just the 50 percent horizon, improves enough to be trusted.
  4. The price per unit of capability keeps falling.
  5. Schools have the devices, connectivity, and trained staff to use the tools.
  6. Privacy law and public acceptance permit adoption.

A prediction failure scenario is a specific, described way a forecast could turn out wrong, used to test whether a plan survives it. Three for this book: the trend stalls (compute, energy, or data limits bind and the horizon grows slowly); the benchmarks mislead (horizons grow on test tasks but not on real classroom work); and the tools arrive but trust does not (privacy scandals or harm to students lead to bans). A plan that works only in the best case is not a plan.

The final term links the forecast to the book's purpose. AI prediction for schools is the specific forecast this book works from: that within about three to four years almost every student could have access to a free, high-quality, interactive, adaptive textbook, because AI will be able to author such textbooks at very low cost. It rests on the horizon arithmetic you saw above, together with falling costs. It is a prediction about content, which can be written once and then served cheaply, and not a prediction that each student will have a human-level private tutor.

Build the plan so it survives being wrong

Notice what makes a no-regret move: it is useful whether or not the forecast comes true. Teaching students to check AI outputs, protecting student data, and letting students move at their own pace are all worth doing even if AI progress stalls tomorrow. That is the test to apply to every item on a school's AI plan.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Three-Scenario Table for Lincoln Middle
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor brings the board a table that tests four decisions against three futures.

Decision Trend continues Trend halves Trend stalls Verdict Train all teachers in AI literacy Strongly useful Useful Still useful: students already use chatbots No-regret: do now Adopt a student data-governance policy Essential Essential Still required by law No-regret: do now Pilot self-paced math in one grade Early lessons Useful Useful: pacing helps regardless No-regret: do now Sign a five-year contract for one vendor's AI tutor Risky: better tools will arrive Uncertain Wasteful if the vendor fails Avoid: prefer one-year terms

The last row is the useful one. A long contract is a bet on one future, and the first three decisions are bets on all of them. This is the approach the book recommends and returns to in Chapters 20 and 21.

docs.title: Answering Mr. Alvarez and Mr. Dang
docs.text:
Mr. Alvarez asked why the line should keep going, and what to do if it does not. The honest answer has three parts. The line might keep going, because the forces behind it, more computing power, better methods, and falling costs, are still in play, and because past forecasts of AI progress have been wrong in both directions. It might not, because each of those forces has limits, and benchmark progress might not carry over to real work. And a school does not need to decide which: it needs a plan built on no-regret moves, short contracts, and stated trip-wires.

Mr. Dang's concern, that every earlier technology was oversold, deserves its own answer. The pattern from Chapter 3 is real: tools arrive, are absorbed into old routines, and underdeliver. What is different here is not that this time the promises are bigger, but that there is a measurement, imperfect and preliminary, that can be checked every few months, and one that has so far kept rising. A skeptic should watch the measurement.

The story has both sides. The benefit: if the trend holds, high-quality adaptive content could be cheap for every student, and teachers could be freed from routine work. The risks: a school that plans around a forecast that fails, spends heavily on tools that disappoint, and leaves students handing their thinking to systems that hallucinate. The response: no-regret moves, short commitments, and teaching students and staff to verify.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Linear growth adds a fixed amount per period and exponential growth a fixed factor; early data cannot tell them apart, but three years out they differ by a factor of about eighteen in our example.
  • A logarithmic scale gives equal distance to equal multiples; on a log-scale chart, constant doubling plots as a straight line, and distance counts doublings.
  • Trend extrapolation works until the forces behind the trend change; many exponentials turn out to be the early part of an S-curve.
  • A planning window of three to five years is how long a school decision has to hold up; the three-to-four-year forecast applies five-month doubling over that window.
  • On the central trend a 50 percent horizon passes 40 hours in about 28 months, and passes the 160 hours needed for an 80 percent horizon in about 38 months, which underlies the book's AI prediction for schools.
  • Forecast uncertainty is dominated by the doubling time: four months versus six months changes the three-year answer by a factor of eight.
  • Compute scaling powers the trend; the limits to AI growth include money, chips and power, data, the benchmark-to-world gap, reliability, and regulation.
  • AI energy use and data center energy are modest for chatbot tutoring (about 12 watt-hours per session, in our example) and larger for video and agent tasks.
  • Falling AI costs compound; a chatbot is the conversational way of using a model.
  • AI hallucination is fluent, confident falsehood, and AI literacy is the habit of checking against a source.
  • Planning under uncertainty means scenarios, no-regret moves, reversible decisions, and trip-wires, built on stated prediction assumptions and tested against a prediction failure scenario.

You can read the curve and its limits

You just learned to read a log-scale chart, project the five-month doubling over a planning window, state the assumptions behind it, and pick moves that survive being wrong. Chapter 6 turns from the forecast to the product: the five-level model that lets you say exactly what kind of intelligent textbook you're being sold. One step at a time, together.

docs.title: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks
Summary
docs.text: This chapter presents the book's central organizing idea: the five-level model of intelligent textbooks, adapted from the SAE J3016 levels for self-driving cars. It walks through static, interactive, adaptive, chatbot, and autonomous AI textbooks, and teaches readers to classify an existing textbook or AI product by its level. Readers finish able to place any learning product on the five-level scale and explain what distinguishes each level from its neighbors.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 4: Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies
  • Chapter 5: Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty

docs.title: Three Emails, Three Promises
docs.text:
On a single Monday, Ms. Okafor receives three emails from three vendors. The first offers an "AI-powered interactive textbook." The second sells an "adaptive, personalized learning platform." The third advertises an "autonomous AI textbook." Each comes with a demo link and a request for a meeting. The board wants to know which one to pilot and what to ask each vendor.

The difficulty is that all three phrases sound alike and may mean very different things. One product might be a PDF with a chat box. Another might be a carefully built set of simulations with no AI in it at all. A third might store detailed records of every student's mistakes. Without a precise vocabulary, a school cannot compare them, price them, or decide what privacy protection each one needs.

This chapter supplies that vocabulary. It presents the book's central framework, the five-level model of intelligent textbooks, and shows how to use it to cut through marketing language. Chapters 7 through 12 depend on it, since the cost, the privacy burden, and the guardrails all change from level to level.

One vocabulary for every vendor email

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to read any product brochure and say which of five levels it really sits at, what it will cost you in privacy, and what questions to ask. It's the single most useful tool in the book for a buyer. Let's find the balance between excitement about what's possible and precision about what's actually on offer.

docs.title: From Print Textbooks to PDFs
docs.text:
Every level in the model is defined against the ordinary textbook, so we begin there.

A textbook is a structured book of instructional content written to support a course, usually organizing a subject into chapters with explanations, examples, and exercises, and aligned to a curriculum (Chapter 1). Textbooks are the main instructional material in most classrooms, and for many students the textbook is the curriculum as they experience it.

A print textbook is a textbook published on paper. It is durable and needs no power or network, which is a real advantage. Its content is fixed at the time of printing, so errors persist until the next edition, and every reader gets exactly the same pages in the same order. K-12 districts typically adopt a print textbook for several years at a time.

A digital textbook is a textbook delivered electronically, to be read on a screen. The term covers a wide range, from a scan of a printed page to a rich web application. What makes a textbook "digital" is the delivery medium, not any new capability.

A PDF textbook is a digital textbook delivered as a PDF file, which reproduces the fixed layout of the printed page. It can be searched, bookmarked, and carried on a laptop, and it costs little to distribute. But it does not respond to the reader: it shows the same content in the same way to every student, whatever they do. A PDF is a print textbook on a screen.

An intelligent textbook is a textbook that uses software to go beyond fixed content: it responds to the learner through interactive elements, tracks and adapts to what the learner knows, converses about the material, or generates content. The word intelligent here does not mean that every intelligent textbook contains AI. Some of the most useful ones do their work with careful design and simple software. How much the textbook can do, and what it needs to know about the student to do it, is exactly what the five levels measure.

docs.title: Worked Example: What a PDF Cannot Do
docs.text: Maya opens her science textbook as a PDF. The PDF lets her search for the word "mitochondria," jump to a chapter from a bookmark, and zoom in on a diagram. It cannot change the diagram when she asks "what if the cell has no mitochondria?" It cannot notice that she read the chapter in four minutes and skipped the practice. It cannot give her a harder problem when the easy ones are done. All of these gaps arise because the PDF has no way to receive her actions and respond. Each of the higher levels adds one such capability.

docs.title: Classification Frameworks and Shared Vocabulary
docs.text:
A classification framework is a system for sorting things into a small number of named categories according to stated criteria, so that people can describe and compare them consistently. You have already met one: Bloom's Taxonomy of Chapter 1 sorts learning outcomes into six levels by the kind of thinking they demand. Others include the periodic table for chemical elements and the system that biologists use to classify living things.

A good classification framework creates a shared vocabulary: a common set of terms with agreed meanings that lets people from different groups talk about the same thing without misunderstanding. When a teacher, a principal, a vendor, and a board member all say "Level 3," they should mean the same thing. Without a shared vocabulary, a conversation about AI textbooks becomes a series of different people using the same words for different things.

The framework in this book is borrowed from a field that faced the same problem: self-driving cars.

docs.title: The SAE Levels: A Model from Self-Driving Cars
docs.text:
The SAE J3016 standard, published by SAE International (a professional association of engineers) beginning in 2014, is the document that defines the six levels of driving automation used throughout the automotive industry. It was written to solve a communication problem. Companies were describing their cars as "self-driving," "autopilot," or "autonomous" for systems with very different abilities, and drivers, regulators, and insurers could not tell them apart.

The levels of driving automation in J3016 run from Level 0 to Level 5, and they are defined by who is responsible for driving in each case.

SAE level Name Who drives Example 0 No driving automation The human does everything A car with only warning sounds 1 Driver assistance The human drives; the system helps with steering or speed Adaptive cruise control 2 Partial automation The system steers and manages speed; the human must watch at all times Lane-centering plus cruise control 3 Conditional automation The system drives in some conditions; the human must take over when asked A traffic-jam pilot that hands back control 4 High automation The system drives itself in a defined area; no human needed there A driverless taxi in a mapped city 5 Full automation The system drives anywhere a human could Not yet available

The standard has had three lasting effects, and they are the reasons this book borrows it. First, it gave the industry a shared vocabulary. Second, it supported graduated regulation: rules that become stricter as a system takes on more responsibility, such as a human supervision requirement at Level 2 and liability and safety-case requirements at higher levels, rather than one rule for all "self-driving" cars. Third, it set realistic expectations: it made clear that Level 5, full automation everywhere, remained a goal while Level 2 systems were already on the road, so that buyers could ask "which level?" before trusting a car.

The textbook model follows the same logic. It has five levels instead of six, and starts at static content instead of a human doing everything, but it keeps the key properties: levels are defined by what the system can do, higher levels shift responsibility from the human to the system, and an important threshold in the middle changes what rules apply. For cars that threshold is Level 3, where the system takes primary control and liability questions arise. For textbooks, it is also Level 3, where the system begins to track individual learning and privacy questions arise.

The sim below, reused from another book in this series, shows the two frameworks side by side.

Levels describe capability, not quality

Notice what the car levels measure: who is responsible for the driving, not how good the car is. A well-built Level 2 system can be safer than a sloppy Level 3 one. The same holds for textbooks: a level tells you what the product does and what it needs from the student, never whether it is any good.

docs.title: The Five Levels at a Glance
docs.text:
The five-level textbook model classifies intelligent textbooks into five levels by what the textbook can do and how much it needs to know about each student:

  1. Level 1, static textbooks: fixed content with no interactivity, like traditional print and PDF textbooks.
  2. Level 2, interactive textbooks: content that responds to the learner's actions, through simulations, quizzes, learning graphs, and recommended learning paths.
  3. Level 3, adaptive textbooks: content driven by each student's goals and progress, which requires storing student records.
  4. Level 4, chatbot textbooks: conversational tutoring through chatbots and large language models.
  5. Level 5, autonomous AI textbooks: real-time content generation and fully personalized instruction.

The model was proposed by Dan McCreary in a December 2025 paper, A Five-Level Classification Framework for Intelligent Textbooks: Lessons from Autonomous Vehicle Standards. As a preprint (Chapter 3), the paper had not yet been peer reviewed when this book was written, so treat the exact boundaries between levels as a proposal that may be refined, though the overall structure is easy to check against real products.

One rule makes classification workable: a product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers to students in use, not the highest one in its brochure. The sim below, reused from this book's tooling library, lets you explore the five levels before we look at each in turn.

Reused from the MicroSim catalog (WHAT match score 0.8163).

docs.title: Level 1: Static Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 1 static textbook is a textbook with fixed content and no response to the learner. Print and PDF textbooks are the standard examples. At most they add navigation aids, such as a table of contents, bookmarks, and text search, which help the reader move around but do not respond to what the reader does.

Level 1 is by far the most common level in use today. Its strengths are real: it is cheap to produce and copy, works everywhere, needs no student data, and raises no privacy questions. Its limits are the ones listed above: one pace, one path, no feedback.

docs.title: Level 2: Interactive Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 2 interactive textbook is a textbook whose content responds to the learner's actions: the learner changes something and the page changes in return. It does not need to know who the learner is, and it stores nothing about them between visits. Because it needs no student records, it carries essentially none of the privacy burden of the higher levels, which is what makes Level 2 the sweet spot of the book's low-cost design.

Four features characterize Level 2.

An embedded simulation, which this book calls a MicroSim, is a small interactive model inside the page, running in the browser with no server, in which the learner changes inputs and watches the result. The sims in this book, such as the effect-size visualizer of Chapter 2 and the task-horizon explorer of Chapter 4, are embedded simulations.

Self-check quizzes give immediate feedback on answers, using the idea from Chapter 2 that quick feedback prevents practicing mistakes.

A learning graph, covered in Chapter 9, maps each concept and the concepts it depends on. At Level 2 it is a fixed map the textbook author made, shared by every reader.

Path recommendation is a suggestion, based on the learning graph, of what concept to read or practice next, such as "you opened Ratios; first review Equivalent Fractions." At Level 2 the recommendation depends on what the learner says they know or what they clicked, within a single visit. It does not require a saved record of the learner.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Level 2 Page in Action
docs.text: A student opens a page on unit rates in a Level 2 textbook. She drags a slider for the price of a pack of juice and the bottle count, and the page recomputes the price per bottle. She answers a self-check question and is told immediately that she divided in the wrong order, with a hint. At the bottom the page says, "If equivalent fractions are shaky, try this review." Every other student who opens the page sees the same content. When she closes the browser, the page remembers nothing. The textbook responded to her, and it never needed to know her name.

docs.title: The Intelligent Textbook Movement and the Growth of Level 2
docs.text:
The intelligent textbook movement is the growing effort, from researchers, open-education authors, and developers, to build textbooks that go beyond static pages. Research workshops on intelligent textbooks have met alongside the major conferences on AI in education for several years, and the movement began in earnest in 2025, when AI tools made it practical for a single author to produce a complete interactive textbook.

The growth of Level 2 textbooks is the most visible result. Because a Level 2 textbook is made of ordinary web pages and small simulations, it costs little to host and nothing to copy, and AI authoring tools lower the cost of writing it. Dozens of open Level 2 textbooks, and hundreds of reusable MicroSims, now exist in the catalog that supports this book's own tooling, and the number is rising quickly. As Chapter 7 explains, this is the economic force that makes Level 2 content cheap and often free.

Check for the reset test

Here's a quick way to tell Level 2 from Level 3: change something on the page, then reload it. If the page forgets you, it's Level 2. If it remembers where you were, what you got wrong, or what you should do next, it's keeping a record about you, and that's Level 3.

docs.title: Level 3: Adaptive Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 3 adaptive textbook is a textbook that changes what it shows each student based on a stored record of that student's goals and progress. The defining step from Level 2 is memory about an individual: the system keeps a record of what each student has done and mastered and uses it to choose what comes next.

Two features define Level 3.

Progress tracking is the recording of what a student has read, attempted, and mastered over time, kept in a store tied to that student. It is the foundation of adaptation: without a record, nothing can adapt. Chapter 8 explains how a standard called xAPI and a Learning Record Store make this possible while keeping the data under the student's and family's control.

Student goal setting is the student's stating of what they want to achieve, such as passing a particular exam, mastering a unit by a date, or following an interest, which the system uses to shape the path. It builds on the student agency of Chapter 1 by giving the student a voice in the plan.

An adaptive textbook might use simple rules, such as "if the student scored below 80 percent on the last three questions, review the prerequisite," or a statistical model that estimates mastery. Neither requires a large language model. Adaptive math platforms existed long before ChatGPT, and by this model's definition they are Level 3.

Level 3 is the privacy inflection point. Below it, a textbook needs almost no student data. At Level 3 and above, it needs detailed learning histories, which brings in the privacy laws, the governance duties, and the checks for bias that Chapter 10 covers. This is the same step as the jump from Level 2 to Level 3 in the car model, where the system takes control and liability questions begin.

Personalization has a price in privacy

Here's the tradeoff at the heart of this book: the more a textbook adapts to a child, the more it has to know about that child. That is not a reason to avoid Level 3. It is a reason to decide, before adopting one, exactly what is kept, by whom, and for how long.

docs.title: Worked Example: What the Record Contains
docs.text:
After a month, the record for Maya in a Level 3 math textbook holds the following. The values are illustrative.

Item in the record Example value What the system does with it Goal "Be ready for the unit test on March 12" Plans backwards from the date Mastery of each concept Equivalent fractions: 40%; Ratios: 25% Sends her back to equivalent fractions Time on each page 4 minutes on unit rates Flags that she may have skipped the practice Errors made Divided in the wrong order, 6 times Selects practice on the specific mistake Last visit Yesterday, 7:40 p.m. Schedules a review of older material

Each row is useful, and each row is also personal data about a child. Ms. Okafor should ask for every item in this kind of table: What is stored? Who sees it? When is it deleted?

docs.title: Level 4: Chatbot Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 4 chatbot textbook is a textbook that adds a conversational AI, usually built on a large language model, which students can talk to about the material. The chatbot, defined in Chapter 5, can answer questions, rephrase an explanation, and respond to a student's own words, ideally by drawing on the textbook's content so that its answers match what the course teaches.

Conversational tutoring is instruction carried out through dialogue: the tutor asks questions, listens to the student's answers, gives hints, and adjusts its next question to the response. It imitates what a good human tutor does and is the reason one-to-one tutoring has been so effective in the research (Chapter 11). A well-designed conversational tutor does not hand over answers. It asks "what is the problem asking you to find?" and lets the student do the thinking, which is the hint ladder of Chapter 2.

A common example is Khan Academy's Khanmigo, launched in 2023 as a tutoring assistant layered on a platform that already tracked student progress. By this model's definitions it is a Level 4 chat tutor on top of a Level 3 platform. This classification is the book's reading of the product, and the vendor may describe it differently.

docs.title: Worked Example: Two Chat Tutors, Same Question
docs.text:
Maya types, "What's the price per bottle if 6 bottles cost $4.50?" Compare two Level 4 designs.

Answer-first tutor Hint-first tutor Reply "Divide $4.50 by 6. The answer is $0.75." "What is the problem asking you to find? Which number is the total, and which is the count?" Maya's reply "ok" "The total is $4.50 and the count is 6, so... divide?" Next move Moves to the next problem "Good. Which goes first, 4.50 or 6? Try it and tell me what you get." What Maya practiced Copying an answer Identifying the quantities and choosing the operation Risk She cannot repeat this on the test The tutor takes longer, and a frustrated student may give up

Both tutors are Level 4. The second is the one the evidence of Chapter 2 favors, and the Turkish high-school study the course description mentions found that this design difference mattered more than the power of the model. The remedy for the second design's risk is not to drop the hints but to add support: after two honest tries the tutor offers a worked example of a different problem.

Level 4 adds the new risks of Chapter 5: hallucination, and students asking for answers instead of thinking. It also adds a per-conversation computing cost. It needs guardrails: hint-first behavior, limits on age and topic, and logs that teachers can review. Chapter 12 develops these.

docs.title: Level 5: Autonomous AI Textbooks
docs.text:
A Level 5 autonomous textbook is a textbook that the AI generates and adapts for each student on its own, in real time, without a human author creating the content in advance. Where a Level 4 chatbot answers questions about a textbook someone wrote, a Level 5 system writes the textbook itself for the student in front of it.

Two features define Level 5.

Real-time content generation is the creation of explanations, examples, exercises, simulations, and assessments at the moment a student needs them, rather than their selection from a library prepared in advance.

Full personalization is adaptation of the content along every relevant dimension at once: the student's goals, prior knowledge, pace, interests, language, reading level, and accessibility needs. A Level 3 textbook changes the order of prepared content; a fully personalized Level 5 textbook changes the content itself.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Level 5 Lesson for Maya
docs.text:
Suppose Maya's record says she is weak on equivalent fractions, loves drawing, and reads two grades above level. A Level 3 textbook would select the prepared equivalent-fractions lesson from a library. A Level 5 system would instead write one: an explanation that uses the area of drawn tiles, since she likes drawing, at her reading level, with six new practice problems built around her recent errors, and a short simulation made on the spot to let her slide a fraction bar. No human wrote that lesson, and no human has read it before she does. The benefit is a lesson no library could contain. The risk is that nobody has checked it. If the explanation has a small error, Maya learns the error. That is why the safeguard table below puts human review of generated lessons first at Level 5.

Level 5 is where the arithmetic of Chapter 5 matters. Writing and checking a chapter-sized lesson with simulations takes tens of hours of human work, so a system that could do it reliably needs a task horizon well beyond one day at high reliability. On the book's central trend that point is about three years away, and the doubts of Chapter 5 apply fully. Level 5 also has the largest verification problem: when no one has reviewed the content in advance, someone has to ensure it is accurate, appropriate, and free of bias.

The table summarizes the five levels. Each row restates what you have just read; use it as a reference.

Level Name What it adds What it needs to know about the student Main new risk 1 Static Nothing beyond fixed content Nothing One pace for everyone 2 Interactive Responds to actions: simulations, quizzes, graph, paths Nothing stored Poorly built or inaccurate simulations 3 Adaptive Adapts to goals and progress A stored record of each student Privacy, bias, data breaches 4 Chatbot Conversation about the material The record plus the conversation Hallucination; answers instead of thinking 5 Autonomous Generates the textbook itself per student Everything above, in real time Unreviewed content; loss of human oversight

docs.title: Levels 3 to 5 on the Horizon and the Adoption Timeline
docs.text:
A level adoption timeline is an estimate of when products at each level become available and widely used. The book's prediction (Chapter 5) is that within three to four years almost every student could have access to a free, high-quality interactive textbook. Level 2 textbooks are already being published in growing numbers, and Levels 3 to 5 on the horizon describes the rest: levels that exist in early form or in the lab and are not yet routine.

Level Status as this book is written What would have to be true for wide adoption 1 Dominant Already widespread 2 Growing quickly; often free Authors and schools adopt open Level 2 textbooks 3 Available in adaptive platforms, mostly commercial Privacy governance and standards such as xAPI become routine 4 Early products; fast-moving Guardrails and independent evidence of benefit 5 Not yet reliable Long-task reliability, content verification, and public trust

On the central trend of Chapter 5, the horizon needed to write and check a lesson at 80 percent reliability is reached around mid-2028, which would make Level 5 technically plausible about three years out, with trust and regulation likely to arrive later. This is a projection with all the caveats of the last chapter, not a schedule.

docs.title: Diagram: Product Level Classifier
docs.text:
Product Level Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: product-level-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge the level of eight fictional learning products by assigning each the highest defining capability it delivers, and will identify whether the vendor's claimed level is an overclaim, accurate, or an underclaim, correctly assigning at least seven of eight levels on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the five levels and their defining capabilities, the rule that a product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers, vendor level claim, AI-powered marketing claim (all defined in the sections on the five levels and below).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 products, the learner assigns a level from 1 to 5 and submits it. An assignment is correct when it equals the "Actual level" in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) "AI-powered" means a high level. (2) An adaptive textbook must use a large language model. (3) A chat box added to a static book makes it autonomous.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a claim requires the learner to compare a described set of features with the level definitions. Including a no-AI adaptive product, an underclaim, and an overclaim based on "personalized" or "autonomous" wording makes the learner apply the definition, not the marketing language.

Content:

The level definitions, shown on request:

Level Defining capability 1 Fixed content; no response to the learner 2 Responds to the learner's actions; stores nothing about the learner 3 Adapts using a stored record of each student's goals and progress 4 Adds conversational tutoring about the material 5 Generates the textbook content itself for each student in real time

Eight fictional products:

# Product and description shown Vendor's claimed level Actual level Why (shown as feedback) 1 ClearPage Digital Edition: a PDF textbook with bookmarks, searchable text, and a hyperlinked glossary. Marketed as an "AI-powered interactive textbook." 2 1 Bookmarks, search, and links do not respond to what the learner does; the content is fixed. 2 SimBook Physics: a web textbook with 20 embedded simulations where students move sliders, and self-check quizzes with immediate feedback. Every student sees the same pages and nothing is saved. Marketed as "interactive." 2 2 It responds to actions and stores nothing about the learner. 3 PathFinder Biology: SimBook-style pages plus a concept map that recommends the next section from what the student clicks during the visit. No accounts and no records. Marketed as "personalized learning." 3 2 Recommending a path from a single visit's clicks is Level 2; nothing is stored about the student. 4 AdaptiveMath: student accounts store every answer, and software chooses the next problem using fixed rules based on the student's mastery record. No language model. Marketed as "AI-powered adaptive learning." 3 3 It adapts from a stored record, which is Level 3; no language model is needed. 5 TutorBook: AdaptiveMath's features plus a chat window where a language model answers questions about the lesson, drawing on the textbook, with a hints-first rule. Marketed as "Level 4." 4 4 It adds conversational tutoring on top of the adaptive record. 6 WriteAssist: TutorBook's features, and the chat can also write a new practice problem when asked. The sequence of lessons is still the authors' fixed chapters. Marketed as "fully autonomous." 5 4 The textbook itself is not generated for each student; extra practice problems do not make it Level 5. 7 InstantText: each night the system reads each student's record and writes the next day's lesson text, examples, and exercises for that student; teachers may review them. Marketed as "Level 5." 5 5 It generates the textbook content itself for each student. 8 FlashPro: a flashcard app with a fixed deck. It stores each user's responses and schedules the next card from them. Marketed as "interactive." 2 3 It adapts from a stored record, so it is Level 3 with the privacy duties that come with it.

Provenance: The level definitions follow the chapter section "The Five Levels at a Glance." The products are fictional, written for this chapter; the sim must label them "Fictional products."

Rules: Each product has exactly one actual level, given in Content. A product is scored on its first submitted level only. After the assignment is revealed, the sim states "Overclaim" when the claimed level is greater than the actual level, "Accurate" when equal, and "Underclaim" when less. The score counts first-attempt correct levels out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one product description and the vendor's claimed level.
  2. The learner assigns a level from 1 to 5 and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text and the overclaim, accurate, or underclaim label.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may assign again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 products, the sim shows the score and a summary of how many claims were overclaims, accurate, and underclaims.
  5. The learner should notice that three of the eight claims overclaim, one underclaims, and one product with no AI model is classed at Level 3.

Feedback: 8 products, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: Level [n]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the product counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can see past the marketing to the level." For a score < 7: "Review the five definitions and try again; the products will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Product 1 of the shuffled order is shown with its description and claimed level, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "What level is this product, really?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that a product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers to students in use. The chapter's table gives the same five definitions. Three claims overclaim (products 1, 3, 6), one underclaims (product 8), and four are accurate. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Using the Levels to Evaluate Products and Claims
docs.text:
The levels become a working tool when you apply them to real products and real marketing. This section defines the terms used in that work.

Level classification is the act of assigning a product to one of the five levels according to the capabilities it actually delivers. Product level assessment is the fuller process a school follows to do so, and it has four steps: gather the product's documentation and a demonstration; test what the product does for students, not what the brochure says; identify the highest defining capability delivered; and record what student data it needs at that level. The checklist for a product level assessment asks:

  1. Does the product do anything but show fixed content? If not, it is Level 1.
  2. Does it respond to the learner's actions on the page? If so, it is at least Level 2.
  3. Does it keep a record of each student and change what it shows from that record? If so, it is at least Level 3.
  4. Can a student hold an open conversation with it about the material? If so, it is at least Level 4.
  5. Does it generate the textbook content itself, for each student, in real time? If so, it is Level 5.

Level terminology precision is the discipline of using the level names exactly as defined, so that a claim of "Level 3" means one thing wherever it is made. Precision protects buyers, and it matters because the common marketing words do not map to levels.

AI-powered marketing claims are product descriptions that use "AI-powered," "intelligent," "personalized," or "adaptive" without saying what the system does or what data it uses. They are common and uninformative. "AI-powered" can describe a PDF with a chat box, a simple adaptive scheduler with no AI model, or a fully generative system. Because the level depends on capability and not on whether an AI model is inside, "AI-powered" is neither necessary nor sufficient for any level.

A vendor level claim is a vendor's statement of the level of its own product. It is a self-report in the sense of Chapter 3: the vendor has an interest in the claim. The right response is not to reject it but to test it using the product level assessment, and to ask for a demonstration of each defining capability. The usual error is an overclaim, in which a vendor states a level above what the product delivers, and the sim above gave you practice spotting them. An underclaim, in which a product delivers more than it admits, matters too, because a vendor that does not realize it stores student records may also not be protecting them.

'AI-powered' is not a level

A common trap is accepting "AI-powered" or "personalized" as if it described capability. Instead, ask four things: what does it do for the student, using what data, stored where, and for how long? The answers place the product on the ladder and tell you what protections it needs.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Three Emails
docs.text:
Return to Ms. Okafor's three emails and apply the checklist after a demonstration of each.

Email says What the demo shows Highest capability delivered Level What to ask next "AI-powered interactive textbook" Web pages with simulations and quizzes; no logins Responds to actions; stores nothing 2 Are the simulations accurate and accessible? Who reviews them? "Adaptive, personalized learning platform" Student accounts; software picks the next problem from past answers; no chat Adapts from a stored record 3 What is stored, where, for how long, and has it been audited for bias? "Autonomous AI textbook" A chat box beside fixed chapters; the same chapter order for everyone Conversation about fixed content 4 How are hallucinations handled? Does it give hints or answers? Is the log reviewable?

None of the three is the highest-level claim the marketing suggested, and the third is two levels below its claim. The framework did not reject any of them. It told Ms. Okafor which questions to ask each one.

docs.title: Graduated Regulation and Level-Specific Policy
docs.text:
The SAE standard supported graduated regulation: rules that get stricter as a system takes on more responsibility. The same approach suits textbooks, because the risks change from level to level. A rule strict enough for Level 5 is wasteful at Level 1, and a rule written for Level 1 is dangerous at Level 5.

A level-specific policy is a school or district policy that sets different requirements for products at different levels. It is the practical result of the model. For example, a policy might say that any product at Level 3 or above must pass a privacy and data-governance review before use. This book recommends the following minimum safeguards. They are recommended practice, not legal requirements, and the real legal duties, such as FERPA and COPPA, are the subject of Chapter 10.

Safeguard First required at Reason Accessibility check of every page (screen reader, keyboard) Level 1 Every student must be able to use the product Independent accuracy check of simulations by a subject expert Level 2 Interactive models can mislead if they are wrong Review of how student records are stored, who sees them, and when they are deleted Level 3 The product now holds personal data Parent notice and consent process for collecting student learning data Level 3 Families have a right to know and to decide Bias audit of how the system chooses next steps for different groups Level 3 Adaptive choices can treat groups unequally Hint-first rules and logging for the chat tutor, reviewed weekly Level 4 Chat can give answers and can hallucinate Age limit and supervision rules for open-ended chat Level 4 Open conversation with minors needs boundaries Human review of AI-generated lessons before students see them Level 5 No author has checked the content in advance

Each safeguard keeps applying at higher levels, so a Level 4 product needs the Level 1, 2, and 3 safeguards as well.

docs.title: Diagram: Level-Specific Safeguard Matcher
docs.text:
Level-Specific Safeguard Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: level-specific-safeguard-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the level-specific policy by choosing the lowest level at which each of eight safeguards should first be required, correctly matching at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the five levels, level-specific policy, graduated regulation (all defined in the chapter sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 safeguards, the learner chooses a level from 1 to 5 and submits it. A choice is correct when it equals the "First required at" level in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) All safeguards should apply at every level from the start. (2) Privacy review is needed only for chatbots. (3) A product with no AI model needs no data governance.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a graduated policy means matching a risk to the capability that first creates it. Items such as the privacy review, which first applies to a product with no AI model, force the learner to link safeguards to capability, not to the amount of AI.

Content:

Eight safeguards:

# Safeguard shown to the learner First required at Why (shown as feedback) 1 Accessibility check of every page for screen readers and keyboard use 1 Every student must be able to use any textbook, whatever its level. 2 Independent accuracy check of the simulations by a subject expert 2 Interactive models first appear at Level 2 and can mislead if they are wrong. 3 Review of how student records are stored, who sees them, and when they are deleted 3 Level 3 is the first level that keeps records about individual students. 4 Parent notice and consent process for collecting student learning data 3 Collecting individual learning data begins at Level 3. 5 Bias audit of how the system chooses next steps for different groups of students 3 The system first makes individualized choices at Level 3. 6 Hint-first rules and weekly review of the chat tutor's logs 4 Open conversation first appears at Level 4. 7 Age limit and supervision rules for open-ended chat 4 Open conversation with minors first appears at Level 4. 8 Human review of AI-generated lessons before students see them 5 Content is first generated without an author's prior review at Level 5.

Provenance: The safeguards and levels follow the chapter section "Graduated Regulation and Level-Specific Policy" and are recommended practice written for this book, not legal requirements. The sim must say so.

Rules: Each safeguard has exactly one correct first-required level, given in Content. A safeguard is scored on its first submitted choice only. The score counts first-attempt correct choices out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7. After each answer the sim states that the safeguard also applies to every higher level.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one safeguard at a time and the five levels.
  2. The learner chooses the lowest level at which it should first be required and submits. The sim marks it and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8, the sim shows the score and a stacked view of the safeguards required at each level.
  5. The learner should notice that three safeguards first apply at Level 3, more than at any other level, and that none depends on whether a product contains an AI model.

Feedback: 8 safeguards, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: Level [n]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the item counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can match safeguards to levels." For a score < 7: "Review where each risk first appears and try again."

Starting State: Safeguard 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the five levels, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "At what level should this first be required?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's safeguard table lists the same eight safeguards at levels 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, and 5. The chapter states that each safeguard keeps applying at higher levels. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Setting Realistic Expectations
docs.text:
The last idea borrowed from the SAE standard is realistic expectations: making clear what each level can and cannot do today, so that buyers neither expect too much nor dismiss what works. A Level 2 textbook is not a tutor, and a Level 4 chatbot is not a trained teacher. Equally, a school that dismisses Level 2 as "just web pages" misses the best value for money in the model.

A useful summary for a school leader is to match the level to the job. Level 2 is excellent for explaining ideas, practicing skills with feedback, and letting students explore simulations, at very low cost and with no privacy burden. Level 3 earns its added burden when a school needs to track mastery and personalize pacing at scale. Level 4 adds the most when a student is stuck and needs a patient conversation, provided guardrails are in place. Level 5 is a promising direction that should be watched, tested in small pilots, and independently evaluated before anyone relies on it.

Five levels, one question at a time

If five levels and thirty-odd terms feel like a lot, start with one habit: for any product, ask "what does it do, using what data?" You already used a simpler version of that question in Chapter 2 when you asked "compared with whom, chosen how?" Everything else in this chapter hangs off that one question.

docs.title: Back to the Three Emails
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor now has a plan. She replied to each vendor with the same four questions: what does your product do for the student, using what data, stored where, and for how long? She asked for a demonstration of each defining capability, and she told the vendors she would classify the product herself. The Level 2 vendor needed nothing further except an accessibility check. The Level 3 vendor was invited to a privacy review. The "autonomous" vendor, whose product turned out to be a Level 4 chat tutor, was asked about its hallucination controls and given a pilot, not a district contract.

The story shows both sides. The benefit is clear: the levels let a school buy the right thing, at the right price, with the right protections, and avoid paying a Level 4 price for a Level 1 product. The risk is that a framework can create false confidence: a level is a statement about capability, not quality, and a product can sit at any level and still be a poor one. The response is to treat the level as the first question and the independent evidence of Chapter 2 as the second.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A textbook can be print, digital, or PDF; a PDF textbook is a print textbook on a screen, with fixed content for every reader.
  • An intelligent textbook uses software to respond, adapt, converse, or generate; it does not have to contain AI.
  • A classification framework creates a shared vocabulary; the SAE J3016 standard and its levels of driving automation gave cars a shared vocabulary, graduated regulation, and realistic expectations, and the textbook model borrows all three.
  • The five-level textbook model: Level 1 static, Level 2 interactive, Level 3 adaptive, Level 4 chatbot, Level 5 autonomous. A product's level is the highest defining capability it actually delivers.
  • Level 2 adds embedded simulations, self-check quizzes, learning graphs, and path recommendation, with nothing stored about the student; the intelligent textbook movement and the growth of Level 2 textbooks make it cheap and often free.
  • Level 3 adds progress tracking and student goal setting, and is the privacy inflection point because it keeps records about individuals.
  • Level 4 adds conversational tutoring through a chatbot; Level 5 adds real-time content generation and full personalization.
  • The level adoption timeline has Levels 3 to 5 on the horizon, with Level 5 plausible technically around three years out on the central trend but dependent on reliability and trust.
  • Apply the four steps of product level assessment; level terminology precision matters because AI-powered marketing claims say nothing about level, and a vendor level claim is a self-report to be tested.
  • Level-specific policy matches safeguards to the level where each risk first appears: accessibility at Level 1, simulation accuracy at Level 2, records and bias audits at Level 3, chat guardrails at Level 4, human review of generated lessons at Level 5.

You can place any product on the ladder

You just learned all five levels, the logic borrowed from self-driving cars, and the four-step assessment that sees through "AI-powered." That's the book's central tool, and everything from here builds on it. Chapter 7 asks what each level costs, and why Level 2 is heading toward free. One step at a time, together.

docs.title: Content Economics and Open Educational Resources
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the economics behind falling content-creation costs: open educational resources, open licenses, the OpenBook QR Score, content commoditization, and how publisher business models are changing as AI makes level 1 and level 2 content cheap to produce. Readers finish able to use the OpenBook QR Score to compare two open textbooks and explain why AI is commoditizing basic textbook content.

docs.text:
