docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 4: Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies
  • Chapter 5: Projecting AI Growth: Doubling Curves, Limits, and Uncertainty
  • Chapter 6: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks

docs.title: "What Will It Cost Per Student?"
docs.text:
At the district's budget meeting, the finance director, Mr. Patel, asks the question every board member eventually asks: "Fine, it's a good idea. What will it cost per student, per year, all in?" Behind him sits a binder with a $900,000 proposal from a publisher for a district-wide digital math program, and beside it a librarian's printout of a free open textbook that covers the same grades.

The two items on the table are not obviously comparable. One is a product with a price. The other is free, and nobody can say what "free" leaves out. To answer Mr. Patel, a school leader needs to understand three things: why content that once cost a publisher a great deal to produce is becoming cheap, what makes a free textbook good and reusable, and where the money goes at each of the five levels of Chapter 6.

The answer is more surprising than "it's all free." Content is becoming nearly free, but devices, teacher training, and data protection are not, and the biggest costs in a digital classroom are often the ones that never appear on a software invoice.

Follow the money, not the hype

This chapter lets you answer a finance director with numbers: what content costs to make, what a free textbook really offers, and what each level of textbook costs per student. You'll also learn to score a free textbook for quality and reusability in a few minutes. Let's find the balance between the savings that are real and the costs that hide.

docs.title: Why Textbook Content Costs What It Does
docs.text:
A textbook publisher is a company that commissions, edits, produces, markets, and distributes textbooks and related materials. The large publishers serving U.S. schools and colleges, such as Pearson, McGraw Hill, Cengage, and Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, grew over many decades by solving a hard problem: assembling expert authors, editors, designers, reviewers, and a sales force to put a reliable book in every classroom.

Content creation cost is the total cost of producing a textbook's content before a single copy is sold: author and subject-expert time, editing, fact-checking and review, design and illustration, simulations and assessments, accessibility work, and production. For a traditional textbook this cost is large and mostly up-front, which is why publishers needed to sell many copies at a high price to recover it. After the book is finished, producing one more copy costs almost nothing in digital form, so the economics are those of fixed cost: the first copy is expensive, and every later copy is nearly free.

A publisher business model is the way a publisher earns money from that content. The classic model is to sell a new edition every few years at a high price, rely on the fact that the person who chooses the book (a professor or a district) is not the person who pays (a student or a taxpayer), and sell updated editions so that used copies lose value. Later models added digital subscriptions, bundled "inclusive access" fees charged with tuition, and adaptive homework platforms sold alongside the book.

Textbook price is what the buyer pays. The College Board estimates that the average undergraduate's annual budget for books and supplies is about $1,300, a figure that has made textbook cost a long-running political issue in higher education. In K-12, districts pay, usually through adoption cycles of five to seven years, and the cost is part of the per-pupil spending of Chapter 1.

docs.title: Worked Example: Anatomy of a Textbook's Cost
docs.text:
The table gives an illustrative breakdown for one chapter of a traditional textbook with its simulations and assessments, using round numbers chosen to show where the effort goes. The hours and hourly cost are assumptions, not industry data.

Task Hours of skilled work per chapter Cost at $50 per hour Drafting the text 30 $1,500 Designing and building the simulations 25 $1,250 Writing practice questions and assessments 10 $500 Expert review and fact-checking 8 $400 Editing, accessibility, and production 7 $350 Total 80 $4,000

For a 20-chapter book the content cost in this illustration is about $80,000, before marketing and sales. Notice that the largest items, drafting and building simulations, are exactly the tasks that AI is getting better at, which leads to the next section.

docs.title: AI and Falling Production Costs
docs.text:
AI-generated content is text, images, simulations, quizzes, and other learning materials produced mainly by an AI system, typically a large language model (Chapter 4), from a prompt or an outline, and then reviewed and edited by a person. The people review it because of the hallucination problem of Chapter 5.

Falling production cost is the decline in the cost of producing content as AI takes over parts of the work. It follows from the two trends of earlier chapters: the task horizon is growing, so AI can complete longer jobs such as a whole chapter, and the price per token is falling, so each job costs less to run. The human role shifts from writing every sentence to specifying, reviewing, and correcting.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Same Chapter, AI-Assisted
docs.text:
Take the 80-hour chapter above and suppose AI generates the first draft of the text, the practice questions, and the first version of each simulation, while a skilled person specifies, reviews, tests, and fixes.

Task Hours of skilled work, AI-assisted Cost at $50 per hour Specifying the chapter and prompts 3 $150 Reviewing and editing the draft 6 $300 Testing and fixing the simulations 5 $250 Expert review and fact-checking 5 $250 Accessibility check and production 3 $150 Total skilled work 22 $1,100 AI computing for generation n/a about $20

The illustrative cost falls from about $4,000 to about $1,120 per chapter, a fall of about 72 percent, and for a 20-chapter book from about $80,000 to about $22,400. Two cautions apply. First, the saving depends on the review step: skipping it moves the cost into errors that students learn. Second, the assumptions are illustrative, and an author who measures their own hours will find different values.

Cheap to write is not cheap to trust

A common trap is counting the generation cost and forgetting the review cost. A draft that costs $20 to produce can still cost students dearly if no one checks it. Always budget reviewer time, and treat AI-generated content as a draft until a subject expert has read it.

AI-generated content also raises a rights question. In the United States, courts and the Copyright Office have so far held that a work produced entirely by an AI system, without human authorship, is not eligible for copyright. Human choices in selecting, arranging, and editing can be protected. For open resources the point cuts both ways: material no one owns is easy to share, but a school cannot assume it can license purely AI-generated material, and it should check the terms of the AI tool that produced it.

docs.title: Open Educational Resources
docs.text:
An open educational resource (OER) is a teaching, learning, or research material, in any medium, that is in the public domain or released under an open license that allows others to access, use, adapt, and share it at no cost or with minimal restrictions. The idea was formalized at a 2002 UNESCO forum and endorsed in UNESCO's 2012 Paris Declaration and 2019 Recommendation on OER. Well-known examples include OpenStax, which Rice University launched in 2012 to publish free peer-reviewed college textbooks; the CK-12 Foundation, which offers free K-12 materials; and K-12 curricula such as Illustrative Mathematics.

The word open is the one that matters. A free textbook is one that students can use at no cost. Free is a statement about price, and open is a statement about permissions. A free PDF that you may read but not edit, translate, or share is free and not open. An open textbook is free and carries a license that grants permissions, so teachers can fix errors and adapt it to their own students. Many open textbooks are also free, and this chapter uses "free open textbook" for the combination.

An open license is a copyright license by which the owner grants the public advance permission to use a work in specified ways, so that no one needs to ask. The most widely used family is the Creative Commons licenses.

A Creative Commons license is one of a set of standard open licenses, published by the nonprofit Creative Commons, that combine four elements: BY (attribution: give credit), SA (share-alike: share adaptations under the same terms), NC (non-commercial: no commercial use), and ND (no derivatives: share only unchanged copies). The six main licenses are:

License Elements What it allows CC BY Attribution Almost anything, if you credit the author CC BY-SA Attribution, share-alike Adaptations allowed if shared under the same license CC BY-NC Attribution, non-commercial Adaptations allowed for non-commercial use only CC BY-NC-SA Attribution, non-commercial, share-alike Non-commercial adaptations under the same license CC BY-ND Attribution, no derivatives Sharing unchanged copies only CC BY-NC-ND Attribution, non-commercial, no derivatives The most restrictive: unchanged, non-commercial sharing only

The book you are reading uses CC BY-NC-SA, which is why it carries the non-commercial label in its footer.

docs.title: The 5R Permissions
docs.text:
The 5R permissions, described by the education researcher David Wiley, are the five things an open license lets you do. They are the working test of whether something is truly open:

  1. Retain: make, own, and control copies of the work, such as downloading and archiving it.
  2. Reuse: use the work in its original form in many settings, such as a class or a website.
  3. Revise: adapt, edit, translate, or reformat the work.
  4. Remix: combine the work with other materials to create something new.
  5. Redistribute: share copies of the original or your changed version with others.

The licenses in the table grant the 5Rs to different degrees. CC BY grants all five. A no-derivatives license withholds revise and remix. A non-commercial license limits what a school may do if it also sells a course. A school choosing a textbook should check which of the five it needs, and the sim below, reused from the companion book OER Evaluator, practices matching classroom actions to permissions.

docs.text:
Run the 5R Permissions MicroSim fullscreen

The 5R Permissions: Five Things You May Do (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: five-r-permissions Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/five-r-permissions/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/oer-evaluator/tree/main/docs/sims/five-r-permissions Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify which of the 5R permissions a classroom action uses, correctly answering at least four of five on the first attempt.

Reused from the author's companion book OER Evaluator, whose index marks it as built.

License check in thirty seconds

Before a school adapts an open textbook, find the license in the footer and ask one question: "Will we need to edit it, combine it, or hand out our version?" If the answer is yes, a BY or BY-SA license is safest. NC and ND can block exactly the things teachers most want to do.

docs.title: The OpenBook QR Score: Judging an Open Textbook
docs.text:
A free textbook is only useful if it is good and if others can reuse it. Textbook quality is the degree to which a textbook helps learners learn: whether it is accurate, aligned with the learning outcomes it claims, readable, accessible to all students, and gives learners practice with feedback. Quality is a matter of judgment, which is why different reviewers using different checklists reach different conclusions. A repeatable method was needed.

The OpenBook QR Score, developed in the author's companion book OER Evaluator, is that method. It scores a resource on ten metrics worth ten points each, for a total from 0 to 100. Five metrics measure quality and five measure reusability, and the score is reported with both halves, as in "QR 65 (Q 32 / R 33)." The letters stand for Quality and Reusability.

Quality (up to 50 points) Reusability (up to 50 points) Accuracy and currency Open license Alignment to learning outcomes Modularity Readability Metadata Accessibility Editable source Practice with feedback Portability

The quality subscore is the sum of the five quality metrics, from 0 to 50, and shows how well the resource helps learners learn. (The OER Evaluator calls it the quality subtotal.) The reusability subscore is the sum of the five reusability metrics, from 0 to 50, and shows how easily others can find, change, and reuse the resource. The five reusability metrics in plain terms: an open license clearly grants permissions; modularity means the parts can be lifted out and used alone; metadata is structured descriptive information that lets people and software find the resource; an editable source means the original files, not just a finished copy, are available; and portability means the content works across devices and platforms.

The total places a resource in a band: Excellent (90 to 100), Good (75 to 89), Fair (50 to 74), Weak (25 to 49), and Poor (0 to 24). A band is a quick label and not an adoption decision, and a bare total can hide a weak half, which is why the score is always reported with both subscores.

docs.title: Worked Example: Comparing Two Open Textbooks
docs.text:
A school is choosing between two free open algebra textbooks. A reviewer scores each on the ten metrics. These scores are illustrative.

Metric Open Algebra FreeMath Complete Accuracy and currency 9 6 Alignment to learning outcomes 8 6 Readability 8 7 Accessibility 7 5 Practice with feedback 8 6 Quality subscore (Q) 40 30 Open license 6 9 Modularity 6 8 Metadata 5 7 Editable source 7 7 Portability 8 7 Reusability subscore (R) 32 38 Total 72 68 OpenBook QR Score QR 72 (Q 40 / R 32) QR 68 (Q 30 / R 38)

Both books fall in the Fair band, and the totals differ by only four points. The halves tell the story: Open Algebra is the better book to hand students tomorrow, while FreeMath Complete is the better raw material for a district that wants to adapt, combine, and republish. Neither total alone would reveal that. The sim below, reused from the same companion book, lets you practice the calculation from metric scores to subscores, total, and band.

docs.title: Diagram: Total Score Calculator
docs.text:
Run the Total Score Calculator MicroSim fullscreen

Total Score Calculator (reused MicroSim)

Type: microsim sim-id: total-score-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/oer-evaluator/sims/total-score-calculator/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/oer-evaluator/tree/main/docs/sims/total-score-calculator Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the quality subtotal, reusability subtotal, total score, and band for five scored resources, with the total and the decision both correct on at least four of five.

Reused from the author's companion book OER Evaluator, whose index marks it as built. Its terms "subtotal" and "adoption decision" correspond to this chapter's "subscore" and to the choice of whether to adopt.

Read the two halves, not just the total

Notice how two books with nearly the same total can be good for different jobs. A single number hides which half is weak, which is why a careful buyer always asks for Q and R separately. This is the same lesson as the effect-size habit of Chapter 2: the headline number is where you start asking questions.

docs.title: Rising Quality Scores
docs.text: Rising quality scores is the trend of open textbooks improving on measures like the OpenBook QR Score over time. The reason follows from the structure of the score. Several of its ten metrics are mechanical improvements that AI does cheaply and well: rewriting for readability, adding text descriptions to images for accessibility, generating practice questions with feedback, writing metadata, and splitting content into modules. These are the tasks that a human editor skips because they are tedious.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Semester of Improvement
docs.text:
An open textbook, Community Algebra, is scored before and after a semester of AI-assisted improvement, with each change reviewed by the author. The scores are illustrative.

Metric Before After What changed Accuracy and currency 7 8 Out-of-date examples refreshed and checked Alignment to learning outcomes 6 7 Outcomes written for each section Readability 6 8 Long sentences shortened Accessibility 5 8 Alt text added to every image Practice with feedback 7 8 Self-check questions with explanations added Q subscore 31 39 Open license 8 9 Clear license statement added Modularity 4 7 Chapters split into stand-alone sections Metadata 3 8 Structured metadata added to each page Editable source 6 8 Source files published Portability 6 8 Exported to open formats R subscore 27 40 Total 58 (QR 58, Fair) 79 (QR 79, Good)

The book moves from Fair to Good, and the reusability half rises most. A caution belongs with this example: a higher score is not proof that students learn more. The score describes properties of the book. Whether the improved book helps students is a question for the kind of controlled comparison that Chapter 2 described, and the OER Evaluator teaches how to run one.

docs.title: Content Commoditization and Publisher Disruption
docs.text:
Content commoditization is the process by which a product becomes interchangeable with competitors and its price falls toward its cost of production, because buyers can no longer tell it apart on quality. When AI makes content cheap to produce, and open licenses make it free to copy, level 1 and level 2 content (Chapter 6), meaning fixed text and interactive pages, tends toward a commodity. A publisher that sells such content competes with a free open textbook of comparable quality.

Publisher disruption is the change that results for publishers: pressure on revenue from the content itself, and a forced shift to other ways of earning. A company like Chegg, which sold homework help and textbook services to students, saw its stock price drop by about half in a single day in May 2023 after its chief executive said that ChatGPT was hurting its growth, which is an early and public example of how quickly AI can undercut a content-based business. Established textbook publishers face a slower version of the same pressure.

The question for a school leader is not whether publishers will adapt but what they will sell. Value beyond content names what stays valuable when content is cheap:

  • Trust and quality assurance: someone accountable for accuracy, bias review, and alignment with standards.
  • Assessment and data: banks of validated questions, and analytics that show which students need help.
  • Integration: working inside the school's learning management system and roster, with single sign-on and accessibility support.
  • Teacher development: training and coaching that change classroom practice (Chapter 16).
  • Human services: tutoring, coaching, and support for students and teachers.
  • Privacy and safety: the legal responsibility for protecting student data at levels 3 and above (Chapter 10).

This is good news and bad news for schools. The good news is that a school no longer needs to pay a premium for content it can get free. The bad news is that the pressure on publishers can push them to compensate with data collection, subscriptions, and lock-in. A purchasing decision should therefore ask what the school is paying for, and whether it is something content cannot supply.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Is the $900,000 Paying For?
docs.text:
Mr. Patel asks the publisher to break down its $900,000 proposal for a 12,000-student district. A simple version of the answer might look like this.

Item Annual cost Is it content? Digital textbook license $240,000 Yes Adaptive practice platform and student records (Level 3) $300,000 Partly Assessment bank and teacher dashboard $150,000 No Teacher training and coaching $120,000 No Support, integration, and data protection $90,000 No Total $900,000

Only $240,000, about 27 percent, pays for content that has an open equivalent. The remaining $660,000 pays for platform, assessment, training, and support, which are the things Value beyond content names. The district can now ask a better question: which of those do we need, which can we get elsewhere or build ourselves, and which are worth the price?

docs.title: Putting a Cost on Each Level
docs.text:
Mr. Patel's original question, "what will it cost per student, all in," needs a model. Cost per student is the total annual cost of a product or program divided by the number of students it serves, the same logic as the per-pupil spending of Chapter 1 applied to one line item. Cost modeling is the practice of building a simple, explicit model of the costs of an option, with stated assumptions, so that choices can be compared and tested.

A total cost of ownership (TCO) is the full cost of using something over its life, including not only the purchase price but also the devices to run it, the training to use it, the support, the data protection, and the replacement. TCO is the reason a "free" product is not always cheap. Software may be free while the laptop to run it is not.

The next sections build the model, one level at a time, using illustrative numbers that a school should replace with its own quotes.

docs.title: Level 2 Cost Per Student
docs.text: The Level 2 cost per student is the cost of an interactive textbook served as ordinary web pages. Hosting static pages is close to free, and the content is open or one-time. The book's penny-per-day vision sets a target: about one cent per student per school day. Over a 180-day year that is \( 180 \times \$0.01 = \$1.80 \) per student, the figure used here for content and hosting. Adding $4.00 per student per year as the share of teacher training gives a Level 2 cost of $5.80 per student per year, not counting the student's device.

docs.title: Level 3 Cost Per Student
docs.text: The Level 3 cost per student adds what adaptation needs: a place to store each student's records, such as a Learning Record Store (Chapter 8), at about $3.00 per student per year; privacy governance, meaning staff time for data-protection reviews and audits (Chapter 10), at about $2.00; and more training, $6.00 in all instead of $4.00. The Level 3 total is \( \$1.80 + \$3.00 + \$2.00 + \$6.00 = \$12.80 \) per student per year.

docs.title: Level 4 Cost Per Student
docs.text: The Level 4 cost per student adds the chatbot. Inference cost (Chapter 4) depends on tokens, sessions, and price. At 20,000 tokens per session, one session a day, 180 days, the year's usage is 3.6 million tokens. At a price of $2.00 per million tokens, a price chosen to represent a stronger model than the $0.07 GPT-3.5-level price of Chapter 4, inference costs \( 3.6 \times \$2.00 = \$7.20 \). Add $1.00 for reviewing logs and guardrail monitoring (Chapter 12), and training rises to $8.00. The Level 4 total is \( \$1.80 + \$3.00 + \$2.00 + \$1.00 + \$8.00 + \$7.20 = \$23.00 \).

docs.title: Worked Example: The Table Mr. Patel Asked For
docs.text:
The table puts the levels side by side, with a print textbook as the baseline. The print baseline assumes an $80 book used for six years in four core subjects, which is \( \$80/6 \times 4 \approx \$53.33 \) per student per year. The device column assumes a school laptop of $300 used four years, or $75 a year. All values are illustrative.

Print (Level 1) Level 2 Level 3 Level 4 Content and hosting $53.33 $1.80 $1.80 $1.80 Records platform n/a n/a $3.00 $3.00 Privacy governance n/a n/a $2.00 $2.00 AI inference n/a n/a n/a $7.20 Guardrail log review n/a n/a n/a $1.00 Teacher training n/a $4.00 $6.00 $8.00 Cost per student per year, devices already owned $53.33 $5.80 $12.80 $23.00 Device share if purchased n/a $75.00 $75.00 $75.00 Total cost of ownership with a new device $53.33 $80.80 $87.80 $98.00

For a 12,000-student district, the Level 2 software and training cost \( 12{,}000 \times \$5.80 = \$69{,}600 \) a year, Level 3 costs $153,600, Level 4 costs $276,000, and print costs about $640,000. Even the Level 4 figure of $23.00 is about 0.15 percent of the $15,600 per-pupil spending of Chapter 1.

The lesson of the bottom row is the surprising one. When devices must be bought, the device is the largest cost at every digital level, about 77 to 93 percent of the total. This is why Mr. Patel's question cannot be answered by comparing software prices. A school that already owns devices gets Level 2 and Level 3 at a small fraction of the price of print, and a school that has to buy them sees the gap close. It is also why equity (Chapter 3) turns on devices and connectivity as much as on content.

docs.title: Diagram: Cost Per Student by Level
docs.text:
Cost Per Student by Level

Instructional Rationale: Adding itemized costs makes the structure of total cost of ownership visible, and the device toggle shows that the largest item may not be software. Committing to calculations before exploring ties the learner's mental model to the numbers.

Three challenges:

# Setup Correct answer Working shown as feedback 1 Level 3 cost per student per year, no device $12.80 1.80 + 3.00 + 2.00 + 6.00 = 12.80 2 Level 4 cost per student per year with 20,000 tokens, 1 session a day, 180 days, $2.00 per million, no device $23.00 Inference 3.6 × 2.00 = 7.20; 1.80 + 3.00 + 2.00 + 1.00 + 8.00 + 7.20 = 23.00 3 Level 4 district cost per year for 12,000 students at $0.20 per million, other settings as in challenge 2, no device $198,240 Inference 3.6 × 0.20 = 0.72; per student 15.80 + 0.72 = 16.52; × 12,000 = 198,240

Provenance: All cost items are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label them "Illustrative costs; replace with your own quotes." The price points $20.00 and $0.07 are the Stanford AI Index 2025 values quoted in Chapter 4; $2.00 and $0.20 are illustrative. The device figure is an illustrative assumption.

Rules: Level 2 total = 1.80 + 4.00. Level 3 total = 1.80 + 3.00 + 2.00 + 6.00. Level 4 total = 1.80 + 3.00 + 2.00 + 1.00 + 8.00 + inference. District cost = per-student cost × students served. With a device purchased, add 75.00 per student. Costs are shown to the cent per student and to the dollar per district. The sim also shows the share of the $15,600 per-pupil spending.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers challenges 1, 2, and 3 as calculations and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and unlocks the controls.
  3. The learner changes the token price, usage, and the device setting. The three level costs and the district total update at once.
  4. The learner compares the cost with and without a purchased device.
  5. The learner should notice that the device share is larger than every software item combined at Levels 2 and 3.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [value]. [Working text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Add each item in the table for that level." After the second wrong attempt the value and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown with the controls locked, and the prompt reads "What does Level 3 cost per student per year?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table gives Level 2 at $5.80, Level 3 at $12.80, and Level 4 at $23.00 per student per year without devices, with a $75.00 device share and totals of $80.80, $87.80, and $98.00. It gives print at about $53.33 and district totals of $69,600, $153,600, and $276,000 for 12,000 students.

docs.title: The Penny-Per-Day Vision and Universal Textbook Access
docs.text:
The penny-per-day vision is the book's name for a target: high-quality interactive textbooks, at Level 2 and increasingly Level 3, costing a school roughly one cent per student per day, about $1.80 a year. It is a target and not a price list. It is achievable for content and hosting because of the three forces of this chapter: AI lowers the cost of creating content, open licenses remove the cost of copying it, and static web pages are nearly free to serve.

Universal textbook access is the goal that follows: every student, in every school, has a free, high-quality, interactive textbook. The course description's prediction of Chapter 5 is that this could happen within three to four years. The barriers that remain are not the price of content. They are devices and connectivity (the equity issues of Chapter 3), teacher training, accessibility for students with disabilities, translation into the languages students speak, and the privacy protections that levels 3 and above require.

docs.title: Worked Example: Pennies at Scale
docs.text:
For the 12,000-student district, the penny-per-day content cost is \( 12{,}000 \times \$1.80 = \$21{,}600 \) a year. The district's total spending at the Chapter 1 figure is \( 12{,}000 \times \$15{,}600 = \$187.2 \) million. The content line is \( 21{,}600 / 187{,}200{,}000 \approx 0.012\% \), about one dollar in every 8,700. Compare this with the $240,000 content license in the publisher's $900,000 proposal, which is more than eleven times as much for content with an open equivalent.

Cost tables look scarier than they are

If a table of cost items makes your eyes glaze, that's normal; the trick is to add one column at a time, as you did with Chapter 1's per-pupil arithmetic. Start with the one line you can check against a real quote, then fill in the rest.

docs.title: Answering Mr. Patel
docs.text:
Mr. Patel's question now has an answer in three parts. Content is falling toward a penny a day, because AI cuts the cost of making it and open licenses cut the cost of copying it. The all-in cost per student depends on the level: in our illustrative model, about $6 at Level 2, $13 at Level 3, and $23 at Level 4 when devices are already owned, against about $53 for print, and about $75 more per student a year if devices must be bought. And the right way to compare a free open textbook with a paid product is to score both on quality and reusability, and to ask what the money pays for beyond content.

The story has both sides. The benefit is large: a district that adopts an open Level 2 textbook might redirect most of a $900,000 content budget to teachers, devices, and support. The risks are also real. A free textbook can be a poor one, so check its QR score. An NC or ND license can block the changes a school needs. AI-generated content can carry errors, and purely AI-generated material may not be licensable. And the savings can be eaten by devices, training, and data protection that a software invoice never shows. The response is the set of habits from this chapter: check the license, score the quality, budget the review, and build the full cost model before the vote.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Content creation cost is mostly up-front, which is why a textbook publisher's publisher business model was built on selling many copies at a high textbook price.
  • AI-generated content drives falling production cost: in our illustration a chapter falls from about $4,000 to about $1,120, as long as the human review step stays.
  • An open educational resource carries an open license; a free textbook is free in price, and open adds the 5R permissions (retain, reuse, revise, remix, redistribute). A Creative Commons license grants them to different degrees.
  • The OpenBook QR Score rates ten metrics worth 100 points: a quality subscore (Q, out of 50) and a reusability subscore (R, out of 50). Textbook quality needs both halves reported, since totals hide which half is weak.
  • Rising quality scores reflect AI doing the tedious improvements, but a higher score does not prove students learn more.
  • Content commoditization pushes content prices toward cost, causing publisher disruption; value beyond content is trust, assessment, integration, training, services, and data protection.
  • Cost per student and cost modeling make options comparable: in the illustration, Level 2, Level 3, and Level 4 cost per student are about $5.80, $12.80, and $23.00 without devices.
  • Total cost of ownership includes devices, which at $75 a year dominate the software at every digital level.
  • The penny-per-day vision (about $1.80 per student per year) makes universal textbook access plausible for content, with devices, training, accessibility, and privacy as the remaining barriers.

You can answer 'what does it cost per student?'

You just learned why content is heading toward a penny a day, how to read a QR score with its two halves, and how to build a per-level cost table that includes the devices a software quote leaves out. Chapter 8 moves to Level 3: how a school can track what students master without handing their data over. One step at a time, together.

docs.title: Tracking Mastery: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, and MicroSims
Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the technical building blocks that let a textbook adapt to a student without a live AI model: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, mastery data, learning analytics, and MicroSims, together with student-controlled, portable learning data. Readers finish able to explain how a Learning Record Store tracks what a student has mastered and why that data should stay under the student's control.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Mastery Data 369 Learning Analytics 107 xAPI 106 Learning Record Store 60 Learning Graph 52 Web Browser 39 Learning Dependency 38 Static Website 28 xAPI Statement 28 Actor Verb Object 27 Learning Record 26 Data Portability 23 Student-Controlled Data 22 MicroSim 21 Learning Management System 18

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
  • Chapter 6: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks

docs.title: "How Does It Know?"
docs.text:
After the pilot at Lincoln Middle School, Maya's mother, Ms. Reyes, comes to the parent night with a sharp question. "The software seems to know exactly which fractions my daughter is stuck on. How does it know? Is there an AI watching her? And who else gets to see that?"

It is the right pair of questions, and the honest answer is less dramatic than she fears and more important than she might expect. No live AI model needs to be watching her. What the software needs is a record: a running list of what Maya did, in a standard format, kept in a place the school controls. Choosing the next lesson from that record can be done with simple rules.

This chapter explains the parts of that arrangement: how an interactive page reports what a student did, where those reports are kept, how they are turned into a measure of mastery, how the software uses the measure to choose what comes next, and how the student and family stay in control of the data throughout. It is the technical foundation of Level 3 from Chapter 6, and it is why the book's low-cost design can adapt to students without sending every request to a large language model.

From clicks to a record you control

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to explain to a worried parent, like Ms. Reyes, exactly what is recorded, where it lives, and how an adaptive textbook uses it, without a live AI model in sight. You'll also know the one design rule that keeps families in charge. Let's find the balance between a textbook that knows a child well and a family that stays in control.

docs.title: The Pieces: Web Pages, Browsers, and MicroSims
docs.text:
Before the record, the thing that produces it. A web browser is the application on a computer, tablet, or phone that retrieves web pages and displays them, and that can run small programs, written in a language called JavaScript, that come with those pages. Chrome, Safari, Edge, and Firefox are web browsers. Every student with a school device already has one.

A static website is a website made of fixed files, such as HTML pages, images, and JavaScript, that a server hands over exactly as stored, without running any program on the server to build each page. This book's own site is a static website. Static sites are cheap and fast to serve, because the server only has to deliver files, and they are secure in a useful way: with no server program and no database, there is little for an attacker to break into and no student data to leak from the page itself. This is the technical reason that Level 2 textbooks carry almost no privacy burden.

A MicroSim, the term used for an embedded simulation in Chapter 6, is a small interactive model that runs entirely inside the web browser. A MicroSim does not need a server, because the browser runs it using the JavaScript delivered with the page. This is why a school can host hundreds of MicroSims on a static site at almost no cost. The sims in each chapter of this book, such as the effect-size visualizer and the task-horizon explorer, are MicroSims.

A MicroSim runs in the student's browser, which makes it a natural place to observe what the student does: a slider moved, a question answered, an answer checked. The question is what to do with those observations. That is the job of the next few terms.

docs.title: xAPI: A Standard Way to Say What Happened
docs.text:
Different learning programs have traditionally reported results in incompatible ways, or not at all. A quiz tool recorded a score, a video platform recorded minutes watched, and a simulation recorded nothing. To make the records comparable and portable, the education technology community developed a shared format.

xAPI, short for Experience API (and originally called Tin Can API), is a standard format and protocol for describing learning experiences and sending the descriptions to a store. It was developed beginning around 2011 under the U.S. Department of Defense's Advanced Distributed Learning initiative, released as version 1.0 in 2013, and later adopted as an IEEE standard. Its main advance over the earlier SCORM standard, which tracked a course's completion and score inside a learning management system, is that xAPI can describe almost any activity, on any device, including activity outside a course.

An xAPI statement is a single record of one learning event, written as a small structured data object. Its core idea is a sentence in three parts, called Actor Verb Object:

  • The actor is who did something, such as a student.
  • The verb is what they did, such as answered, completed, or experienced.
  • The object is what they did it to, such as a particular quiz question or simulation.

Statements can carry extra detail. A result holds the outcome, such as a score or whether the answer was correct, and a context holds surrounding information, such as the course or the page the activity belongs to. Each statement also has a timestamp. The sentence "Student 4821 answered Question 3 on Unit Rates correctly" is a statement in everyday language.

The standard writes the statement in a text format called JSON. Before you look at one, here is what each field in it means: actor names who acted, using a code instead of a real name so that the record does not expose identity by itself; verb gives a standard web address that identifies the action, plus a human-readable label; object identifies the activity by its web address; and result records whether the answer was correct and the score as a fraction of 1.

{
  "actor":  { "account": { "name": "student-4821" } },
  "verb":   { "id": "http://adlnet.gov/expapi/verbs/answered",
              "display": { "en-US": "answered" } },
  "object": { "id": "https://example.edu/unit-rates/question-3" },
  "result": { "success": true, "score": { "scaled": 1.0 } },
  "timestamp": "2026-11-04T10:15:32Z"
}

Read it as a sentence: student-4821 answered question 3 of the unit-rates activity, correctly, at 10:15 a.m. The statement says nothing more. It records an event, which is what makes it a safe and compact unit of data: an ordinary statement takes about a kilobyte or less, and a full semester of a student's activity compresses to a fraction of a megabyte, according to the author's draft design for a lightweight store.

The sim below, reused from the author's companion book on Learning Record Stores, walks through the building blocks of a statement with one worked example.

docs.text:
Run the xAPI Statement Building Blocks MicroSim fullscreen

xAPI Statement Building Blocks (reused MicroSim)

Type: workflow sim-id: xapi-statement-triple Library: Mermaid Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/learning-record-store/sims/xapi-statement-triple/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-record-store/tree/main/docs/sims/xapi-statement-triple Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify the parts of an xAPI statement as actor, verb, object, result, or context using one worked example.

Reused from the author's companion book on Learning Record Stores, whose page is marked instrumented.

docs.title: Worked Example: From Maya's Click to a Statement
docs.text:
Maya answers the third question in the unit-rates activity. The page, running in her browser, builds a statement.

Event on the page Statement parts In plain English Maya clicks "Check" on question 3 and the answer is right Actor: student-4821. Verb: answered. Object: unit-rates question 3. Result: success, score 1.0 "student-4821 answered question 3 correctly" Maya slides the bottle-count slider in the simulation Actor: student-4821. Verb: experienced. Object: unit-rate simulation "student-4821 explored the simulation" Maya finishes the five-question check with four right Actor: student-4821. Verb: completed. Object: unit-rates check. Result: success, score 0.8 "student-4821 completed the check with 80 percent"

Two details deserve attention. The actor is a code, student-4821, not "Maya Reyes," so that someone reading the record without the roster cannot tell who she is. And not every action is recorded: nothing in the table records that Maya moved her mouse across the page, because that would be noise, and noise in a record makes the conclusions drawn from it unreliable.

docs.title: The Learning Record Store
docs.text:
A Learning Record Store (LRS) is a system that receives xAPI statements, stores them, and returns them on request. It is the memory of the arrangement: the place where all the statements from all the sims, quizzes, and activities for all the students end up. An LRS does not decide anything about instruction. It receives and answers questions such as "give me all the statements for student-4821 about unit rates."

A learning record is the stored collection of statements about one learner, or one activity, held in the LRS. Where a statement is one event, a learning record is the history: everything Maya did over the semester, in order.

A learning management system (LMS) is a software platform that schools use to administer courses: it holds course materials, enrolls students, delivers assignments, collects submissions, and keeps the gradebook. Canvas, Moodle, Schoology, and Google Classroom are examples. An LMS has traditionally been the home of learning data, but it records only what it was built to record, usually grades and submissions, and it is not designed to take in the activity of a simulation or an app outside it.

The difference between an LMS-centered design and an LRS-centered one is a difference in architecture, and the sim below, from the same companion book, shows it.

docs.title: Diagram: LMS-Centric Versus LRS-Centric Architecture
docs.text:
Run the LMS versus LRS MicroSim fullscreen

LMS-Centric versus LRS-Centric Architecture (reused MicroSim)

Type: workflow sim-id: lms-vs-lrs-architecture Library: Mermaid Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/learning-record-store/sims/lms-vs-lrs-architecture/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-record-store/tree/main/docs/sims/lms-vs-lrs-architecture Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare a single-hub LMS-centric architecture with a hub-and-spoke LRS-centric architecture and explain why the second scales to many kinds of learning activity.

Reused from the author's companion book on Learning Record Stores, whose page is marked implemented.

The summary is as follows. In an LMS-centric design, every activity must report through the LMS, so a simulation that the LMS does not know about leaves no trace. In an LRS-centric design, every activity, whether a simulation, a quiz, a reading page, or an app, sends statements directly to the LRS, and the LMS becomes one more source and one more consumer. The textbook, the LMS, and any analytics tool all speak xAPI.

docs.title: Worked Example: Same Activity, Two Records
docs.text:
Maya spends twenty minutes on the unit-rates simulation, answers three questions, gets the second one wrong twice, and then gets it right. Compare what two systems keep.

LMS gradebook LRS record Did she open the simulation? Not recorded; the LMS does not know about it Yes, one experienced statement with the time How many questions did she attempt? Only the final score on the quiz: 2 of 3 Each attempt, in order: right, wrong, wrong, right Where did she get stuck? Not recorded Question 2, two attempts, then success What can a teacher learn? "Maya scored 67 percent" "Maya needed three tries at the division order and then got it"

The gradebook says how she did. The record says how she got there, which is the information a teacher needs to help.

For a small pilot, the store need not be a heavy system. The author's draft design for a lightweight "LRS-Lite" keeps each student's compressed statements in a database inside the browser and synchronizes them through low-cost cloud storage, which the draft estimates at a few dollars a month for one course. That design is a plan, not a finished product, and a district at scale would use a full LRS. What matters here is the principle: a Level 3 textbook needs a store of records, and the store can be small and cheap.

The page doesn't need to know you; the record does

Notice the division of labor. The page, a static file, is the same for every student and holds no data. The record store holds each student's history and nothing else. Keeping those two apart is what lets the content be free and the data be protected, because each can be treated according to what it is.

docs.title: Mastery Data and How a Textbook Uses It
docs.text:
Mastery data is evidence of which concepts a student has demonstrated they know, derived from the learning record. A statement records an event, but mastery data turns a pile of events into a judgment about a concept: has this student mastered equivalent fractions? Mastery data is the output that adaptation depends on, and it extends the formative assessment of Chapter 1 from a single quiz to a continuing, automatic process.

Estimating mastery can be simple or sophisticated. A simple rule, for example, is to count a concept as mastered when the student answered four of the last five questions on it correctly. A more sophisticated method, such as the Bayesian Knowledge Tracing used in the author's LRS design, keeps a probability for each concept and updates it after every answer. Either way, the rule must be stated in advance and applied the same way to every student, which makes it transparent and checkable.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Mastery Rule
docs.text:
Maya's record for three concepts after three weeks, under the rule "mastered means at least four of the last five answers correct," reads as follows. Correct answers are marked ✓ and wrong ones ✗, oldest first.

Concept Last five answers Correct Mastered? Fractions as parts of a whole ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ 4 of 5 Yes Equivalent fractions ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✓ 2 of 5 No Whole-number multiplication and division ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ 5 of 5 Yes

The rule is deliberately simple and has its own weaknesses: five answers is a small sample, and a lucky guess can flip a result. Transparency is the price worth paying. A teacher or parent can see exactly why the system said what it said.

docs.title: Learning Dependencies and the Learning Graph
docs.text:
A learning dependency is a relationship between two concepts in which one must be understood before the other can be learned. Equivalent fractions depend on fractions as parts of a whole; unit rates depend on ratios. This is the idea of a prerequisite concept from Chapter 2, written as a link between two concepts.

A learning graph is a map of concepts and their learning dependencies: each concept is a node, and each dependency an arrow from a concept to the prerequisite it depends on. Chapter 9 covers learning graphs in detail. For now what matters is what the graph lets the software do. Given a student's mastery data and the learning graph, finding the next concept to study needs no AI model: it is a lookup. The rule is that the next concepts to study are those the student has not mastered, and whose prerequisites the student has mastered. Call those concepts ready.

docs.title: Worked Example: Choosing Maya's Next Concept
docs.text:
Use the eight-concept fractions-to-proportions graph of Chapter 2. Maya's mastery data says she has mastered concepts 1, 2, and 5, and has not mastered 3, 4, 6, 7, and 8. Apply the rule to each unmastered concept.

Concept Prerequisites Prerequisites all mastered? Ready? 3. Equivalent fractions 1, 2 Yes Yes 4. Adding and subtracting fractions with unlike denominators 3 No (3) No 6. Ratios 3 No (3) No 7. Unit rates 5, 6 No (6) No 8. Proportional equations 7 No (7) No

Exactly one concept is ready: equivalent fractions, which is the root gap found in Chapter 2. The software did not use a language model, a neural network, or any live AI: it used a stored record, a stated mastery rule, and a map. This is the whole answer to the parent's question about whether an AI is watching. The adaptation here is a lookup, and its output can be checked by anyone who can read the table.

docs.title: Diagram: Class Mastery Heatmap for One Section
docs.text:
Run the Class Mastery Heatmap MicroSim fullscreen

Class Mastery Heatmap for One Section (reused MicroSim)

Type: chart sim-id: class-mastery-heatmap Library: p5.js Status: Reused Source: https://dmccreary.github.io/learning-record-store/sims/class-mastery-heatmap/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-record-store/tree/main/docs/sims/class-mastery-heatmap Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish a concept-wide weakness, shown as a dark column across most students, from a student-specific weakness, shown as a dark row across most concepts, in a class mastery heatmap.

Reused from the author's companion book on Learning Record Stores, whose page is marked implemented.

docs.title: Learning Analytics
docs.text:
Learning analytics is the measurement, collection, analysis, and reporting of data about learners and their contexts, for the purpose of understanding and improving learning and the environments in which it happens. That definition comes from the Society for Learning Analytics Research. Mastery data for one student is the starting point, and analytics goes on to ask questions across many students: which concept does most of the class find hard, which students have stalled, did a new activity help?

The heatmap above shows the idea. Each row is a student and each column a concept, and darker cells mean lower mastery. A dark column means a concept-wide weakness: most students stumbled there, so the right response is a whole-class reteach or a better explanation. A dark row means a student-specific weakness: one student is struggling across many concepts, so the response is individual support. The same data supports opposite conclusions, and a teacher who reads only an average would miss the difference.

Read rows and columns before averages

When you look at any class dashboard, ask two questions before you look at the average: "Is there a dark column?" and "Is there a dark row?" A column points to your teaching; a row points to a student. The average blends them and hides both.

docs.title: Data Portability and Student-Controlled Data
docs.text:
A system that holds a child's learning history carries responsibilities. This section names the design principles that decide whether the arrangement serves families or merely observes them.

Data portability is the ability to move one's data from one system to another in a standard format without losing meaning. For a student it means that a mastery record built in one school, one textbook, or one product can follow them to the next. Without portability, every change of school or vendor starts the child back at "unknown," and the records are held hostage by whoever stores them. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) gives individuals a legal right to data portability, and xAPI helps make it practical, since every compliant system reads the same statements.

Student-controlled data is a design principle under which the student, and for a minor the family, decide what is collected, who can see it, and what happens to it, and the school and vendors act as custodians, not owners. The principle has five parts:

  1. Minimum necessary. Collect only what instruction needs.
  2. See it. The student and family can view their own record at any time.
  3. Take it. They can export it in a standard format, which is portability.
  4. Limit it. Only people with an educational need, such as the student's own teachers, can see identifiable records. Outside parties see them only under a written agreement for a stated purpose.
  5. Remove it. The record can be deleted when it is no longer needed, within the law.

In the United States, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) already gives parents and eligible students the right to inspect education records and to ask for corrections, and it limits disclosure to others. Chapter 10 covers FERPA, COPPA, and GDPR in detail. The principles above are design commitments that go beyond the minimum.

docs.title: Worked Example: Answering Ms. Reyes
docs.text:
Ms. Okafor answers the parent's two questions with a one-page handout.

Ms. Reyes asks The answer "How does it know?" The pages report what Maya does, as short xAPI statements, to a record store. A stated rule turns the record into a mastery estimate, and the learning graph shows which concept is ready next. No live AI model is involved "What is in the record?" A code, not her name, plus the time, the activity, and whether each answer was right. No camera, no microphone, no location "Who sees it?" Maya's own teachers, Maya, and the family. Outside parties only under a written agreement, and never for advertising "Can I get a copy?" Yes, in a standard format, and the family can ask for it to be deleted when Maya leaves "Where does it live?" In the district's record store, not in the vendor's own systems

The handout works because it states what the system does, in order, and commits to specifics. A promise that "your data is safe" would not have.

docs.title: Diagram: Who May See This Record?
docs.text:
Who May See This Record?

Type: microsim sim-id: who-may-see-this-record Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight requests to see or use a student's learning record should be allowed, allowed only with an agreement and family notice, or not allowed, correctly judging at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/health-education/tree/main/docs/sims/trusted-source-sorter

Prerequisites: learning record, student-controlled data and its five parts, data portability (all defined in the section "Data Portability and Student-Controlled Data" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 requests, the learner chooses one of three responses and submits it. A response is correct when it matches the "Correct response" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the five principles is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Anyone at the school may see any student's record. (2) A vendor may use records for any purpose once it has them. (3) A family may only look at the record, never take a copy.

Instructional Rationale: Judging a request requires applying the principles of minimum necessary access and stated purpose to a concrete case. Cases from teachers, parents, vendors, researchers, and advertisers show that the same record deserves different answers for different requesters and purposes.

Content:

Three responses, shown for every request:

Response Meaning shown Allow A person with an educational need, or the student's own family, may see or take the record Allow only with an agreement and family notice An outside party may use the record only under a written agreement that states the purpose, with the family notified Do not allow The use has no educational need or goes beyond the stated purpose

Eight requests:

# Request shown to the learner Correct response Why (shown as feedback) 1 A teacher views the mastery records of the students in her own class to plan next week. Allow The teacher has a direct educational need for her own students. 2 A teacher with no connection to a class looks up the records of its students out of curiosity. Do not allow There is no educational need, so access is not justified. 3 A parent asks to see their own child's learning record. Allow Parents have the right to inspect their child's education records. 4 A student moving to a new school asks for a copy of their record in a standard format. Allow Data portability lets the record follow the student. 5 The software vendor wants to use identifiable student records to train a new commercial product. Do not allow The use goes beyond providing the service the school bought. 6 A university team, working under a district-approved study, asks for class-level summaries with no student names. Allow only with an agreement and family notice An outside party may use data only under a written agreement stating the purpose. 7 An advertiser asks for a list of students who are struggling in math. Do not allow Student records must never be used for advertising. 8 A district-approved tutoring partner asks to see one student's fractions mastery to prepare a session. Allow only with an agreement and family notice An outside party with an educational purpose needs an agreement and notice.

Provenance: The responses follow the five principles in the chapter section "Data Portability and Student-Controlled Data," which are recommended design practice, not a statement of any one law. The requests are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must say that legal duties are covered in Chapter 10.

Rules: Each request has exactly one correct response, given in Content. A request is scored on its first submitted response only. The score counts first-attempt correct responses out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one request at a time and the three responses.
  2. The learner chooses a response and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct response and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 requests, the sim shows the score and lists misjudged requests with their correct responses.
  5. The learner should notice that three requests are allowed, two need an agreement, and three are refused, and that the requester's job title alone never decided the answer.

Feedback: 8 requests, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [response]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the response]." After the second attempt the correct response is revealed and the request counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can judge who should see a student's record." For a score < 7: "Review the five principles and try again; the requests will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Request 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three responses, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Should this request be allowed?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists five principles: minimum necessary, see it, take it, limit it, remove it. The chapter states that outside parties may see identifiable records only under a written agreement for a stated purpose, and never for advertising. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

Data you can't delete is a liability

A common trap is collecting everything "in case it's useful later." Every extra field raises the damage if the store is breached and the work of protecting it. Before collecting any item, ask what decision it will inform, and plan when it will be deleted.

docs.title: Putting It Together: Adapting Without a Live AI Model
docs.text:
The chapter's pieces now make a complete loop, and it is the loop at the heart of the book's low-cost design.

  1. A static website serves the same free pages to every student, with no student data on the server.
  2. In the student's web browser, MicroSims and quizzes report what the student does as xAPI statements, each an actor, verb, object sentence.
  3. A Learning Record Store keeps each student's learning record.
  4. A stated rule turns the record into mastery data.
  5. A learning graph of learning dependencies tells the software which concept is ready next.
  6. Learning analytics shows the teacher which concepts and which students need attention.
  7. Throughout, the data is student-controlled and portable.

No step requires a live large language model. AI may have helped write the content, once, as Chapter 7 explained, but at the time a student uses the textbook the work is lookups, rules, and a record. That is why the cost per student at Level 3 in the Chapter 7 model is modest and why the privacy risks, while real, are limited to the record store, which is a bounded and defensible thing to protect.

The story has both sides, as always. The benefit: a textbook that moves each student at their own pace, shows Maya the exact missing prerequisite, and costs a few dollars a year per student. The risks: a permanent record of a child's mistakes, the temptation to collect more than needed, a breach, and the danger of treating a simple mastery rule as truth when it is a rough estimate. The response is built into the design: collect the minimum, keep the data under the family's control, state the rules in public, and treat the estimate as a prompt for a human to look, not a verdict.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A web browser runs the pages and the code; a static website serves fixed files with no student data on the server; a MicroSim runs entirely in the browser.
  • xAPI is a standard format for describing learning events, and an xAPI statement is one event written as actor, verb, object, with an optional result and context.
  • A Learning Record Store receives and stores statements; a learning record is the stored history for one learner; an LRS-centered design lets any activity report, where an LMS-centered design records only what the LMS sees.
  • Mastery data turns events into a judgment about a concept using a stated rule; with a learning graph of learning dependencies, finding the next concept is a lookup: not mastered, with all prerequisites mastered.
  • Learning analytics reads across students: a dark column points at the teaching, a dark row at a student.
  • Data portability lets a record follow the student, and student-controlled data means minimum necessary, see it, take it, limit it, and remove it.
  • A Level 3 textbook can adapt with no live AI model, which keeps cost low and the privacy question focused on one bounded store.

You can explain how it knows

You just followed a click all the way to a mastery estimate and a next-lesson choice, and you can say exactly what is recorded, where it lives, and who may see it. That's a clear answer for a worried parent. Chapter 9 looks at learning graphs and the standards that let these tools work together. One step at a time, together.

docs.title: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers learning graphs as directed acyclic graphs of concept nodes, the interoperability standards (IMS Global, IEEE) that let these pieces work across products, and the practical requirements of delivering content at scale: device access, connectivity, offline access, and a "generate once, serve many" delivery model. Readers finish able to explain how a learning graph selects a student's next concept and what it takes to deliver that content to every student affordably.
