docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Device Access 18 Interoperability Standards 17 Concept Node 13 Directed Acyclic Graph 13 Web Page Hosting 12 Foundational Concept 12 Learning Path 12 Generate Once Serve Many 11 Browser-Based Simulation 10 Interactive Visualization 10 IMS Global Standards 8 IEEE Learning Standards 8 Internet Connectivity 8 Student Progress Dashboard 6 Offline Access 4

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 7: Content Economics and Open Educational Resources
  • Chapter 8: Tracking Mastery: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, and MicroSims

docs.title: "Will It Work at Fairview?"
docs.text:
The district's technology director, Ms. Singh, has read the plan from the last few chapters and has a practical worry. "This all sounds wonderful for Lincoln Middle," she says. "But Fairview Elementary is forty minutes from the nearest town. Its internet is slow, half its devices are older than the students, and the district's tools all come from different vendors that don't talk to each other. Will any of this work at Fairview?"

Her question divides into two. The first is about structure: how does the software decide what a student should learn next, and how do products from different makers share the information they need? The second is about delivery: how does a free, interactive textbook actually reach a student on an old device with a poor connection?

This chapter answers both. It explains the learning graph that drives the "what next" decision, the standards that let separate tools cooperate, and the delivery model that keeps cost and bandwidth low enough for a school like Fairview. The story it tells has both sides, since a design that looks wonderful on a fast network in a well-funded school can quietly leave the schools that most need it behind.

Design for Fairview first

This chapter shows how a textbook chooses each student's next step from a map of concepts, and how the same design can reach a school with slow internet and old devices. You'll leave able to ask the questions that decide whether an AI-native school is for everyone or only for the best-connected. Let's find the balance between ambitious design and access that actually reaches every child.

docs.title: Learning Graphs: Maps of Concepts
docs.text:
Chapter 8 introduced the learning graph as a map of concepts and their dependencies, and used it to pick Maya's next concept. This section gives the graph its proper vocabulary.

A concept node is one concept in a learning graph, the unit of knowledge the graph tracks. A node has an identifier, a name such as "Equivalent Fractions," and sometimes extra attributes, like a category or an importance score. Every node stands for something a student can learn and that can be checked. This book's own learning graph has 532 concept nodes, from "Education" to "A/B Testing," and each chapter covers a group of them.

A learning dependency, as in Chapter 8, links two nodes: concept A depends on concept B when B must be understood before A can be learned. In this book's graph every dependency is written as an arrow from the dependent concept to its prerequisite. The book's graph has 961 of them.

A foundational concept is a concept with no prerequisites in the graph: the place where learning on a topic can begin. Foundational concepts are the roots from which everything else grows. This book's graph has 14, including Education, Student, Teacher, Learning, Artificial Intelligence, Exponential Growth, and Web Browser. A terminal concept is the opposite: one that nothing else depends on, so it ends a chain, such as a capstone skill. The graph has 28.

A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a graph whose arrows point in one direction (directed) and that never leads back to where it started (acyclic, meaning free of cycles). A learning graph must be a DAG, for a logical reason: if concept A required concept B and B also required A, no student could learn either, because each would have to be learned first. Checking that a learning graph has no cycles is one of the first quality tests, and this book's graph passes it. The DAG property has a useful consequence: the concepts can always be put into an order in which every concept comes after all of its prerequisites, which is the basis of a learning path.

A learning path is an ordered sequence of concepts that takes a student from where they are to a goal, with every concept coming after its prerequisites. A path can be generated automatically from the graph: start with the goal, collect every concept it depends on, directly or indirectly, remove the ones the student has already mastered, and list what is left in an order that respects the arrows. Because the path is built from the student's mastery data (Chapter 8), two students with the same goal get different paths.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Path Through This Book's Own Graph
docs.text:
Take a goal from this book: the concept Five-Month Doubling, from Chapter 4. Following its dependencies back through the book's learning graph, the concept rests on 15 other concepts, arranged in seven layers, where each layer's concepts depend only on layers above it.

Layer Concepts in the layer Depends on 1 Artificial Intelligence; Exponential Growth Nothing (both foundational) 2 AI Capability; Machine Learning; Doubling Time Layer 1 3 AI Benchmark; Large Language Model Layers 1 and 2 4 METR; AI Agent Layers 2 and 3 5 Benchmark Task Suite; Task Horizon Layers 2 to 4 6 50 Percent Time Horizon; Human Working Time; Long-Running Task; Task Success Rate Layer 5 and AI Agent 7 Five-Month Doubling (the goal) Layer 6, Layer 5, and Doubling Time

A student who has never studied any of it needs all 16 concepts, in an order that respects the layers. A student who has already mastered Artificial Intelligence, Exponential Growth, Doubling Time, and Machine Learning skips four and begins with AI Capability. The same graph produces both paths with no judgment call and no AI model. The longest chain in the whole book's graph is much longer: 26 concepts, running from Artificial Intelligence to A/B Testing, which means that a student aiming at the book's final skill is walking through the book's own argument from the first idea to the last.

The book's own graph viewer, embedded below, lets you explore all 532 concepts. Search for a concept, filter by category, and follow the arrows.

docs.title: Diagram: The AI-Native Schools Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text:
Run the Learning Graph Viewer fullscreen

Learning Graph Viewer (reused MicroSim)

Type: graph-model sim-id: graph-viewer Library: vis-network Status: Reused Source: ../../sims/graph-viewer/ Source Repo: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-native-schools/tree/main/docs/sims/graph-viewer Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain how a concept depends on other concepts by selecting a concept in the 532-concept learning graph and following its arrows to its prerequisites.

Reused from this book's own sims directory, which marks it as built.

The arrow points to what you need first

Notice the direction. In this book's graph every arrow runs from a concept to the one it depends on, so following arrows takes you backward to what must come first. A learning path is those arrows read in reverse. Keep the direction straight and the rest of the graph is easy to read.

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding the Ready Concepts
docs.text:
Chapter 8 introduced the rule for picking the next concept: a concept is ready when the student has not mastered it and has mastered all of its direct prerequisites. Apply it to the sixteen concepts above. Suppose a student has mastered Artificial Intelligence, Exponential Growth, AI Capability, Machine Learning, and Doubling Time.

Unmastered concept Direct prerequisites All mastered? Ready? AI Benchmark AI Capability Yes Yes Large Language Model Machine Learning Yes Yes METR AI Benchmark No No AI Agent Large Language Model No No Task Horizon METR, AI Capability No (METR) No

Two concepts are ready: AI Benchmark and Large Language Model. The student could begin with either, and the software could offer both and let the student choose, which keeps the student's agency (Chapter 1) while the graph guarantees the choice is valid. The sim below practices the rule.

docs.title: Diagram: Ready Concepts Finder
docs.text:
Ready Concepts Finder

Type: graph-model sim-id: ready-concepts-finder Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve six problems by selecting exactly the set of ready concepts in a 16-concept learning graph for a given set of mastered concepts, correctly answering at least five of six on the first attempt.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/automating-instructional-design/tree/main/docs/sims/learning-dependency-network

Prerequisites: learning dependency, foundational concept, directed acyclic graph, learning path, the ready rule (all defined in the section "Learning Graphs: Maps of Concepts" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 6 problems, the learner selects the set of nodes they judge to be ready and submits it. A selection is correct when it equals the "Ready set" in Content exactly, with no missing and no extra nodes. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Selecting a node to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A concept is ready as soon as one prerequisite is mastered. (2) A concept already mastered can still be ready. (3) Only one concept can be ready at a time.

Instructional Rationale: Solving a ready-set problem applies the rule step by step: for each unmastered node, check every direct prerequisite. Problems with an empty mastered set, several ready nodes, and a single ready node show the range of cases.

Content:

Sixteen concepts taken from this book's learning graph (provenance below), with their direct prerequisites. An arrow from a concept points to its prerequisites.

Concept Direct prerequisites Artificial Intelligence none Exponential Growth none AI Capability Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning Artificial Intelligence Doubling Time Exponential Growth AI Benchmark AI Capability Large Language Model Machine Learning METR AI Benchmark AI Agent Large Language Model Benchmark Task Suite METR, AI Benchmark Task Horizon METR, AI Capability 50 Percent Time Horizon Task Horizon Human Working Time Task Horizon Long-Running Task Task Horizon, AI Agent Task Success Rate Task Horizon Five-Month Doubling Task Horizon, 50 Percent Time Horizon, Human Working Time, Benchmark Task Suite, Long-Running Task, Task Success Rate, Doubling Time

The ready rule: a concept is ready when it is not mastered and every one of its direct prerequisites is mastered.

Six problems:

# Mastered concepts Ready set Why (shown as feedback) 1 none Artificial Intelligence; Exponential Growth Only concepts with no prerequisites can be ready when nothing is mastered. 2 Artificial Intelligence; Exponential Growth AI Capability; Machine Learning; Doubling Time Each depends only on a mastered concept. 3 Artificial Intelligence; Exponential Growth; AI Capability; Machine Learning; Doubling Time AI Benchmark; Large Language Model Each depends only on mastered concepts; METR still needs AI Benchmark. 4 Artificial Intelligence; Exponential Growth; AI Capability; Machine Learning; Doubling Time; AI Benchmark; Large Language Model; METR; AI Agent Benchmark Task Suite; Task Horizon Both depend only on mastered concepts; Long-Running Task still needs Task Horizon. 5 All nine from problem 4, plus Benchmark Task Suite and Task Horizon 50 Percent Time Horizon; Human Working Time; Long-Running Task; Task Success Rate All four depend only on Task Horizon, and on AI Agent for the Long-Running Task. 6 All fifteen concepts except Five-Month Doubling Five-Month Doubling It is the only unmastered concept, and all its prerequisites are mastered.

Provenance: The sixteen concepts and their dependencies are copied from docs/learning-graph/learning-graph.json in this repository, restricted to Five-Month Doubling and everything it depends on. The sim must copy the values into its own folder, not read the file at run time.

Rules: The ready set for a problem is computed by the ready rule from the table. Each problem has exactly one correct ready set. A problem is scored on its first submitted set only. The score counts first-attempt correct sets out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5. Mastered nodes are shown as already known and cannot be selected.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the graph with the mastered concepts marked, and the problem number.
  2. The learner selects every concept they judge to be ready and submits.
  3. The sim marks the answer and highlights the correct ready concepts and the prerequisites that make them ready.
  4. If incorrect, the learner may select again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct set and reason are shown.
  5. After all 6 problems, the sim shows the score.
  6. The learner should notice that the number of ready concepts rises from two to four and then falls to one as the student nears the goal.

Feedback: 6 problems, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct. [Why text]." Incorrect with a missing node: "At least one ready concept is missing. Check every unmastered concept's prerequisites." Incorrect with an extra node: "At least one selected concept still has an unmastered prerequisite." After the second wrong attempt the correct set is shown with the Why text. Score "n of 6" is shown at the end.

Starting State: The full graph is shown with problem 1, no concepts mastered, and the prompt "Which concepts could this student start on?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked examples use the same sixteen concepts: seven layers, 15 prerequisites of Five-Month Doubling, and the ready set of AI Benchmark and Large Language Model for the mastered set of problem 3. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

docs.title: Interoperability Standards
docs.text:
A learning graph, a Learning Record Store, and a textbook are useful only if they can exchange information with the other tools a school uses: the learning management system, the student information system that holds rosters and grades, and the assessment tools. Interoperability standards are agreed technical specifications that let separate software products exchange data and work together without custom, one-off integrations. They are the electrical sockets of educational software: any compliant plug fits any compliant outlet.

Interoperability matters for three reasons. It prevents lock-in, in which a school cannot leave a vendor because its data and workflows are tied to proprietary formats. It lowers cost, since a tool built once to a standard works in every compliant system. And it lets small and open projects take part: a free Level 2 textbook that follows the standards can be dropped into any school's learning management system.

Two organizations produce most of the standards that matter here.

IMS Global standards are the specifications of the IMS Global Learning Consortium, a nonprofit of schools, universities, and technology companies, which renamed itself 1EdTech in 2022. Its best-known standards are these:

  • Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) lets an outside tool plug into a learning management system, with single sign-on and the ability to return grades.
  • OneRoster exchanges class rosters, enrollments, and grades between a school's student information system and learning tools.
  • Question and Test Interoperability (QTI) exchanges quiz questions and tests between systems.
  • Common Cartridge packages course content so that it can be imported into any compliant learning management system.
  • Caliper Analytics describes learning events, in the same spirit as xAPI.

IEEE learning standards are the specifications of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, whose Learning Technology Standards Committee maintains standards for learning technology. These include xAPI, now an IEEE standard (Chapter 8), and the Learning Object Metadata standard, which defines how to describe a learning resource, such as its title, subject, level, and rights, so that it can be found and reused.

Standard Organization What it lets tools do LTI IMS Global (1EdTech) Plug into an LMS with single sign-on and return grades OneRoster IMS Global (1EdTech) Exchange rosters and grades with the student information system QTI IMS Global (1EdTech) Move quiz questions between systems Common Cartridge IMS Global (1EdTech) Package content for import into an LMS Caliper Analytics IMS Global (1EdTech) Report learning events for analytics xAPI IEEE (originating with ADL) Send learning statements to a Learning Record Store Learning Object Metadata IEEE Describe a learning resource so it can be found and reused

docs.title: Worked Example: Fairview's Tool Tangle
docs.text:
Fairview Elementary uses four tools from four vendors: a reading app, a math practice site, a quiz maker, and the district's learning management system. Teachers re-type class rosters into each one, and the principal cannot see a student's work across the tools.

Problem Standard that addresses it Result Rosters typed into four tools OneRoster The district's roster system feeds all four tools automatically A separate login for each tool LTI The tools open from inside the LMS with one sign-on Quizzes trapped in the quiz maker QTI Questions move to another tool when needed No view of work across tools xAPI All four tools send statements to one record store A free textbook that cannot join the LMS LTI, Common Cartridge The textbook opens from the LMS like any other tool

The district does not need to build any integration itself. It needs to require the standards in its purchasing criteria, which is the subject of Chapter 21. A vendor that supports none of them is a lock-in risk, whatever its brochure says.

Ask for the standards by name

When a vendor says "it integrates with everything," ask: "Which standards? LTI, OneRoster, xAPI?" A vendor who supports them will say so in one sentence, and one who doesn't will talk about "custom integrations," which usually means extra cost and lock-in.

docs.title: Delivering Content at Scale
docs.text: Now the second half of Ms. Singh's question: how does the content reach every student?

docs.title: Generate Once, Serve Many
docs.text:
Generate once, serve many is the delivery model at the center of the book's low-cost design. AI is used to create the content one time, with human review, as Chapter 7 described, and the finished content is then served to every student as ordinary web pages. The expensive step, creation, happens once. The cheap step, serving, happens a million times. The alternative, "generate for each student," would call an AI model every time a student asks for a lesson, so the cost grows with every student and every request.

Web page hosting is the service that stores a website's files and delivers them to browsers on request. For a static site it is among the cheapest services in computing: the host simply sends stored files. Many hosts, including GitHub Pages, which serves this book, offer static hosting at no charge for public projects, within generous limits, and commercial hosts charge pennies. A content delivery network can copy the files to servers close to each school to make them load faster.

docs.title: Worked Example: Once Versus Every Time
docs.text:
Use the Chapter 7 illustration: a 20-chapter interactive textbook costs about $22,400 to produce with AI assistance and human review. Compare two ways to serve a school year to N students. In the first, the book is generated once and served as static pages, so the cost is the one-time $22,400 plus almost nothing to serve it. In the second, an AI model generates each student's lessons live, which uses about 3.6 million tokens a student per year (the Chapter 4 usage), at the illustrative $2.00 per million tokens, or $7.20 per student per year.

Students N Generate once: cost per student Generate once: total Live generation: total per year 100 $224.00 $22,400 $720 1,000 $22.40 $22,400 $7,200 12,000 $1.87 $22,400 $86,400 1,000,000 $0.02 $22,400 $7,200,000

For a very small group, live generation is cheaper, since nothing has to be produced in advance. The lines cross at about \( 22{,}400 / 7.20 \approx 3{,}100 \) students. Beyond that, generate-once wins, and at a million students the one-time cost is about one three-hundred-twentieth of the live cost. The comparison understates the first approach's advantage, because the one-time content can serve students for several years, and it overstates it in one respect: live generation can personalize far more than a fixed book can. The right choice depends on what you need, and this book's design uses generate-once for the bulk of content and reserves live AI for the places where it adds the most, as Chapter 6's levels suggested.

docs.title: Diagram: Generate Once Versus Generate for Each Student
docs.text:
Generate Once Versus Generate for Each Student

Type: chart sim-id: generate-once-vs-live-cost Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare the total yearly cost of generating content once and serving it to all students with the cost of generating it live for each student, and determine the number of students at which the two are equal, to within 100 students.

Prerequisites: generate once serve many, web page hosting, AI inference cost (defined in this chapter and Chapter 4).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the controls unlock, the learner commits three answers: (Q1) the generate-once cost per student for 12,000 students; (Q2) the live-generation total per year for 12,000 students; (Q3) the number of students at which the two totals are equal. An answer is correct when it is within the tolerance in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Exploring the controls afterward is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Live generation is always more expensive. (2) Serving static pages costs as much as generating them. (3) The cost of generate-once grows with the number of students.

Instructional Rationale: Comparing a fixed cost with a per-student cost requires finding where the two lines cross. Calculating a few points first and then locating the break-even makes the structure of the argument clear.

Content:

Cost model: generate-once total = production cost (one-time) + serving cost (zero in this model). Live-generation total = tokens per student per year × price per million tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × number of students.

Controls:

Input Min Max Step Default Unit Production cost of the book 5,000 100,000 100 22,400 dollars Tokens per student per year 1,000,000 10,000,000 100,000 3,600,000 tokens Price per million tokens 4 choices: 0.07, 0.20, 2.00, 20.00 2.00 dollars Number of students 100 1,000,000 100 12,000 students

Check values at the chapter's settings (production cost $22,400, 3.6 million tokens, $2.00 per million): live cost per student per year $7.20.

Students Generate-once cost per student Generate-once total Live-generation total 100 $224.00 $22,400 $720 1,000 $22.40 $22,400 $7,200 12,000 $1.87 $22,400 $86,400 1,000,000 $0.02 $22,400 $7,200,000

Answers: Q1 = $1.87 (±$0.01); Q2 = $86,400 (±$100); Q3 = about 3,100 students (±100).

Provenance: The $22,400 production cost is the illustrative Chapter 7 value for a 20-chapter AI-assisted book. The token usage and $2.00 price are the illustrative Chapter 4 and Chapter 7 values. The sim must label all of them "Illustrative."

Rules: Generate-once cost per student = production cost ÷ students. Live total = students × tokens ÷ 1,000,000 × price. Break-even students = production cost ÷ live cost per student.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers Q1, Q2, and Q3 and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and unlocks the controls.
  3. The learner changes the price, the tokens, and the number of students. Two lines and the break-even point update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that lowering the price moves the break-even number of students up, and that the generate-once line is flat.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [value]. [Working text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Check the units: the price is per million tokens." After the second wrong attempt the value and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The generate-once line and the live-generation line are drawn for the default settings, the question is hidden, and the prompt reads "At how many students does generating once become cheaper?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table uses a production cost of $22,400, 3.6 million tokens, a $2.00 price, $7.20 per student, and break-even at about 3,100 students, with totals of $86,400 at 12,000 students and $7,200,000 at 1,000,000.

docs.title: Reaching Fairview: Devices, Connectivity, and Offline Access
docs.text:
A delivery model that is cheap on paper still has to work in a school with old computers and slow internet. Three terms describe what has to be true.

Device access is whether each student has a working device with a browser and a screen large enough to use, at school and, where homework is involved, at home. A device is the largest cost in digital learning (Chapter 7), and an uneven spread of devices is among the most important equity gaps in education. Pew Research surveys around 2018 found that roughly one in six U.S. teenagers said they could not always complete homework because they lacked a reliable computer or internet connection. During the 2020 school closures that gap became visible nationwide, and federal programs such as the Emergency Connectivity Fund responded with billions of dollars for devices and connections.

Internet connectivity is the quality and capacity of a school's and students' connection to the internet: its speed (bandwidth), its reliability, and its cost. Static pages and browser-based simulations are lighter than video or live AI chat, which keeps them workable on slower connections. But a rural school's connection is shared by every device at once, and bandwidth that is fine for one student may not be fine for twenty-eight.

Offline access is the ability to use content without any connection at all. A static website is made of ordinary files, so a copy can be saved to a laptop or a USB drive, or the browser can store the pages it has already loaded, and students can keep working with the network down. Live AI chat cannot work offline, since it needs a connection to a remote model. This makes the choice of level a connectivity decision: Levels 1 and 2 are available offline, Level 3 can buffer records and send them later, and Levels 4 and 5 need a live connection.

Browser-based simulation is a simulation, such as a MicroSim, that runs inside the student's browser, using the device's own processor, with nothing to install and no server doing the computation. That is why it works on a basic school laptop or Chromebook, costs nothing per use, and exposes no student data: the calculation happens on the student's own device. The drawback is that it depends on the device being capable enough.

An interactive visualization is a graphic that the learner can manipulate to explore data or a model, by hovering, filtering, zooming, or changing a setting, rather than merely looking at it. The graph viewer earlier in this chapter is one: you can search for a concept, filter categories, and follow its arrows. Interactive visualizations help most when the data is too large or too connected to understand from a static picture.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Slow Connection and an Offline Copy
docs.text:
Fairview Elementary shares a 1.5 megabit-per-second connection among its devices. Suppose a chapter page with its simulations is about 3 megabytes (an illustrative size). Converting units, 1.5 megabits per second is \( 1.5 / 8 = 0.1875 \) megabytes per second.

Situation Calculation Time One student opens the page 3 MB ÷ 0.1875 MB/s about 16 seconds Twenty-eight students open it together 28 × 3 MB ÷ 0.1875 MB/s about 448 seconds, or 7.5 minutes The teacher downloaded the page to a shared folder the night before Read from local storage under a second The whole 23-chapter book at about 5 MB a chapter 23 × 5 MB = 115 MB, which fits easily on a USB stick Copied once

The point of the table is that the design decides the experience. A static, offline-capable textbook turns a seven-minute wait into no wait at all, and the same is not true of a design that needs a fresh network round-trip for every click. A school with a poor connection should ask every vendor: "What works offline? How much data does a lesson download? Can the content be cached on the school network?"

'Works on the web' is not 'works at Fairview'

A common trap is testing a product on the best connection in the district and calling it ready. Instead, test on the worst: an old device, a shared slow link, and no connection at all. If it fails there, it will widen the equity gap the district says it wants to close.

docs.title: Student Progress Dashboards
docs.text:
A student progress dashboard is a display of what a student has done and mastered, shown to the student, the teacher, and the family. It is the visible output of the whole chain of Chapter 8: statements become mastery data, mastery data joins the learning graph, and the dashboard presents the result in a form a person can act on. A good dashboard has a different job for each audience: it shows the student what they have mastered and what is ready next; it shows the teacher which concepts and which students need attention; and it shows the family progress in plain language.

Dashboards can help or harm, depending on design. A dashboard that ranks students against each other can discourage the ones who are behind. One that shows a long list of every click can drown the reader in noise. A well-designed dashboard shows a student their own progress, not their place in a ranking, and always shows a next step.

docs.title: Worked Example: Maya's Dashboard
docs.text:
A good progress dashboard for Maya after the Lincoln Middle pilot might show the following.

Part What it shows Goal "Ready for the March 12 unit test" Mastered Fractions as parts of a whole; Whole-number multiplication and division; Multiplying and dividing fractions Ready next Equivalent fractions In progress Ratios (waiting on equivalent fractions) This week 4 sessions, 1 hour 10 minutes A note from your teacher "Try the tiles simulation first, then the check."

It contains no comparison with classmates, no points total, and no grade. It tells Maya what she knows, what to do next, and gives her a human voice. Compare this with the dashboard that lists her rank in the class, which tells her only where she stands.

docs.title: Answering Ms. Singh
docs.text:
Ms. Singh's two questions now have answers. On structure: a learning graph, a directed acyclic graph of concept nodes, lets the software pick each student's next concept by a simple rule, and interoperability standards, LTI, OneRoster, QTI, xAPI, and the rest, let the tools from different vendors share rosters, logins, questions, and records without custom work. On delivery: generate-once, serve-many content keeps the cost per student far below live generation at scale, static pages and browser-based simulations work on modest devices, and offline access keeps students working when the network does not.

The story has both sides. The benefit: a design that, with the right choices, can reach Fairview as well as Lincoln Middle. The risks: devices that are too old, connections that are too slow, a product that quietly requires a live connection, and vendors whose tools cannot share data. The response is the set of questions in this chapter, and a district that tests every product at its worst-connected school before it buys.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A concept node is one concept in a learning graph; a learning dependency is an arrow from a concept to its prerequisite; a foundational concept has no prerequisites. This book's graph has 532 concepts, 961 dependencies, and 14 foundational concepts.
  • A learning graph must be a directed acyclic graph, with no cycles, so the concepts can always be put in an order where each follows its prerequisites.
  • A learning path is built by collecting the goal's prerequisites, removing what the student has mastered, and ordering the rest; a concept is ready when it is unmastered and all its direct prerequisites are mastered. Five-Month Doubling rests on 15 concepts in seven layers.
  • Interoperability standards prevent lock-in; IMS Global standards (LTI, OneRoster, QTI, Common Cartridge, Caliper) and IEEE learning standards (xAPI, Learning Object Metadata) let tools share logins, rosters, questions, and records.
  • Generate once, serve many pays for content creation once and then relies on cheap web page hosting; in our example live generation costs more beyond about 3,100 students.
  • Device access, Internet connectivity, and offline access decide whether a design reaches every school; browser-based simulations and static pages work on modest devices and can run offline, while live AI chat cannot.
  • An interactive visualization helps explore large connected data, and a good student progress dashboard shows each student what they have mastered and what is ready next, without ranking them.

You can say how it reaches Fairview

You just learned how a learning graph chooses the next step, which standards let tools cooperate, and why generate-once content with offline access can reach a school with a slow connection and old devices. Chapter 10 takes on the hard question these records raise: protecting student privacy and governing the data. One step at a time, together.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the level-3 privacy inflection point: why adaptive and higher-level textbooks need detailed student data, and what that triggers — FERPA, COPPA, GDPR, data governance, and algorithmic bias auditing — illustrated by the inBloom shutdown and the PowerSchool data breach. Readers finish able to assess whether a school's data governance is ready for a level-3-or-higher textbook.

docs.text:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
  • Chapter 6: The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks
  • Chapter 8: Tracking Mastery: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, and MicroSims

docs.title: A Parent Who Reads the News
docs.text:
At the next parent night, a father named Mr. Chen, who works in network security, stands up with a printout. "I read that a company that holds records for tens of millions of students was breached last winter," he says. "You're about to ask us to let a system keep a record of every mistake my daughter makes. Why should I trust it more than that company?"

Ms. Okafor does not argue. She thanks him, because he has asked the central question of the whole Level 3 design. Everything in the earlier chapters that makes a textbook adaptive requires a record about a child. The better the adaptation, the more detailed the record. And records can leak, be misused, or be kept long after anyone needs them.

This chapter takes that problem seriously. It explains what student data is and what the law requires, how a school governs the data it holds, how it checks that an algorithm treats groups of students fairly, and what two real failures, inBloom and the PowerSchool breach, teach. It ends with a way for a school to judge whether it is ready for a Level 3 textbook. The goal is the book's usual one: strengthen the benefits of personalization and reduce the harm.

Take the hard question first

This is the chapter where trust gets built or lost, so we'll answer Mr. Chen's question with specifics instead of reassurance. You'll learn what the main privacy laws ask of a school, how to govern data, and how to tell whether a district is ready for an adaptive textbook. Let's find the balance between a textbook that knows a student well and a school that protects what it knows.

docs.title: What Counts as Student Data
docs.text:
Student data is any information that a school, or a company working for a school, collects, creates, or keeps about a student. It is broader than the grade book. It includes enrollment and demographic information, attendance, grades and test scores, discipline records, health and special-education information, eligibility for free or reduced-price lunch, and, increasingly, what a student does inside digital learning tools: answers, time on task, and clicks.

Personally identifiable data, often called personally identifiable information or PII, is any student data that identifies a particular student, either on its own or in combination with other information. It has two kinds. Direct identifiers single out a person by themselves: a name, a student ID number, a home address, a photograph, a fingerprint. Indirect identifiers, also called linkable data, do not name anyone but can identify a student when combined: a birth date together with a ZIP code and a gender, for example. Latanya Sweeney's research found that those three facts alone were enough to uniquely identify about 87 percent of Americans, which is why "we removed the names" does not make a data set anonymous.

Student data privacy is the protection of student data from unauthorized access, use, and disclosure, and the right of students and families to know about and control how it is used. It has two sides. One is security: keeping outsiders out. The other is appropriate use: making sure that people who legitimately hold the data use it only for the purposes for which it was collected.

docs.title: Worked Example: Is This Field Identifying?
docs.text:
Mr. Chen's daughter has a record in a Level 3 textbook. Consider several fields in it.

Field Identifies on its own? Why Name Yes: direct identifier It names the student State student ID Yes: direct identifier It is unique to one student Birth date plus ZIP code plus gender No, but identifies in combination Together they are unique for most people The district's average score on a test No It describes a group, not an individual Grade 7, Lincoln Middle, the only student there with a hearing impairment In combination The small group size makes the student identifiable

The last row is the subtle one. Data about a group can identify an individual when the group is small enough. This is why privacy rules often suppress results for groups under a minimum size, a threshold such as ten students.

docs.title: Diagram: Is This Data Identifying?
docs.text:
Is This Data Identifying?

Type: microsim sim-id: is-this-data-identifying Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eight data fields as direct identifiers, identifiers in combination, or not identifying, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: student data, personally identifiable data, direct identifier, indirect identifier, small-group identification (all defined in the section "What Counts as Student Data" above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 data fields in one of three categories and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct category" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the category definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Removing names makes data anonymous. (2) Group data can never identify a person. (3) Only a name or ID number counts as identifying.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying fields requires applying the distinction between identifying alone and identifying in combination. Including a small-group field and a combination of ordinary facts makes the learner use the idea of linkability, not just recognize obvious identifiers.

Content:

Three categories:

Category Definition shown Direct identifier Identifies a specific student on its own Identifies in combination Not identifying alone, but identifies a student when combined with other facts or because the group is very small Not identifying Describes a large group or carries no link to any individual

Eight fields:

# Data field shown to the learner Correct category Why (shown as feedback) 1 A student's full name Direct identifier It names the student. 2 A state-assigned student ID number Direct identifier It is unique to one student. 3 A home street address Direct identifier It points to a specific household and student. 4 A birth date, a ZIP code, and a gender, together Identifies in combination Together they are unique for most people. 5 A fingerprint used to log in to a school device Direct identifier A biometric is unique to one person. 6 The district-wide average score on the state math test Not identifying It describes thousands of students, not one. 7 Grade 7, Lincoln Middle, and a hearing impairment, when only one student at that school has one Identifies in combination With a group of one, the facts point to a single student. 8 The number of students absent from the district today Not identifying It is a district-wide count that points to no one.

Provenance: The categories follow the chapter section "What Counts as Student Data." The 87 percent figure cited in the chapter is from Latanya Sweeney's research on the identifiability of birth date, ZIP code, and gender. The fields are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each field has exactly one correct category, given in Content. A field is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one data field at a time and the three categories.
  2. The learner places the field and submits. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct category and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 fields, the sim shows the score and lists misplaced fields with their correct categories.
  5. The learner should notice that fields 4 and 7 contain no name, yet still identify a student.

Feedback: 8 fields, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [category]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the category]." After the second attempt the correct category is revealed and the field counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can spot data that identifies a student." For a score < 7: "Review the three categories and try again; the fields will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Field 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the three categories, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "Does this field identify a student?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter names two kinds of identifier, direct and indirect, and states that small groups can identify individuals. It cites the 87 percent finding for birth date, ZIP code, and gender. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: The Privacy Inflection Point
docs.text:
The privacy inflection point is the level of the five-level model at which a textbook's data needs change from almost none to substantial. As Chapter 6 explained, Levels 1 and 2 need no record about an individual student. At Level 3 and above, the textbook needs the data that makes adaptation possible, and the privacy duties of this chapter begin to apply.

Two kinds of data drive the change. A detailed learning history is a long, time-ordered record of everything a student has attempted, answered, and struggled with: every wrong answer to every question over years. It is the same record that makes a Level 3 textbook useful, and it is a portrait of a child's mind. Behavioral data is data about how a student acts while learning, rather than what they answer: how long they hesitate, what they click, which hints they request, when they log in, how they type. It can reveal much more than anyone intended, such as attention, frustration, a learning difference, or a home situation.

Neither kind of data is dangerous by existing. The danger is in how much is kept, for how long, by whom, and for what use, which is why the rest of the chapter is about rules and governance.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Changes at Level 3
docs.text:
The table compares what Maya's school holds under a Level 2 textbook and a Level 3 textbook for the same unit.

Level 2 textbook Level 3 textbook Stored about Maya Nothing A coded record of every answer, in order, for the year Tracks behavior No Yes: time on page, hints requested, session times Who could see it Not applicable Teacher, family, and the vendor's systems, unless limited If the system is breached No student data exposed A year of Maya's learning history exposed Privacy review needed Accessibility and accuracy only Records, consent, retention, bias, and breach plan

The comparison is not an argument against Level 3. It is an argument for doing Level 3 deliberately, with a governance process, which the rest of this chapter describes.

The same record is the benefit and the risk

Notice that the record that shows Maya exactly which fraction idea to review is also the record that would harm her if it leaked. You can't keep the benefit and delete the risk; you can only shrink the risk with rules. That's why every Level 3 decision begins with "what do we actually need to keep?"

docs.title: The Laws: FERPA, COPPA, and GDPR
docs.text:
Three laws shape most of what a school must do. Each has a different scope, and a school may be subject to more than one.

FERPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, is the main U.S. federal law protecting student education records. It gives parents, and students who turn 18, the right to inspect their education records and to ask for corrections. It generally requires written consent before a school discloses personally identifiable information from those records, with exceptions. One important exception lets a school share data with a vendor that acts as a "school official" with a legitimate educational interest, provided the school keeps direct control of how the vendor uses and protects the data. FERPA applies to schools that receive federal education funds, and the U.S. Department of Education can withhold funds for violations. It does not give individuals a right to sue, which the Supreme Court held in 2002.

COPPA, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, protects children under 13 online. It requires operators of websites and online services directed at children, or that know they collect data from them, to give notice and get verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information, and it is enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. The FTC has allowed schools to consent on behalf of parents for educational uses only, which means a school that signs a vendor's terms takes on a responsibility for what the vendor does with the data. COPPA was updated by an FTC rule in 2025, so a district should check the current requirements.

GDPR, the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, in force since 2018, is a comprehensive privacy law covering the personal data of people in the EU, wherever the organization is located. It requires a lawful basis for processing, collection of only what is needed, and gives individuals rights to access, correct, delete, and move their data (Chapter 8's portability). Penalties can reach 20 million euros or four percent of worldwide annual revenue, whichever is higher. A U.S. school generally falls outside GDPR, but a vendor serving European students, and any school with students resident in the EU, may not.

Many U.S. states have added their own student-privacy laws. California's Student Online Personal Information Protection Act of 2014, for example, bars educational technology operators from using student data for targeted advertising or from building profiles for non-educational purposes. A district should know which of its state's laws apply.

Law Where Protects Key requirements FERPA United States Education records of students in federally funded schools Parent and student access and correction; consent before disclosure, with a school-official exception COPPA United States Personal information of children under 13 online Notice and verifiable parental consent; school consent allowed for educational use only GDPR European Union Personal data of people in the EU Lawful basis, data minimization, rights to access, erase, and port data; large fines State laws Varies by state Student data from educational technology operators Often ban targeted advertising and non-educational profiling

Legal is not the same as trusted

A common trap is treating "we comply with FERPA" as the end of the conversation. The laws set a floor, and several have exceptions that let a vendor hold data under a school's authority. Families judge you on what actually happens, so ask what the vendor does with the data, not only whether the form is signed. This is general information, not legal advice; check with your district's counsel.

docs.title: Data Governance and Its Parts
docs.text:
Data governance is the set of policies, roles, and processes by which an organization manages its data throughout its life: what is collected, who may use it, how it is protected, how long it is kept, and how problems are handled. A school with good data governance can answer, for any piece of student data, "who is responsible for this, and why do we have it?" It usually includes a named accountable person or committee, a list of every tool and the data it holds, vendor review, staff training, and a plan for when something goes wrong.

Five practices form the core of governance for a Level 3 textbook.

Data minimization is the practice of collecting only the data needed for a stated purpose and no more. It is a GDPR principle and an ethical one, and it is the cheapest protection there is: data that was never collected cannot be leaked. Before adding a field, a school asks what decision the field will inform.

Informed consent is a family's agreement to data collection that is given with real understanding: knowing what is collected, why, who sees it, how long it is kept, what the risks are, and what the alternatives are, including the ability to decline. A signature on a long form that no one reads is not informed consent. Good consent is specific, in plain language, and revocable.

A data retention policy is a written rule for how long each kind of data is kept and when it is deleted. A learning record that helps a teacher this semester has little value in ten years, and every extra year of storage is a year of breach risk. A typical policy keeps detailed records while the student is enrolled and deletes or de-identifies them a short time after the student leaves, except where the law requires longer.

Data ownership is the question of who has the rights to student data, meaning who controls it, who may use it, and who profits from it. The usual sound position, reflected in the student-controlled data of Chapter 8, is that the data belongs to the student and family and the school, and that a vendor is a custodian that may use it only to provide the service. Contracts should say so explicitly, and should bar the vendor from selling the data or using it to train commercial products.

Governance readiness is the degree to which a school has these practices in place and is therefore prepared to adopt a Level 3 or higher textbook safely. The last section of this chapter turns it into a checklist.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Retention Schedule
docs.text:
Lincoln Middle's draft retention schedule for the Level 3 pilot looks like this. The periods are illustrative; real ones depend on law and district policy.

Data Why it is kept Kept until Answer-level records (each answer, in order) Choosing the next concept End of the school year Concept mastery summary Planning and reporting progress One year after the student leaves the school Behavioral data (clicks, hints, timing) Improving the textbook Aggregated at the end of each term, then raw data deleted Consent forms Proof of consent Seven years Breach and incident logs Accountability Seven years

The schedule shows data minimization at work: the most detailed data, the answer-level record, is kept the shortest time, and the most personal, behavioral data, is reduced to summaries quickly.

docs.title: Algorithmic Bias, Auditing, and Transparency
docs.text:
A system that adapts to students also makes judgments about them: who is ahead, who is at risk, who should get which task. Algorithmic bias is a systematic and unfair difference in a system's results for different groups of people, arising from the data the system learned from, the way it was designed, or the way it is used. A system can be biased without anyone intending it. If an at-risk prediction model learns from past data in which students from some schools were less often given advanced courses, it may repeat that pattern as if it were a fact about the students.

Real cases exist in education. In 2020, the United Kingdom replaced cancelled exams with an algorithm that adjusted teacher-assigned grades using schools' past results, and it lowered grades most often for students at schools that historically scored lower, so the government withdrew it after protests. A 2023 investigation by The Markup reported that Wisconsin's early-warning system for dropout risk produced more false alarms for Black and Hispanic students than for white students. And a 2023 Stanford study found that several AI-writing detectors falsely flagged the work of non-native English writers far more often than that of native writers, a point the book returns to in Chapter 21.

Algorithmic bias auditing is the systematic testing of a system's outputs across groups of people to find unfair differences. An audit compares measures such as how often each group is recommended for an opportunity, how often each group is wrongly flagged, and how accurate the system is for each group. One common screening test comes from employment law, where the "four-fifths rule" treats a group's selection rate as a warning sign when it is less than 80 percent of the rate of the most-selected group. A result below that line does not prove unfairness; it tells the auditors where to look.

Algorithmic transparency is the ability of the people affected by a system, and those responsible for it, to know what it does, what data it uses, and why it made a particular decision. A transparent system documents its rules, explains its recommendations in plain language, and lets families ask how a decision about their child was made. The simple mastery rule of Chapter 8, "four of the last five answers correct," is transparent: a parent can check it. A complex model that no one can explain is much harder to audit or contest, which is one more reason the book's design favors transparent, rule-based adaptation at Level 3.

docs.title: Worked Example: A Four-Fifths Audit
docs.text:
A district's adaptive system recommends students for an advanced math pathway. An audit counts how many students in each of three groups were eligible and how many were recommended. The numbers are illustrative.

Group Eligible Recommended Selection rate Ratio to highest rate A 500 200 40.0% 1.00 B 300 72 24.0% \( 24.0/40.0 = 0.60 \) C 200 70 35.0% \( 35.0/40.0 \approx 0.88 \)

Group A has the highest rate, 40 percent. Group C's ratio of 0.88 is above the 0.80 line, so it passes the screen. Group B's ratio of 0.60 is well below it, so the audit flags the system. The next step is investigation: Is the difference explained by something legitimate, such as prior course taking, or is the system relying on a feature that stands in for group membership? A flagged result starts a conversation and does not end one.

docs.title: Diagram: Four-Fifths Bias Audit Calculator
docs.text:
Four-Fifths Bias Audit Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: four-fifths-bias-audit-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate selection rates and four-fifths ratios for three student groups and identify which groups the audit flags, correctly answering three of three questions.

Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-strategy-for-education/tree/main/docs/sims/algorithmic-bias-sources

Prerequisites: algorithmic bias, algorithmic bias auditing, selection rate, the four-fifths rule (all defined in the section "Algorithmic Bias, Auditing, and Transparency" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the controls unlock, the learner commits three answers: (Q1) the selection rate for group B; (Q2) group B's ratio to the highest rate; (Q3) which groups the audit flags. An answer is correct when it equals the value in Content, within the stated tolerance. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Using the controls afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) A flagged result proves the system is unfair. (2) A group with the largest count must have the highest rate. (3) A ratio is a difference in percentage points.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating the rates and ratios from counts makes the audit's logic concrete, and asking which groups are flagged ties the arithmetic to the decision rule. The explanation after the answer stresses that a flag begins an investigation.

Content:

Rule shown: selection rate = recommended ÷ eligible. The highest group's rate is the reference. Ratio = a group's selection rate ÷ the reference rate. A group is flagged when its ratio < 0.80.

Data:

Group Eligible Recommended A 500 200 B 300 72 C 200 70

Controls for exploration:

Input Min Max Step Default Unit Recommended, group A 0 500 10 200 students Recommended, group B 0 300 6 72 students Recommended, group C 0 200 10 70 students

Answers: Q1 = 24.0% (±0.1 percentage point); Q2 = 0.60 (±0.01); Q3 = group B only.

Check values: group A rate 40.0%, ratio 1.00; group C rate 35.0%, ratio 0.875 (shown as 0.88).

Provenance: The counts are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim must label them "Illustrative audit data." The four-fifths threshold is a screening convention from U.S. employment-selection guidance, applied here as an illustration.

Rules: Rate = recommended ÷ eligible. Reference = the highest rate. Ratio = rate ÷ reference, shown to two decimals. A group is flagged when ratio < 0.80. When recommended is changed, rates, ratios, and flags update at once. If every recommended count is zero, no ratio is shown and the sim says "No recommendations to audit."

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers Q1, Q2, and Q3 and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and shows the table with rates, ratios, and flags.
  3. The learner changes the recommended counts. The rates, ratios, and flags update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that group B can be moved above the line by raising its recommended count to at least 96, and that the flag is a prompt to investigate, not a verdict.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Q1 correct: "Correct: 72 ÷ 300 is 24.0%." Q1 incorrect: "Divide the number recommended by the number eligible." Q2 correct: "Correct: 24.0 ÷ 40.0 is 0.60." Q2 incorrect: "Divide group B's rate by the highest rate, group A's." Q3 correct: "Correct: only group B is below 0.80." Q3 incorrect: "Flag any group whose ratio is below 0.80." After the second wrong attempt the answer and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The counts are shown for three groups with no rates, and the prompt reads "Is the system recommending students from every group at similar rates?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses groups A, B, and C with eligible counts of 500, 300, and 200 and recommended counts of 200, 72, and 70, rates of 40.0, 24.0, and 35.0 percent, ratios of 1.00, 0.60, and about 0.88, and a threshold of 0.80.

docs.title: Learning from Failure: inBloom and PowerSchool
docs.text:
Two real cases, both in the book's AI-First Stories appendix, show what the principles above protect against.

inBloom was a nonprofit launched in 2013 with about $100 million in funding, mainly from the Gates Foundation, to store student data from several states in one shared cloud service and let educational software use it. Its goals were reasonable, and its design collected an enormous number of data fields in one place. Parents, in New York and elsewhere, objected that they had not been told, could not control what was held, and did not trust a centralized repository. State after state withdrew, and inBloom closed in 2014. The lesson is that technical soundness is not enough: a data project fails without the trust of families, and that trust depends on clear rules about who owns and controls the data.

The PowerSchool data breach came in December 2024. PowerSchool, one of the largest vendors of student information systems, disclosed that attackers had gained access to records for tens of millions of students and teachers. Reporting at the time indicated that the attackers used stolen credentials to reach a support system, and that the account lacked multi-factor authentication, though the details should be checked against the latest reports. The lesson is that records held by one large vendor become a single, valuable target.

A data breach is an incident in which unauthorized people gain access to protected data. Centralized student records are student records held in one large store, whether by a vendor or a district, rather than spread across many separate ones. Centralization has benefits, since one store is easier to secure well and to share across tools, and a serious cost: a successful attacker gets everything at once. This is the case for keeping the sensitive store small, minimizing what it holds, and deleting data on schedule.

Vendor risk is the risk that a school's data is harmed through a company it relies on. Most school data lives with vendors, so a school's security is only as good as its vendors', and a school cannot fully outsource accountability. Managing vendor risk means checking a vendor's security practices before signing, requiring breach notification in the contract within a short, stated time, limiting what data the vendor receives, and planning for the vendor's failure or sale.

Cybersecurity in schools is the set of measures that protect school computers, networks, and data from attack. Schools are frequent targets of ransomware, a kind of attack that locks a school's systems until a payment is made. A 2022 report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that ransomware attacks on school districts caused weeks of lost learning time and months of recovery. Core measures are well known: multi-factor authentication for every account that can reach student data, prompt software updates, regular backups kept offline, giving each person only the access they need, and training staff to recognize phishing.

docs.title: Worked Example: What Each Failure Teaches
docs.text:
Case What went wrong Which practice would have helped inBloom (2014) Parents did not trust a large central store; rules on ownership and use were unclear Informed consent, data minimization, clear data ownership, a transparent explanation of what was kept PowerSchool (2024) One vendor held records for tens of millions; credentials were reportedly stolen Multi-factor authentication, vendor risk checks, data minimization, a retention schedule that deletes old data Any district A vendor is breached and the school learns last Contract clause requiring prompt breach notice, a breach response plan

Ask 'what would an attacker get?'

For any system that holds student data, imagine it is breached tonight and ask what an attacker would walk away with. If the answer is a year of answer-level records tied to names, shrink it: remove names, shorten retention, or collect less. The data you never stored is the data you can't lose.

docs.title: Children, AI, and Trust
docs.text:
Chatbots and adaptive systems that talk with children raise questions beyond data. Responsible AI with minors is the practice of designing, deploying, and supervising AI systems used by children so that they are safe, appropriate, and respectful of children's development and rights. UNESCO's 2023 guidance recommended a minimum age of 13 for classroom use of generative AI, and COPPA already restricts data collection from children under 13. The particular risks include exposure to inappropriate content, inaccurate answers delivered confidently (Chapter 5), data collected from children who cannot meaningfully consent, and chatbots that encourage emotional dependence.

Age-appropriate AI design is the design of AI tools to fit the age and development of their users. Practices include high privacy by default, collecting as little as possible, avoiding features that pressure children to keep using the tool, clear language, filters tuned to the age group, and teacher visibility. The United Kingdom's Age Appropriate Design Code, in force since 2021, is a widely cited model. Chapter 12 returns to guardrails for AI tutors.

The trust paradox is the tension at the center of personalization: the system needs more data to serve a student well, and families will give more data only if they trust the system, and trust requires that the system holds back. A school that collects too much loses trust, and a school that collects too little cannot adapt. Family trust is the confidence that parents and guardians have that a school will act in their children's interest, and it is built by consistent behavior over time rather than by statements. The way out of the paradox is the set of practices in this chapter: collect the minimum, say what you hold, let families see and take their data, delete on schedule, and report problems quickly and honestly.

Governance feels heavy at first

If this much policy sounds overwhelming for a school with no privacy officer, start small. You managed a retention table and a bias audit in this chapter with nothing but arithmetic. Pick three practices, name one accountable person, and add one more each term.

docs.title: Governance Readiness
docs.text:
Putting the chapter together, governance readiness can be checked against a short list. The list below separates six must-have practices, without which a school should not adopt a Level 3 textbook, from four should-have practices that make a school well placed for Level 4.

Practice Why it matters M1 A named person or committee accountable for student data Someone must own the questions M2 An inventory of what student data each tool collects You cannot protect what you have not listed M3 A retention schedule with deletion Old data is old risk M4 Vendor contracts that state the school and family own the data and bar use beyond the service Prevents misuse and lock-in M5 A notice and consent process for families Informed consent and trust M6 A written breach response plan, with vendor notification duties Speed in the first days limits harm S1 A plan to audit adaptive choices for bias Fairness across groups S2 A public explanation of how recommendations are made Algorithmic transparency S3 Annual staff training People are the largest source of risk S4 A data minimization review before each new tool Keeps the store small

The rule: a school is not ready for Level 3 if any must-have is missing. It is ready for Level 3 if all six must-haves are present, and ready for Level 3 and well placed for Level 4 if it also has at least three of the four should-haves.

docs.title: Worked Example: Judging Three Districts
docs.text:
M1 M2 M3 M4 M5 M6 S count Verdict Riverton Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes 0 of 4 Ready for Level 3 Oakdale Yes Yes No Yes Yes Yes 4 of 4 Not ready: no retention schedule Hillcrest Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes 3 of 4 Ready for Level 3 and well placed for Level 4

Oakdale shows the point of the rule. It has every should-have and would look impressive, and it still fails, because it keeps data with no end date. Strong extras do not make up for a missing foundation.

docs.title: Diagram: Governance Readiness Judge
docs.text:
Governance Readiness Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: governance-readiness-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of six districts is not ready, ready for Level 3, or ready for Level 3 and well placed for Level 4, by applying the must-have and should-have rule, correctly judging at least five of six on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: governance readiness, the six must-have and four should-have practices and the readiness rule (all defined in the section "Governance Readiness" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 6 districts, the learner chooses one of three verdicts and submits it. A verdict is correct when it matches the "Correct verdict" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Reading the rule is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Many should-have practices can make up for a missing must-have. (2) A district with one strong feature is ready. (3) Readiness is a score out of ten.

Instructional Rationale: Applying a two-part rule to concrete profiles requires checking the must-haves first and counting the should-haves second. A profile with a missing must-have but all should-haves tests whether the learner applies the rule as written.

Content:

The rule: Not ready if any of M1 to M6 is missing. Otherwise, Ready for Level 3 if fewer than 3 of S1 to S4 are present. Otherwise, Ready for Level 3 and well placed for Level 4.

Practices: M1 accountable person or committee; M2 data inventory; M3 retention schedule with deletion; M4 vendor contracts on ownership and use; M5 notice and consent process; M6 breach response plan; S1 bias-audit plan; S2 public explanation of recommendations; S3 annual staff training; S4 minimization review before each new tool.

Six districts:

# District Practices present Correct verdict Why (shown as feedback) 1 Riverton M1, M2, M3, M4, M5, M6 Ready for Level 3 All must-haves are present and there are no should-haves, which is fewer than 3. 2 Oakdale M1, M2, M4, M5, M6, S1, S2, S3, S4 Not ready M3, a retention schedule, is missing, and should-haves cannot make up for it. 3 Hillcrest M1, M2, M3, M4, M5, M6, S1, S2, S3 Ready for Level 3 and well placed for Level 4 All six must-haves and three should-haves are present. 4 Pinewood M2, M3, M4, M5, M6, S1, S2, S3, S4 Not ready M1, an accountable person, is missing. 5 Lakeview M1, M2, M3, M4, M5, M6, S1 Ready for Level 3 All must-haves are present and only one should-have, which is fewer than 3. 6 Cedar Heights M2, M5, S3 Not ready Four must-haves are missing: M1, M3, M4, and M6.

Provenance: The practices and the rule are this chapter's recommended practice, not a legal standard, and the sim must say so. The districts are fictional, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each district has exactly one correct verdict, determined by the rule. A district is scored on its first submitted verdict only. The score counts first-attempt correct verdicts out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees one district's list of practices and the three verdicts.
  2. The learner chooses a verdict and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may choose again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct verdict and reason are shown.
  4. After all 6 districts, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that district 2 has the most practices and is still not ready.

Feedback: 6 districts, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [verdict]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. First check whether every must-have is present. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the verdict]." After the second attempt the correct verdict is revealed and the district counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 6" is shown. Final message for a score >= 5: "You can judge a district's readiness." For a score < 5: "Review the rule and try again; the districts will be reshuffled."

Starting State: District 1 of the shuffled order is shown with its practices and the score "First-try correct: 0 of 6," and the prompt reads "Is this district ready for a Level 3 textbook?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists six must-have practices (M1 to M6) and four should-have practices (S1 to S4), and the rule: not ready if any must-have is missing; ready for Level 3 with all six; well placed for Level 4 with all six and at least three should-haves. The chapter's worked example has Riverton, Oakdale, and Hillcrest. The mastery bar is 5 of 6.

docs.title: Answering Mr. Chen
docs.text:
Mr. Chen asked why he should trust the system more than the company that was breached. Ms. Okafor's honest answer has four parts. The district will hold less: only what the lesson needs, deleted on a published schedule. It will hold it differently: with multi-factor authentication, vendor contracts that bar misuse, and a written breach plan. It will let families see, take, and delete their data. And it will tell families when something goes wrong, quickly, even when the news is bad. She did not promise it could never happen. She promised the district would be ready.

The story has both sides, like every story in this book. The benefit: a Level 3 textbook that finds Maya's missing prerequisite and saves her years of confusion. The risks: a permanent record of her mistakes, a breach, a biased recommendation, and a loss of family trust that would end the whole effort, as it did at inBloom. The response is governance: minimize, consent, retain briefly, own clearly, audit for bias, explain, and prepare. A school that cannot do these things should stay at Level 2, which is free, effective, and needs none of them.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Student data includes records and learning-tool activity; personally identifiable data can identify a student directly or, in combination or in a small group, indirectly; student data privacy covers both security and appropriate use.
  • The privacy inflection point is Level 3, where a detailed learning history and behavioral data become necessary; the same record is both the benefit and the risk.
  • FERPA (U.S. education records), COPPA (children under 13 online), and GDPR (EU residents) set a floor, and compliance is not the same as trust.
  • Data governance rests on data minimization, informed consent, a data retention policy, and clear data ownership; governance readiness means having the must-have practices in place.
  • Algorithmic bias can arise without intent; algorithmic bias auditing compares results across groups (the four-fifths rule flags ratios below 0.80), and algorithmic transparency lets families understand and contest decisions.
  • inBloom failed for lack of family trust, and the PowerSchool data breach showed the danger of centralized student records; manage vendor risk and practice cybersecurity in schools, especially multi-factor authentication.
  • Responsible AI with minors and age-appropriate AI design call for privacy by default and no pressure on children; the trust paradox is resolved by collecting little, saying what you hold, and building family trust by consistent action.
  • A school that is not ready should stay at Level 2, which needs no student records.

You can say whether a district is ready

You just learned what counts as student data, what FERPA, COPPA, and GDPR ask, how to govern and audit, and how to judge readiness with a rule you can apply in minutes. That closes Part 1 of the book's argument, the evidence and the foundations. Chapter 11 turns to the shorter academic morning itself. One step at a time, together.

docs.title: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
Summary
docs.text: This chapter makes the case for a shorter academic morning: adaptive and mastery learning, personalized pacing, Bloom's two-sigma problem, one-on-one tutoring, and what AI tutors do well, alongside the critical- and computational-thinking skills a compressed morning is meant to protect time for. Readers finish able to summarize the evidence that two to three hours of adaptive learning can match a traditional day's results.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 16 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Adaptive Learning 3301 Academic Morning 1139 Personalized Pacing 955 Gap Filling 955 Compressed Academic Morning 954 Reduced Direct Instruction 890 Freed-Up School Time 871 Critical Thinking 849 Computational Thinking 415 Mastery Learning 244 Bloom's Two-Sigma Problem 226 One-on-One Tutoring 226 AI Tutor 225 Evidence Evaluation 125 Argument Analysis 123 Cognitive Offloading 76

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: The Building Blocks of Schools, Students, and Learning
  • Chapter 2: Evidence, Motivation, and the Stakeholders of Schooling
  • Chapter 3: School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy
  • Chapter 7: Content Economics and Open Educational Resources
  • Chapter 8: Tracking Mastery: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, and MicroSims

docs.title: The Claim That Needs Evidence
docs.text:
At the board meeting where Ms. Okafor presents the pilot results, Mr. Dang, the skeptical teacher from Chapter 5, asks the question the whole book depends on. "You're telling us students could learn today's material in two or three hours a day instead of the five or six we spend now. I've been teaching for twenty years. Where's the proof?"

It is the strongest objection to the book's central idea, and it deserves a direct answer. The idea is that if interactive, adaptive textbooks let each student move at their own pace and fill their own gaps, then the hours spent on whole-class explanation and waiting are no longer needed, and a shorter academic morning could free the rest of the day for something else. The "something else" is the subject of Part 3, the pro-social afternoon. This chapter examines whether the compression itself is plausible.

It does so honestly. The evidence is promising and mixed: some carefully designed studies show large gains in less time, and some real programs have produced disappointing or unclear results. By the end you will be able to say what the evidence supports, what it does not, and which design choices decide the difference.

Does the evidence hold?

This chapter takes Mr. Dang's challenge seriously and walks through the best evidence for and against a shorter morning, including the studies that cut the wrong way. By the end you'll be able to summarize what we know and what we don't, in your own words. Let's find the balance between excitement about a shorter day and respect for the data.

docs.title: Adaptive Learning and Mastery Learning
docs.text:
