Adaptive learning is an approach in which a system adjusts what a student sees, the order, difficulty, and pace, based on data about that student's performance. It is what Level 3 textbooks do (Chapter 6), using the mastery data and learning graph of Chapters 8 and 9. Adaptation can be simple, such as rules that choose the next problem from a mastery record, or statistical, such as a model that estimates the probability the student knows each concept. Well-known examples include the ALEKS mathematics system, based on a theory of "knowledge spaces," and Carnegie Learning's Cognitive Tutor, a mathematics program that tracks each student's skills as they work.

The evidence for adaptive learning is real and modest. A large randomized study of Cognitive Tutor Algebra I by the RAND Corporation found no effect in the first year of use and an effect of about 0.2 standard deviations in the second year, which, by the benchmarks of Chapter 2, is a large effect for a school intervention but one that took time and teacher training to appear. Adaptive learning is not a miracle; it is a tool whose results depend on how it is implemented.

Mastery learning is an instructional approach in which students must demonstrate mastery of a concept, typically 80 to 90 percent on a check, before moving on to the next one, and get extra time and different instruction when they do not. The educational psychologist Benjamin Bloom described it in 1968, building on John Carroll's 1963 observation that learning is a function of the time a student actually spends relative to the time they need. If the time allowed is fixed, achievement varies; if achievement is fixed, the time varies. Mastery learning fixes achievement and lets time vary, the reverse of the seat-time model of Chapter 3.

A 1990 meta-analysis of mastery-learning studies by Chen-Lin Kulik, James Kulik, and Robert Bangert-Drowns found that mastery learning raised exam performance by about half a standard deviation on average, which in the terms of Chapter 2 moves the average student from the 50th to roughly the 70th percentile. Most of those studies were in college and high school courses, many were short, and the quality varied, so the number is a guide and not a promise.

docs.title: Worked Example: Fixed Time Versus Fixed Mastery
docs.text:
Recall Chapter 3's class of 20 students who needed between 70 and 260 hours to master a course. The table contrasts what happens in the two models. The values repeat the illustrative numbers from that example.

Fixed time (150 hours) Fixed mastery (time varies) Students who master the course 14 of 20 20 of 20 Students who do not 6 0 Idle hours among those who finish early 535 0 (they move on when ready) Total hours used 3,000 2,770 Average hours per student 150 138.5

Mastery learning gets every student to the goal with fewer total hours in this example. But notice the average: 138.5 hours is only about eight percent below 150. Mastery learning is mainly a way of getting everyone to the goal, not of making the course dramatically shorter. The case for a compressed morning needs more than mastery: it needs the time that students spend on explanation and waiting to shrink as well, which is the subject of the next sections.

docs.title: Personalized Pacing and Gap Filling
docs.text:
Personalized pacing is letting each student move through material at the speed that suits them: faster through what they already know, slower through what is new or difficult. It is the self-paced learning of Chapter 1, made practical by software that tracks progress and offers the next step. Gap filling is the diagnosis and repair of missing prerequisite knowledge: finding the root gap, in the sense of Chapter 2, and teaching the missing concept before returning to the grade-level work. It is the remedy for the "missing stair" of Maya's fractions, and, according to the learning-gap analysis of Chapter 1, it is the main reason students who are behind stay behind: they sit through lessons built on foundations they do not have.

Together they address the main weakness of whole-class instruction. Recall Chapter 1's class of 28, in which only 13 students were "in reach" of any single lesson. Adaptive software can serve all 28 at their own readiness. The question is whether it does so well enough to replace the time the whole class spends together.

Pace is a variable, not a constant

Notice what mastery and pacing change: they treat time as the thing that varies and learning as the thing that's fixed. Our schools do the opposite, so some students finish early and wait and some are moved on before they're ready. Almost everything in this chapter follows from flipping that one assumption.

docs.title: Bloom's Two-Sigma Problem and Tutoring
docs.text:
The most famous number in this part of educational research comes from a 1984 article by Benjamin Bloom, titled "The 2 Sigma Problem: The Search for Methods of Group Instruction as Effective as One-to-One Tutoring."

One-on-one tutoring is instruction in which a single tutor works with a single student, responding moment by moment to what the student says and does. A tutor can ask a question, hear the answer, notice hesitation, give a hint, and adjust. This is the practice that a teacher with 28 students cannot provide, as the arithmetic of Chapter 1 showed: under two minutes per student in a 50-minute period.

Bloom's two-sigma problem is the finding, reported by Bloom and his graduate students, that students tutored one-on-one using mastery learning performed about two standard deviations better than students in a conventional classroom: the average tutored student scored above about 98 percent of the conventional class. ("Sigma" is the Greek letter used for standard deviation.) The problem in the name is a practical one: tutoring that effective is far too expensive to give to every child, so Bloom asked whether group methods could be found that come close to it. Mastery learning in a group, by comparison, produced about one standard deviation, the middle of three conditions.

Condition in Bloom's studies Effect compared with a conventional class The average student in this condition scores above Conventional class 0 (baseline) 50% of the conventional class Mastery learning in a class about 1 standard deviation about 84% One-on-one tutoring with mastery learning about 2 standard deviations about 98%

The two-sigma number has been quoted for forty years, often without the cautions it needs. The original studies were small, ran for a few weeks on a single topic, and tested students on the material that was taught. When researchers later pooled many randomized trials of tutoring in real schools, they found much smaller average effects. A 2020 review of 96 randomized trials of tutoring by Andre Nickow, Philip Oreopoulos, and Vincent Quan found an average effect of about 0.37 standard deviations. Other work on human tutoring and on intelligent tutoring systems, such as VanLehn's 2011 review, found effects of about 0.76 to 0.79 for well-designed tutoring, with simpler systems doing worse. Tutoring is among the most effective interventions known, with effects in the range of a half to a whole standard deviation, and Bloom's two sigma is the upper end of what has been seen in small, careful studies.

Cost is the other half of the problem. High-dosage tutoring programs for schools, with a tutor working with a small group several times a week, often cost on the order of $1,000 to $2,500 per student per year, which is why they reach only a fraction of the students who need them.

docs.title: Worked Example: The Tutoring Arithmetic
docs.text:
Convert the effect sizes into percentiles with the table of Chapter 2, and compare what each would cost at scale for a 12,000-student district. The cost figure for human tutoring is an illustrative midpoint, and the AI figure is the Chapter 7 Level 4 cost.

Approach Effect size (approximate) Average student's percentile Cost per student per year District of 12,000 Bloom's small studies 2.0 98th not scalable not scalable Pooled randomized tutoring trials 0.37 64th about $1,500 about $18 million Well-designed tutoring system about 0.7 about 76th about $23 (Level 4, Chapter 7) about $276,000

The last row is the hope behind the AI tutor: an effect in the range of half a standard deviation or more, at a cost of tens of dollars rather than thousands. It is a hope and not a result. The effect size in that row comes from studies of earlier tutoring systems, and whether current AI tutors reach it in real classrooms is what the next section examines.

docs.title: AI Tutors
docs.text:
An AI tutor is a system, usually built on a large language model, that tutors a student through conversation: it asks questions, gives hints, explains in several ways, and adjusts to what the student says. It is a Level 4 feature in the five-level model, and it is the attempt to deliver something like the one-on-one tutoring of Bloom's experiments at the cost of software.

What an AI tutor does well is real. It is available at any hour, never loses patience, can try many explanations, and can respond to a student's own words. What it does badly is also real: it can state wrong answers confidently (the hallucination of Chapter 5), it can slide into simply giving answers, and it lacks the human sense of when a student is discouraged. The evidence below, drawn from the book's AI-First Stories appendix, shows both sides.

  • A Harvard physics course ran a randomized study in which students learned from a carefully designed AI tutor and from an instructor-led active-learning class. The AI tutor group learned more, in less time. The tutor was built on proven teaching practices, not left as an open chatbot.
  • An after-school program in Edo State, Nigeria, used a GPT-4-based tutor to practice English for six weeks with teachers in the room, and the World Bank team reported large learning gains, around 0.3 standard deviations, at very small cost per student. By Chapter 3's benchmark for typical annual growth, that is about a year of ordinary progress in six weeks, though a result from a short pilot in one setting should be treated with care.
  • A study at a high school in Turkey gave students open access to GPT-4 while practicing math. They did much better on the practice problems, and on later exams taken without AI they did about 17 percent worse than students who had never had access. A second version of the tutor that gave hints instead of answers removed most of the harm.
  • Khanmigo, Khan Academy's AI tutor, is designed to guide students with questions, not answers. Reports describe early versions making math mistakes and students in some districts using it less than expected.

The pattern across these cases is the book's thesis in miniature: how the AI is designed matters more than how powerful it is. The Turkish study used the same model in both conditions, and the difference between harm and help was whether it gave answers or hints. Chapter 12 develops the design principles.

docs.title: Worked Example: Judging the Evidence for a Compressed Morning
docs.text:
Return to Mr. Dang's question and sort the evidence using the levels of Chapter 2. This is the exercise the sim below repeats.

Evidence Design What it supports Limits Harvard physics AI tutor Randomized comparison AI tutoring can teach more in less time One course at one university; college students Nigeria after-school pilot Randomized pilot, six weeks Low-cost AI tutoring can help where resources are scarce Short; one setting; English practice Turkish high-school study Randomized field experiment Design decides help versus harm One school; short-term math Meta-analyses of mastery learning Many classroom studies pooled Mastery learning raises achievement by about half a standard deviation Mostly older, many short; quality varies Alpha School's reported growth School-reported Nothing yet that can be checked independently Self-reported; no outside evaluation known Unbound Academy's early results Board slides, no baseline Nothing about the effect of the program Reported proficiency below state averages; unknown starting points

Notice what the table says. The strongest evidence, the randomized studies, supports the possibility that a well-designed AI tutor can teach more in less time. The evidence for the full package, two hours of software replacing a long academic morning, comes from a school whose results are self-reported and a second whose early results look weaker than the state average. The honest summary is that compression is plausible and unproven. A school should pilot it, measure it independently, and be prepared for it not to work.

docs.title: Diagram: Judging the Evidence for a Shorter Morning
docs.text:
Judging the Evidence for a Shorter Morning

Type: microsim sim-id: judging-evidence-for-shorter-morning Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge the strength of the evidence behind eight claims about AI tutoring and the compressed morning by assigning each to one of the five evidence levels from Chapter 2, correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: the five evidence levels (Strong, Moderate, Promising, Demonstrates a rationale, No evidence of effect), randomized controlled trial, self-reported results (all defined in Chapters 2 and 3), and the studies described in the section "AI Tutors" above.

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 claims in one of five evidence-level bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A famous or often-quoted result is strong evidence. (2) A school's own reported gains are evidence of effect. (3) A published meta-analysis is the same as a randomized trial.

Instructional Rationale: Judging requires applying the same design criteria to real, unevenly supported claims about the very idea the book proposes. Including claims that support the book's thesis but have weak evidence prevents the learner from rating by agreement.

Content:

The five levels, as defined in Chapter 2: Strong (random assignment, well designed and carried out); Moderate (a comparison group, no random assignment); Promising (a correlational study with statistical controls); Demonstrates a rationale (a research-based reason, results not yet in); No evidence of effect (testimonials, surveys, self-reported or uncontrolled results).

Eight claims:

# Claim shown to the learner Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 In an introductory Harvard physics course, students randomly assigned to a carefully designed AI tutor learned more, in less time, than in an instructor-led active-learning class. Strong Random assignment and a direct comparison, though in a single course. 2 In a six-week Nigerian after-school pilot, randomly assigned students who used a GPT-4 tutor with teachers present showed large gains in English. Strong Random assignment and a comparison group, though short and in one setting. 3 In a Turkish high-school field experiment with random assignment, open GPT-4 access improved practice scores but lowered later exam scores by about 17 percent, while a hint-first version removed most of the harm. Strong Random assignment; the finding concerns design, not just power. 4 A pooled analysis of many classroom studies found that mastery learning raised exam scores by about half a standard deviation. Moderate It combines many studies with comparison groups, but most were not randomized and quality varies. 5 A school reports that its students gain more than double the expected growth after two hours a day on adaptive software. No evidence of effect The result is self-reported and has not been independently evaluated. 6 A new online school's early reports show 10 percent proficiency in math, with no information about where students started. No evidence of effect Without a starting point or a comparison, the result says nothing about the program's effect. 7 A district reports that students in some schools used an AI tutor less than expected and that early versions made math errors. No evidence of effect These are implementation reports, with no comparison group measuring learning. 8 A new AI tutor is built on research about hint-first questioning and spaced practice, and an independent evaluation is planned. Demonstrates a rationale It has a research-based reason to expect benefit, with results still to come.

Provenance: The studies are those described in the chapter section "AI Tutors" and in the book's AI-First Stories appendix, which notes that several accounts still need source checking. The sim must label the claims "Summaries; check the sources before citing." Level definitions follow Chapter 2.

Rules: Each claim has exactly one correct level, given in Content. A claim is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads one claim at a time and sees the five levels.
  2. The learner places the claim in a level and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 claims, the sim shows the score and the misplaced claims with their correct levels.
  5. The learner should notice that the three strongest claims are all about tutoring design, and that none of the claims about whole-school results reaches the Strong level.

Feedback: 8 claims, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [level]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the claim counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can weigh the evidence on both sides." For a score < 7: "Review the five levels and try again; the claims will be reshuffled."

Starting State: Claim 1 of the shuffled order is shown with five empty levels, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "How strong is the evidence behind this claim?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter reports a 17 percent drop on later exams in the Turkish study, a Harvard randomized physics study, a six-week Nigerian pilot, and an effect of about half a standard deviation for mastery learning. The chapter states that Alpha School's results are self-reported and Unbound Academy's early results lack a baseline. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

Test the tutor's first reply

When evaluating any AI tutor, ask it a homework question and read only its first reply. If it hands over the answer, the design fails the Turkish-study test, whatever the brochure says. A good first reply asks the student something.

docs.title: Cognitive Offloading
docs.text:
Cognitive offloading is the use of an external tool or resource to reduce the mental effort a task demands: writing a phone number down instead of remembering it, or using a calculator for arithmetic. Offloading is ordinary and often wise. It becomes a problem in learning when the thing offloaded is the very thing the student is supposed to be learning, since the effort is the learning (the productive struggle of Chapter 2).

The research on AI and offloading is early. The MIT Media Lab study summarized in the appendix, a small preprint, found that students writing essays with ChatGPT showed lower brain engagement and recalled less of their own writing than students who wrote unaided. Survey studies have linked heavy AI use with lower critical thinking scores, though correlation cannot show which way the effect runs. The Turkish study is stronger evidence, because it was randomized: students with open access learned less. A working rule is to offload the routine and keep the target: let a tool do the arithmetic once the concept of division is mastered, but not before, and let AI check a draft after the student has written it, not write it.

docs.title: Worked Example: What to Offload
docs.text:
Skill being learned Tool use that offloads the target (avoid) Tool use that offloads the routine (fine) Solving unit-rate problems Asking the chatbot to solve each problem Using a calculator for the division after choosing which numbers to divide Writing a paragraph argument Having AI draft the paragraph Having AI point out unclear sentences in the student's own draft Understanding a historical cause Asking AI "what caused the war?" and copying Asking AI for sources to evaluate, then judging them Debugging a program Pasting the error and accepting the fix Asking for a hint about where to look

The calculator lesson doesn't transfer automatically

A common trap is reasoning "we let students use calculators, so we can let them use chatbots." A calculator does arithmetic and leaves the thinking; a chatbot can do the thinking too. Before allowing a tool, ask what part of the task it does and whether that part is the skill being taught.

docs.title: The Compressed Academic Morning
docs.text:
Academic morning is the part of the school day devoted to the core academic subjects, usually reading, writing, mathematics, science, and social studies. In a traditional school these subjects are spread through the whole day. The compressed academic morning is the proposal that, with adaptive learning, students could reach today's academic results in about two to three hours a day, concentrated in the morning, which frees the rest of the day. Alpha School, as the AI-First Stories appendix reports, runs about two hours of adaptive academic software a day. Whether the compression works is the question the evidence above leaves open.

Two mechanisms can make it work. Reduced direct instruction is the shift from long, whole-class, teacher-led explanation (the direct instruction and lecture of Chapters 1 and 2) to explanation that is short, interactive, and paced by the student, with the teacher moving from lecturer to coach. And the removal of waiting: the idle hours of fixed-time classes, the time students spend on material they already know, and the transitions between periods.

Freed-up school time is the time the compression releases, available for other uses. It is the reason compression matters at all: not that students spend less time learning, but that the time can be spent on things that AI cannot do and that students need, the subject of Part 3.

docs.title: Worked Example: How Much Time Is Freed?
docs.text:
Use the illustrative school day of Chapter 2. Its five academic periods total 250 minutes a day: each period had 5 minutes of settling and attendance, 20 minutes of whole-class direct instruction, 20 minutes of guided and independent practice, and 5 minutes of wrap-up. In a compressed morning, suppose settling and wrap-up fall to 10 minutes in all, explanation becomes 50 minutes of short interactive segments paced by the student, and practice with immediate feedback takes 90 minutes. These values are an illustrative scenario, not data.

Part of the academic morning Traditional (minutes) Compressed (minutes) Settling, attendance, wrap-up 50 10 Explanation 100 50 Practice 100 90 Total 250 150

The compressed morning is 150 minutes, 2.5 hours, and frees \( 250 - 150 = 100 \) minutes a day. Over a 180-day year that is \( 100 \times 180 = 18{,}000 \) minutes, or 300 hours, about 46 school days of 6.5 hours. This is a substantial amount of time, enough for a half-day of afternoon activity every day.

The scenario also shows what must be true. Students would need to cover in 150 minutes what the traditional morning covers in 250, which means learning about \( 250 / 150 \approx 1.67 \) times as much per minute. The compression works only if the adaptive morning delivers that gain, and that is what the evidence, so far, does not show. If the morning must be 190 minutes (explanation 70 and practice 110), the freed time falls to 60 minutes a day, or about 28 school days a year, still worth having but less transformative.

docs.title: Diagram: Morning Time Budget
docs.text:
Morning Time Budget

Type: microsim sim-id: morning-time-budget Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the minutes freed per day, the hours freed per year, and the equivalent school days freed by a compressed academic morning, and the speedup it requires, correctly answering three of three questions.

Prerequisites: academic morning, compressed academic morning, reduced direct instruction, freed-up school time (all defined in the section "The Compressed Academic Morning" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the controls unlock, the learner commits three answers: (Q1) the minutes freed per day for a 10-minute settling time, 50 minutes of explanation, and 90 minutes of practice; (Q2) the hours freed per year for the same settings; (Q3) the school days freed per year when settling is 10, explanation is 70, and practice is 110. An answer is correct when it is within the tolerance in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Using the controls afterward is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Compression means students learn less. (2) The time freed is the same whatever the morning contains. (3) A compressed morning needs no faster learning per minute.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating freed time from a budget makes the tradeoff concrete and exposes the speedup the compression silently requires. Different settings show how sensitive the freed time is to how much explanation and practice are kept.

Content:

Baseline: five academic periods, 250 minutes per day, from the Chapter 2 illustrative schedule (50 minutes settling and wrap-up, 100 explanation, 100 practice).

Controls:

Input Min Max Step Default Unit Settling, attendance, wrap-up 0 50 5 10 minutes per day Explanation 0 100 5 50 minutes per day Practice 0 150 5 90 minutes per day School days per year 150 200 10 180 days Length of a school day 6 7 0.5 6.5 hours

Rules shown: compressed morning = settling + explanation + practice. Freed per day = 250 − compressed morning. Freed per year in minutes = freed per day × school days. Hours = minutes ÷ 60. School days freed = freed minutes per year ÷ (length of day in hours × 60). Required speedup = 250 ÷ compressed morning.

Check values:

Settling Explanation Practice Compressed Freed per day Hours freed per year School days freed Required speedup 10 50 90 150 100 300 46.2 1.67 10 70 110 190 60 180 27.7 1.32

Answers: Q1 = 100 minutes (±1); Q2 = 300 hours (±1); Q3 = 27.7 days (±0.1).

Provenance: The 250-minute baseline is the illustrative Chapter 2 schedule. The compressed settings are an illustrative scenario, and the sim must label them "Illustrative scenario, not evidence."

Rules: If the compressed morning is greater than 250, freed time is shown as 0 and the sim says "No time is freed." Values are shown to one decimal place for days and to the nearest whole number for minutes and hours. When any control changes, all results update at once.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner answers Q1, Q2, and Q3 and submits them.
  2. The sim checks the answers and unlocks the controls.
  3. The learner changes the three minute settings and the school-day length. The freed time, school days freed, and required speedup update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that the required speedup rises as the compressed morning gets shorter, and that freed time depends strongly on how much explanation and practice are kept.

Feedback: Three questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [value]. [Working text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Add the three parts of the compressed morning, then subtract from 250." After the second wrong attempt the value and working are shown. A score "n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: The three minute settings are at their defaults of 10, 50, and 90, the results are hidden, and the prompt reads "How much time does a shorter morning free up?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses a 250-minute baseline, a compressed morning of 150 minutes, 100 minutes freed per day, 300 hours or about 46 days per year, and a required speedup of about 1.67, and a second scenario of 190 minutes with about 28 school days freed.

docs.title: Critical Thinking and Computational Thinking
docs.text:
The reason to free time is not to stop learning academic content. It is to spend the time on abilities that AI cannot replace and that students need to practice with other people. Two of them, critical and computational thinking, are things AI can teach well, as the course description says, and students still have to practice.

Critical thinking is the disciplined ability to analyze information, evaluate claims and arguments, and decide what to believe or do on the basis of reasons and evidence. It is the higher-order thinking of Chapter 1, the Analyze and Evaluate levels of Bloom's taxonomy, made into a habit. It is the skill this book has used throughout: asking "compared with whom, chosen how, measured by whom?" is critical thinking applied to evidence.

Two parts of critical thinking are worth naming. Evidence evaluation is judging how much weight a piece of evidence deserves, by asking about its source, its method, its sample, and who benefits. Argument analysis is the breaking of an argument into its parts: the conclusion it wants you to accept and the premises offered as reasons, and then judging whether the premises are true and whether they actually support the conclusion. A vendor's claim, "94 percent of teachers love it, so it improves learning," is an argument whose conclusion does not follow from its premise.

docs.title: Worked Example: Analyzing an Argument
docs.text:
Take a statement from a brochure: "Our students spend only two hours a day on software and score above the state average. Therefore the software, not the teachers, produces the results."

Part Text Question to ask Premise 1 Students spend two hours a day on software Is it true? How is it measured? Premise 2 They score above the state average Which test, and compared with whom? Did they start higher? Conclusion The software, not the teachers, produces the results Does it follow from the premises?

The argument skips a step. Even if both premises are true, students might score high because of who enrolls, what the adults do in the rest of the day, or families' resources. The conclusion requires evidence that rules those out, which is why the randomized designs of Chapter 2 matter. A student who can lay out an argument this way is practicing critical thinking, and this is also exactly what the pro-social afternoon needs to exercise, in debate and in joint projects.

Computational thinking is the set of thinking habits used to formulate problems so that a computer, or a person following precise steps, can solve them. It is usually described with four parts: decomposition, breaking a problem into smaller pieces; pattern recognition, noticing what repeats; abstraction, ignoring detail that does not matter; and algorithm design, writing precise steps to solve the problem. Jeannette Wing's 2006 essay popularized the term and argued that it is a basic skill for everyone, and not only for programmers.

docs.title: Worked Example: Computational Thinking in Maya's Textbook
docs.text:
The ready-concepts rule of Chapters 8 and 9 is computational thinking in action. The problem, "what should Maya study next?", is decomposed into one question per concept: is it mastered, and are its prerequisites mastered? The pattern is that every concept is checked the same way. The abstraction ignores everything about a concept except its name, its status, and its prerequisites. The algorithm is the rule itself: for each unmastered concept, mark it ready if all its direct prerequisites are mastered. A student who can run, and then write, a rule like this has learned something that applies to scheduling a tournament, sorting a list, or planning a project.

Thinking skills are learned by practice

If critical and computational thinking sound like talents you either have or don't, they're not; they're habits built by doing. You already practiced both in this chapter, laying out an argument and running a rule. Try one on a real brochure this week.

docs.title: Practice: Reading a Tutor's Reply
docs.text: The sim below ties the thread of this chapter together. It asks you to read an AI tutor's reply and say how much of the solution it gives away, using the hint ladder from Chapter 2, because that is the property that decided help from harm in the Turkish study. The hint ladder had four levels after the student works alone: Level 1 asks what the problem is asking; Level 2 narrows the plan; Level 3 gives the step; Level 4 gives the answer.

docs.title: Diagram: Tutor Reply Hint Levels
docs.text:
Tutor Reply Hint Levels

Type: microsim sim-id: tutor-reply-hint-levels Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify eight AI tutor replies to the same question by hint level (1 to 4), correctly placing at least seven of eight on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: productive struggle, the four-level hint ladder, cognitive offloading, AI tutor (all defined in Chapter 2 and in the sections of this chapter above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of 8 tutor replies a hint level from 1 to 4 and submits it. An assignment is correct when it equals the "Correct level" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the level definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A reply that is polite and detailed is a good hint. (2) A long explanation is a Level 1 hint. (3) A hint that shows a worked example of the same problem is not giving the answer.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying replies by how much they reveal trains the learner to see the design property that separated help from harm in the Turkish study. Replies written in friendly language but revealing the answer test whether the learner looks at content, not tone.

Content:

The four levels, shown on request:

Level What the reply does 1 Asks what the problem is asking, without giving any part of the method 2 Narrows the plan, such as naming which quantities to use or which operation type 3 Gives the specific step to carry out, leaving the final computation 4 States the final answer or does the whole solution

The student's question for every reply: "A 6-pack of juice costs $4.50. What is the price per bottle?"

Eight replies:

# Tutor reply shown Correct level Why (shown as feedback) 1 "Let's start by looking at the problem. What is it asking you to find?" 1 It asks a question and reveals nothing about the method. 2 "Which number is the total cost, and which is the number of bottles?" 2 It narrows the plan by pointing at the two quantities. 3 "You want the cost for one bottle, so think about splitting the total into equal parts." 2 It names the idea of splitting, which narrows the plan without giving the step. 4 "Divide the total price by the number of bottles." 3 It gives the specific step and leaves only the computation. 5 "Great question! The price per bottle is $0.75." 4 It states the final answer. 6 "Take $4.50 and divide it by 6, which gives 0.75, so each bottle costs $0.75." 4 It does the whole computation and states the result. 7 "What operation do you use when you share an amount equally among several things?" 2 It narrows the plan by pointing to the kind of operation. 8 "Here is a similar problem solved step by step: 8 pencils cost $2.00, so $2.00 divided by 8 is $0.25 each. Now try yours." 3 A worked example of a similar problem shows the step, leaving the student to carry it out.

Provenance: The four levels follow the hint ladder in Chapter 2. The replies are illustrative, written for this chapter.

Rules: Each reply has exactly one correct level, given in Content. A reply is scored on its first submitted level only. The score counts first-attempt correct levels out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7. After each answer the sim states whether the reply is suitable as a first response: levels 1 and 2 are, levels 3 and 4 are not.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the student's question and one tutor reply at a time, with the four levels.
  2. The learner assigns a level and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text and whether the reply suits a first response.
  3. If incorrect, the learner may assign again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct level and reason are shown.
  4. After all 8 replies, the sim shows the score.
  5. The learner should notice that replies 5 and 6 sound very different yet are both Level 4, and that reply 3 is Level 2 despite not naming the operation.

Feedback: 8 replies, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: Level [n]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the level]." After the second attempt the correct level is revealed and the reply counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 8" is shown. Final message for a score >= 7: "You can see how much a reply gives away." For a score < 7: "Review the four levels and try again; the replies will be reshuffled."

Starting State: The student's question and reply 1 of the shuffled order are shown, with the score "First-try correct: 0 of 8," and the prompt "How much of the solution does this reply give away?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's four-level hint ladder and the juice problem (6 bottles for $4.50, $0.75 each) match Chapter 2. The mastery bar is 7 of 8.

docs.title: Answering Mr. Dang
docs.text:
Mr. Dang asked for proof. The honest answer has three layers. What is solid: mastery learning and adaptive practice improve achievement, with effects of about half a standard deviation or less in real settings; one-on-one tutoring is among the most effective interventions known; and a well-designed AI tutor, giving hints instead of answers, can teach well in careful studies. What is not yet shown: that two hours of software can replace a traditional academic morning for most students at scale; the one school with a long track record reports its own results, and an online version has produced early results below the state average. What decides the difference: design, with hint-first tutors, mastery checks, human adults in the room, and the rest of the day spent with other people.

The story has both sides. The benefit: a morning that fills each student's gaps and could free around 300 hours a year, many weeks of school time. The risks: a compression that does not deliver and shortchanges students, tutors that give answers and erode learning, and screen time that grows. The response: pilot the compression, measure it independently, keep a person in the loop, and keep the morning short and the afternoon social. The next chapters supply the rest: guardrails in Chapter 12, and the afternoon in Chapters 13 and 14.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Adaptive learning adjusts content to each student's data; mastery learning fixes achievement and lets time vary, with effects of about half a standard deviation in pooled studies. Fixed mastery saved only about eight percent of total hours in our example, so mastery alone does not compress the day.
  • Personalized pacing and gap filling address the one-pace problem: in a class of 28, a single lesson reaches 13.
  • One-on-one tutoring is highly effective; Bloom's two-sigma problem (two standard deviations in small studies) is the upper end, pooled randomized trials average about 0.37, and cost keeps human tutoring out of reach for most students.
  • An AI tutor can approach tutoring at the cost of software, but design decides the outcome: in the Turkish study, answer-giving harmed later exams by about 17 percent and hint-first removed most of the harm.
  • Cognitive offloading is fine for the routine and harmful for the target skill; offload the routine and keep the target.
  • The compressed academic morning and reduced direct instruction could free freed-up school time: in our illustration 100 minutes a day, 300 hours a year, but it requires learning about 1.67 times as much per minute, which the evidence has not yet shown.
  • Critical thinking, including evidence evaluation and argument analysis, and computational thinking, are what the freed time is for, and AI can teach them while students still need to practice them with other people.
  • The strongest evidence supports well-designed AI tutoring; the evidence for the full compressed-morning package is self-reported or early, so pilot it and measure it independently.

You can weigh the case for a shorter morning

You just weighed the evidence on mastery learning, tutoring, and AI tutors, and worked out how many hours a compressed morning could free and what it must deliver. Chapter 12 turns to the guardrails that keep an AI tutor helping. One step at a time, together.

docs.title: Character Sheet: Indigo the Barn Owl
docs.text: The canonical identity document for Indigo, the pedagogical mascot for the AI-Native Schools textbook. Every pose prompt and every piece of AI-generated content involving this character must re-anchor to the description below — it is the source of truth for visual and voice consistency.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• Name: Indigo
  • Species: Barn Owl
  • Subject: How AI is reshaping the school day — written for teachers, administrators, policymakers, and parents weighing mornings with AI against afternoons with each other
  • Catchphrase: "Let's find the balance."

docs.title: Visual Description
docs.text:
• Body color: Deep indigo-violet feathers — hex #3F51B5, with a soft ivory-cream face and chest
  • Accent color: Warm amber-orange — hex #FF9800
  • Clothing / accessories: A slim, loosely knotted amber-orange scarf around the neck. No glasses, no hat — the look stays clean and credible for a professional readership rather than juvenile
  • Expression: Calm, warm, closed-beak smile with soft, attentive eyes
  • Size proportion: Medium — chest-up, three-quarter body visible; reads clearly both at quarter-page size and shrunk to the 90px admonition icon
  • Art style: Modern flat vector illustration, clean lines, minimal shading, transparent background

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
• Warm
  • Steady
  • Thoughtful
  • Fair-minded

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
• Speaks plainly and avoids hype — never oversells what AI can do
  • Names the tradeoff before the benefit, in keeping with the book's own practice of pairing every story's risk with the school's response
  • Treats teachers, administrators, and families as partners working through a real decision, never as an audience being sold a product
  • Signature phrases: "Let's find the balance.", "Here's the tradeoff.", "One step at a time, together."

docs.title: Pronouns
docs.text: Indigo has no gender. Always write "Indigo" or use they/them — never gendered pronouns.

docs.title: Why This Mascot
docs.text: Owls are education's most legible "trusted guide" trope — instantly readable to a book written for teachers, administrators, and policymakers without needing explanation. Indigo's deep indigo-violet plumage deliberately matches this site's own primary: indigo theme color, so the mascot feels native to this specific book rather than generic stock art, and the amber-orange scarf echoes the site's accent: orange. The calm, steady, no-hype personality mirrors the book's central promise — pairing every AI benefit with its risk and the school's response — so Indigo never oversells. Indigo balances.

docs.title: Learning Graph for AI-Native Schools
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 14 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MISC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Scoring Breakdown
docs.text: Element Points Score Notes Title 5 5 Clear title and subtitle that states the book's thesis Target Audience 5 4 Specific roles are named, but the audience is broad: teachers, administrators, board members, policymakers, designers, education students, and parents have different needs Prerequisites 5 5 States "None" and the few assumed skills Main Topics Covered 10 9 86 topics grouped into six areas that match the five parts and the storytelling thread. A few topics are named after single case studies and may produce narrow concepts Topics Excluded 5 5 Seven clear exclusions, with pointers to companion books Learning Outcomes Header 5 5 "After this course, readers will be able to:" Remember 10 9 13 outcomes. One ("name the key case studies") is recall of examples rather than concepts Understand 10 10 15 outcomes covering every part of the book Apply 10 10 12 practical outcomes, including cost estimates, procurement criteria, and risk checklists Analyze 10 10 10 outcomes, including the Alpha-versus-Unbound comparison Evaluate 10 10 11 outcomes, including judging self-reported versus independent results Create 10 10 7 outcomes plus 8 sample capstone projects Descriptive Context 5 5 Strong overview with the prediction, the five parts, and the storytelling goal Total 100 97

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
1. Broad audience (−1). The book serves several groups with different needs. This does not block learning graph generation, but chapter writers will need to choose a main reader. Teachers and school leaders are the natural primary audience, with board members, policymakers, and parents as secondary readers.
  2. Case-study topics (−1). Topics such as "Unbound Academy" and "lessons from Tutor CoPilot" are specific examples. In the learning graph, they work best as examples attached to general concepts (for example, Guardrails or AI That Coaches Teachers) rather than as concepts of their own.
  3. Recall of case names (−1). "Name the key case studies and the main lesson of each" is fine for a quiz but adds little to the learning graph.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
These are optional; the description is already ready to use.

  1. Add one sentence naming the primary reader (for example, "written mainly for K-12 teachers and school leaders, with sections for board members and parents").
  2. When the learning graph is generated, treat case studies as examples of concepts, not as concepts, unless the case is central (Alpha School and the five-level model are central).
  3. Check the stories written from memory in the AI-First Stories appendix before chapters cite their numbers. Fourteen stories are still marked "Sources still to add."

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
• Topic breadth: 86 topics across six areas: the evidence for the prediction, the shorter morning, the pro-social afternoon, school culture change, putting the model into practice, and stories.
  • Topic depth: Many topics name several concepts (for example, the five ADKAR elements, the five adopter categories, the five innovation attributes, the five textbook levels, and Schein's three levels).
  • Bloom's coverage: 68 outcomes across all six levels, which suggests foundation, process, judgment, and design concepts.
  • Estimated concept count: 250–350 concepts, well above the 200-concept target.

docs.text: The score is above 85, so the course description is ready for the learning-graph-generator skill.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text: This interactive viewer allows you to explore the 532-concept learning graph for AI-Native Schools.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Search: Type in the search box to find specific concepts
  • Category Filtering: Use checkboxes to show/hide concept categories
  • Interactive Navigation: Click and drag to explore, scroll to zoom
  • Statistics: View real-time counts of visible nodes and edges

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. Search for Concepts: Start typing in the search box to find concepts. Click on a result to focus on that node.

  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts. Use "Check All" or "Uncheck All" for bulk operations.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

  4. Drag to pan around the graph
  5. Scroll to zoom in and out

  6. Click on a node to select it and highlight its connections

  7. View Statistics: The sidebar shows counts of visible nodes, edges, and foundational concepts.

docs.title: Graph Structure
docs.text:
• Foundational Concepts (left side): Prerequisites with no dependencies
  • Advanced Concepts (right side): Topics that build on multiple prerequisites
  • Edges: Arrows point from a concept to its prerequisites
